text:
3 Reasons Your Forearms Stay Small (And How to Fix Them) 
Forearms not growing despite wrist curls? These three training fixes address automatic lifting-strap use, workouts that never progress, and the forearm muscles most routines overlook.

Learn how grip work, controlled wrist curls, reverse wrist curls, reverse curls, and hammer curls fit together. The video explains why the brachioradialis needs elbow-flexion work and why visible progress takes consistent training over time.

Which fix is missing from your routine? Comment REVERSE if you have never tried a reverse wrist curl.

0:56 The Problem With Lifting Straps
2:22 Treating Forearms Like a Real Muscle
3:48 Training the Missing Half

title: 3 Ab Exercises That Work Better When You Slow Down
translatedTitle: How to Force Your Abs to Grow (3 Exercises)

Quick, science-based fitness tips that actually work.
Train smarter, avoid injuries, and build real strength the Bro Pump way...

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription:
Quick, science-based fitness tips that actually work.
Train smarter, avoid injuries, and build real strength the Bro Pump way...

text:
How many crunches have you done this month? 100? 500? Now the real question: how much weight have you added to them? Exactly. You'd never train chest like that so why are you training abs like that?
Scientists put sensors on real people and compared 13 popular ab exercises. The bicycle crunch produced roughly 2.5x the six-pack activation of the traditional crunch you keep repeating. But activation alone doesn't build the best abs so this video gives you the two winners from that testing, plus the loaded exercise the study couldn't measure: the one that separates abs that GROW from abs that just get tired.
Straight up, because you know how this channel works: these build what's underneath. They won't burn the fat on top that's the other video, linked at the end.

Chapters:
0:00 – Intro
0:11 – The 13-exercise sensor study
1:19 – The honest fine print: activation ≠ growth
1:36 – #1: Hanging leg raise / captain's chair
2:52 – #2: The bicycle crunch (2.5x activation)
3:42 – #3: The weighted cable crunch (the growth engine)
6:39 – The whole thing in one breath

Comment "HEAVY ABS" if you're finally going to load them and tell me which of the three you're starting with.
The best ab exercises according to muscle activation research: the hanging leg raise or captain's chair (second for six-pack activation, first for obliques but only if you curl the pelvis upward, not just swing the legs), the bicycle crunch (top floor exercise in the ACE-sponsored study rotate shoulder to opposite knee, slow), and the weighted cable crunch for progressive overload, because activation isn't growth: abs get thick and blocky from 8–12 genuinely heavy reps with load added over time, trained like any muscle, 2–3x a week, stopping 1–2 clean reps before failure. You can't isolate upper from lower abs it's one continuous muscle and no ab exercise burns the fat on top.

channelDescription:
Quick, science-based fitness tips that actually work.

text:
You Aren't Training to Failure (Here's Proof) 
When researchers ask lifters to train to failure, something strange happens: many stop with three, four, sometimes five clean reps still left while swearing they had nothing. Their muscles didn't fail. Their brain quit early. And if that's you (for most beginners, it is), then every time you say "I had two reps left," you're probably guessing.

This video fixes that: what real failure actually looks and feels like, why you DON'T need it every set, and the one-time calibration test that turns "two reps left" from a guess into a place you've actually visited. By the end you'll have your calibration number proof of how many reps your brain has been quietly stealing from your sets.
This is not a "go harder, bro" video. The goal is smarter effort not destroying yourself every workout.

Chapters:
0:00 – Your brain quits before your muscles do
1:12 – What failure actually is (an event, not a feeling)
2:33 – The twist: you don't need failure every set
3:39 – The 1–3 reps sweet spot
4:39 – Where to test failure safely (and where NOT to)
6:47 – Your calibration number (the stolen reps, counted)
7:23 – How to use it in normal training
8:19 – The whole thing in one breath

Comment "FAILURE" and answer honestly: has a clean rep ever physically stopped on you? And after you run the test come back and drop your calibration number. I want to see how many reps your brain was stealing.

Real training to failure means a clean rep physically cannot finish not the burn, not slow reps, not wanting to stop. Research shows stopping 1–3 clean reps short of failure builds very similar muscle with far less fatigue but you can't count backwards from a point you've never reached. So run the calibration test once on a safe exercise (dumbbell curls, machines, cables, push-ups never an unspotted barbell), memorize what the last clean reps feel like, then spend most of your training 1–3 reps from that wall. Visit failure rarely. Train near it regularly. The goal isn't falling off the edge every workout it's knowing exactly where the edge is.











#trainingtofailure #musclegrowth #beginnergym #musclegrowth  #buildmuscle

text:
The Best Exercise to Lose Belly Fat (The Honest Answer)..
250,000 crunches. That's roughly what it would take to burn one pound of fat and even then, your body wouldn't take it from your stomach. So here's the honest answer to "what's the best exercise to lose belly fat," given in the first 40 seconds, no stalling: it's walking. Not crunches. Not sit-ups. Walking.
But the catch is the whole point: walking only works because it feeds the one thing that actually burns belly fat and that thing isn't an exercise at all. This video ranks every fat-loss tool in order of what actually matters, including why fixing your sleep might do more for your gut than another hour of cardio.

Chapters:
0:00 – 250,000 crunches for one pound
2:17 – #1: The calorie deficit (nothing works without this)
4:11 – #2: Walking the most underrated fat loss tool
5:27 – #3: Strength training (so you don't end up skinny-fat)
6:13 – #4: Sleep the one quietly running everything
7:15 – #5: HIIT useful tool, not the answer


Comment "BORING" if you're ready to do the stuff that actually works and tell me: how many steps do you actually walk a day?

The best exercise to lose belly fat is walking not crunches, not sit-ups because belly fat only comes off through a calorie deficit, and walking builds that deficit without wrecking your recovery or your appetite. You can't spot reduce: fat comes off your whole body at once like a pool draining, and the belly empties last.

Strength training keeps you lean instead of skinny-fat while you cut, sleep controls the hunger and stress hormones that decide whether you stick to it, and HIIT is one tool not the magic answer. No pills, no gimmicks: walk more, eat in a small deficit, lift, sleep, repeat.





#bellyfat #fatloss #walking #bellyfat #bellyfatloss #bellyfatexercise

title: Stretching Before Lifting? You're Doing It Wrong
channelDescription:
Quick, science-based fitness tips that actually work.
Train smarter, avoid injuries, and build real strength the Bro Pump way...

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription:
Quick, science-based fitness tips that actually work.
Train smarter, avoid injuries, and build real strength the Bro Pump way...

text:
Stretching before you lift might be making you weaker and it sounds backwards, but holding a long static stretch on a cold muscle can leave you walking into your first heavy set weaker than if you'd never stretched at all.
The other half of the problem? Skipping the warm-up entirely and lifting cold. Both cost you. Here's the exact warm-up that fixes it three simple moves plus the one step almost everyone skips so your first set feels as strong as your third.

Chapters:
0:00 – Why stretching can make you weaker
1:14 – What a warm-up is actually for
4:11 – Move 1: Band rotations (shoulders)
4:34 – Move 2: Easy push-up (push pattern)
5:09 – Move 3: Bodyweight squats (legs)
5:34 – The ramp-up: the step everyone skips
7:12 – Warm-up mistakes to stop making

Comment "WARMUP" and tell me honestly were you a skipper, or an over-stretcher?
A warm-up shouldn't tire you out it should make your first set feel stronger. Skip the long static stretching before you lift and rehearse the movement instead: band rotations for the shoulders, an easy push-up for the push pattern, bodyweight squats for the legs, then ramp-up sets into your first big lift. Save static stretching for after your workout, when it actually helps flexibility and recovery. Works for any lift bench press, squat, or deadlift.




#warmup #stretching #gymtips

title: Do This Before Bed to Wake Up Flatter (No-BS Guide)
channelDescription:
Quick, science-based fitness tips that actually work.
Train smarter, avoid injuries, and build real strength the Bro Pump way...

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription:
Quick, science-based fitness tips that actually work.
Train smarter, avoid injuries, and build real strength the Bro Pump way...

text:
You can't burn belly fat while you sleep but here's what nobody tells you: most of that puffy, bloated stomach you wake up with isn't fat at all. It's bloat. Water and gas. And that you can fix by tomorrow morning.
No detox, no tea, no pills just a simple before-bed routine that cuts the bloat so you wake up flatter and tighter. It works because it's based on how your body actually holds water and gas.

Chapters:
0:00 – You can't burn fat overnight (but you can de-bloat)
1:02 – Bloat vs fat: the difference nobody explains
2:08 – Trigger 1: Salt (the biggest lever)
2:52 – Trigger 2: The big, late meal
3:20 – Trigger 3: Fast eating & fizzy drinks
4:07 – Trigger 4: Alcohol
4:49 – The flush: potassium, water & a walk 
6:05 – The honest part (de-bloat, not fat loss)

Comment "NOT FAT" if this changed how you see your morning belly and tell me your worst trigger: salt, soda, or late-night eating.
Most guys wake up to a puffy stomach and think it's fat they need to burn it's not, it's bloat. This before-bed routine flattens your stomach by morning: keep your last meal earlier, lighter, and lower in salt, slow down when you eat, skip the soda and alcohol, get some potassium and water in, and take a short walk after dinner. It's a de-bloat routine, not a fat-loss diet but these same habits help you lose real belly fat over time too.


#bloating #fatloss  #bellyfat

text:
Two men eat one meal a day. One gets lean. The other slowly loses the muscle he spent years building. Same diet. Opposite results.

The difference isn't the fasting. It's what happens during the one meal.
This is exactly what happens inside your body when you eat once a day hour by hour through the full 24-hour clock plus the honest truth about autophagy, the muscle-loss trap nobody warns you about, and who should never do OMAD at all.
OMAD isn't magic and it isn't poison. It's a tool. Everything depends on how you use it.



0:00 - Two men, same diet, opposite results 
0:40 - What OMAD actually is 
1:17 - The 24-hour clock: hours 0-4 (fed state) 
1:43 - Hours 4-12 (the quiet phase) 
2:20 - Hours 12-16 (the shift to fat for fuel) 
3:05 - Hours 16-24 (the deep fast + hunger waves) 
4:04 - The honest truth about autophagy 
5:05 - The first week vs the long run 
6:27 - The one meal that decides everything 
7:11 - How to build the meal right 
8:28 - Who should and should NOT do OMAD 
9:45 - The honest truth: OMAD isn't required









#fatloss #intermittentfasting #onemealaday

text:
Most guys think the V-taper is built with pull-ups. They're only one-third right.
A real V-taper isn't just a big back. It's three parts working together wide lats, capped side delts, and a waist that doesn't ruin the illusion. Get one and miss the other two, and you don't get a V. 

You get a wider, blocky torso.
Your body doesn't need to be huge. It needs to be shaped correctly. This video covers all three parts the two most guys ignore, and the one almost everybody gets backwards.


0:00 - Why most guys only get the V-taper 1/3 right 
0:44 - Why most guys fail 
1:30 - Part 1: Build the lats (the wings) 
3:03 - Part 2: Build the side delts (the frame) 
4:20 - The free posture win 
4:56 - Part 3: Control the waist (the part everyone gets backwards) 
6:41 - The full V-taper workout 
7:23 - The weekly rule

THE THREE PARTS
1. Lats - vertical pulling for width. Drive your elbows down, don't curl with your arms.
2. Side delts - lateral raises for the frame most guys never train directly.
3. Waist - stay lean and train the deep core. Skip heavy side bends that thicken your obliques.

THE WORKOUT (two sessions, each twice a week)
DAY 1 - WIDTH: Wide-grip pull-ups or lat pulldowns, one-arm pulldowns, straight-arm pulldowns, farmer's walks, hollow body holds.
DAY 2 - FRAME + WAIST: Lateral raises, water bottle/backpack raises, rear delt flys, band pull-aparts, hanging knee raises.
You can't out-train a growing waist. Staying lean happens in the kitchen, every single day.


Comment "V" plus the muscle group you've been neglecting if you want the full V-taper workout plan in the next video.
Pull-ups were never wrong. They were just one-third of the answer. Stop chasing a bigger body. Start building a better shape.

text:
Many people have been taught incorrect core exercises since middle school gym class, like traditional sit-ups and planks, which can stress the lower back without effectively building visible, functional abs.

This video explains why these common abdominal exercises often fail and demonstrates proper form for a plank, along with introducing more effective methods like the ab roller rollout for core strength exercises. Learn how to strengthen your core correctly, avoiding common mistakes that can lead to back pain.


0:00 - Why your abs aren't showing
0:37 - Abs are built in the gym, not the kitchen
1:47 - Why sit-ups stress your lower back
2:47 - Why planks plateau within weeks
4:27 - Exercise 1: The Weighted Cable Crunch
5:01 - Exercise 2: The Ab Wheel Rollout
5:45 - Exercise 3: The Pallof Press (almost nobody does this)
6:28 - The programming mistake that ruins everything


Three exercises. Two to three sessions a week. Heavy. Progressive. Then recover. That's the whole playbook.
Drop a comment with your current ab routine I'll tell you which exercise to swap first.

text:
Many people try to get in shape and lose belly fat with complicated plans, only to experience gym burnout and quit. This video explains why fat loss is not about entertainment, but about a more sustainable approach. Learn how to lose fat effectively by avoiding over-the-top methods and focusing on consistent, simpler strategies that truly work for weight loss, making your diet work for you. You don't need extreme HIIT. You don't need exotic superfoods. You don't need a 30-day challenge. 

The people with flat stomachs aren't using secret biohacks they've mastered a handful of boring, repetitive habits that actually work with your biology instead of against it.

In this video I break down the 4 most unglamorous habits that make fat loss feel effortless. I explain the science of why they work, and how to automate them so you never have to rely on willpower again.

0:00 - Why exciting fat loss plans always fail
0:22 - The biology of why your body hates novelty
2:25 - Habit 1: The Copy-Paste Breakfast
3:42 - Habit 2: The 10-Minute Post-Meal Walk
4:55 - Habit 3: The Non-Negotiable Step Floor
5:59 - Habit 4: The Hormonal Blackout
6:56 - Why you'll want to quit by week 3 (don't)

No gimmicks. No motivation. Just four boring things lean people do every day. Drop a comment and tell me which habit you're starting tomorrow I read every one.

text:
Doing endless crunches and 5-minute ab workouts won't burn stubborn belly fat. If you are losing weight everywhere else but your stomach looks exactly the same, you are fighting your own biology. Here is the real science behind why your lower belly fat won't leave, and the exact step-by-step protocol to fix it.

Spot reduction is a myth. Lower belly fat and love handles are packed with Alpha-2 receptors, meaning they are biologically designed to be the absolute last energy reserve your body burns. In this video, I break down the 5 steps to override your biology (including the crucial role of cortisol—your belly fat's "hormonal bodyguard"), and the 3 silent mistakes like the Cardio Trap and the Weekend Wipeout that are secretly destroying your progress. Stop fighting your body and start working with it.


0:00 - Why Your Belly Fat Won't Leave
0:52 - The Spot Reduction Myth
1:50 - The Biology of Stubborn Fat
3:34 - Fix 1: The Sustained Deficit
4:09 - Fix 2: The Protein Target
5:02 - Fix 3: Why You MUST Lift Weights
5:40 - Fix 4: Cortisol (The Hormonal Bodyguard)

7:01 - Mistake 1: Trusting the Scale

9:01 - The Ultimate Belly Fat Protocol



THE STUBBORN FAT PROTOCOL..
• Deficit: 300 to 500 calories below maintenance (sustained for months, not days)
• Protein: 0.8 to 1g per lb of target body weight
• Training: Resistance training (compound lifts) 3-5 days a week
• Sleep: Prioritize recovery to lower cortisol
• Patience: Give your body 8-16 weeks of honest consistency

text:
Lose Fat Without Going Hungry: Build Your Meals Like This
Most people try to lose belly fat by slashing calories, doing cardio, or following trendy diets… and still stay stuck. The truth is simple: your deficit isn't broken your meals are. And hard cardio isn't what burns belly fat fastest.
In this video, I break down the one eating rule that fixes about 80% of the problems people hit during a fat loss phase without starving yourself, without eliminating food groups, and without spending hours on the treadmill.

You'll learn:
Why most calorie deficits fail before they even start
Why protein is the single most important fat loss tool
How much protein you actually need (exact numbers)
Why meal order affects your blood sugar and cravings
The meal-by-meal breakdown breakfast, lunch, dinner, snacks
5 mistakes that silently destroy your fat loss progress


Your deficit creates the fat loss. Protein-first eating makes it sustainable. Try this for 2 weeks and track your hunger, energy, cravings, and waistline.

Drop your daily protein target in the comments I read every one.







#bellyfatloss #losebellyfat #weightloss

title: THESE 3 Walking Rules Melt Belly Fat Faster Than Running

Train smarter, avoid injuries, and build real strength the Bro Pump way...

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription:

text:
Most people try to lose belly fat with running, HIIT, or endless cardio… and still stay stuck.
The truth is simple: you can’t outrun your diet — and hard cardio isn’t always the best way to burn fat.

In this video, I break down a 10-minute post-meal walking routine that can help improve blood sugar control, support fat loss, and keep your body in a better fat-burning state without exhausting workouts.

You’ll learn:
Why belly fat is harder to lose
Why running and HIIT can backfire for some people
How Zone 2 walking helps burn more fat
Why walking after meals works so well
Simple NEAT hacks to increase daily calorie burn
How incline walking can speed up results


Diet creates the deficit.
Walking accelerates the results.
Try this routine for 7 days and track your steps, energy, digestion, and waistline.




#bellyfatloss #losebellyfat  #weightloss

text:
What if the internet died before Google, Amazon, or the iPhone even existed?

In the late 90s, the Dot-Com Bubble saw investors pour billions into anything ending in .com—from Pets.com to Webvan—no business model required. This $5 TRILLION financial delusion brought the Nasdaq to its knees and wiped out thousands of startups.

We break down the hype-fueled madness, the brutal crash of March 2000, and how a few quiet builders, like Jeff Bezos, ignored the chaos to lay the foundation for the tech giants of the 21st century. The internet didn't die—it rebooted.

He lied about a $1 stock. Made millions. Only served 22 months.
And then? He became a best-selling author, Hollywood icon, and motivational speaker.

This is the true story of Jordan Belfort — the infamous Wolf of Wall Street.
From Italian ices to IPO manipulation, Stratton Oakmont wasn’t just a brokerage… it was a fraud factory.
Fueled by drugs, cold calls, and zero ethics — this wasn’t capitalism.
It was chaos with a phone script.

Timestamps
0:00 Origins of a Salesman: The Making of Jordan Belfort
4:30 Stratton Oakmont: The Empire of Hype
8:45 Cracks, Chaos, and the Chase
12:54 The Fall and the Myth That Lived

In this video, we explore how a charming hustler scammed America, rewrote the rules of sales, and turned financial crime into personal brand power. All while his victims were left with nothing.

and only served 22 months in jail. Then
Hollywood turned his crimes into a
blockbuster. This is the story of Jordan
Belelfford, the man who scammed America
and got rich again doing it. And the
wildest part, people still cheer for
him.
Bayside, Queens, 1962.
A working-class Jewish neighborhood
where dreams were modest and ambition
had a ceiling. But one kid, Jordan
Belelfford, had no interest in ceilings.
One lemon ice, please. For you, two for
one, but only if you tell three friends.
What are you, 12? 16, and I'm going to

Jordan, he enrolled in dental school.
First day, the dean stood up and said,

the wrong profession." Jordan stood up,
nodded, and walked out just like that.
Because he wasn't there to clean teeth.
He was there to get rich. And this was
not the path. Next stop, meat. After

wreckage, Jordan found something that
turned out to be his superpower. The
product didn't matter. Stakes,
surfboards, stocks. you. Yes, you. You
could sell anything. And just like that,
the salesman was born. Jordan didn't
need a better product. He needed a
better payout. Enter Wall Street. Jordan
landed an entry-le job at LF Rothschild,
a legit firm with suits, quotas, and
cocaine in the bathroom stalls. It was
the 1980s, after all. This was where he
got his first taste of real money, real

the markets moved, how the brokers

It's Black Monday. Phones stopped

ticker. The markets crashed. Jordan was
fired. But while others mourned, Jordan
saw something else. An opportunity. He

garbage no serious broker would touch.

10 times the reward. No fancy degrees

mouth. So Jordan picked up the phone,

entertainment industry. I'm talking
about a ground floor opportunity preIPO,

We're talking a 10x return minimum. You
get in now at a dollar a share and in 6
months, you're not calling me to thank
me. You're calling me from your beach
house in Maui. So, here's what we're
going to do. I'm locking you in for
4,000 shares. Sound good?
Uh, I'm not really sure I understand the
company. You don't have to understand
the company, sir. You just have to
understand the upside. That's what smart
money does. They act before the crowd
catches on. So, do you want to be first
or do you want to read about it in
Forbes a year from now, saying, "God, I
wish I had listened." And just like
that, he closed $4,000 with a single
call. No rules, no regulators, no
breaks, just cold calls and pure
adrenaline. He'd found his kingdom, and
he was ready to build an empire.
1989, Jordan Belelfford was already
pouring the next round. And this time,
he wasn't alone.
Enter Danny Porish, a fast, talking,
drunk snorting misfit from Long Island
with the charm of a salesman and the
instincts of a hustler. He wasn't from
Wall Street, and on some days it didn't
feel like he was from the same planet,
but he could close. And Jordan saw
something in him. Hunger, loyalty, no
breaks. Together they were dangerous.
Jordan had the vision. Dany brought the
chaos. And from that chaos, they built
their empire.
Introducing Stratton Oakmont. The name
sounded prestigious, like it had a
100red-year legacy and leatherbound
books. In reality, it was a strip mall
boiler room with flickering lights,
mismatched desks, and exactly zero
regulatory oversight. The early
recruits, they weren't analysts. They
weren't even qualified. They were
bartenders, college dropouts, and
neighborhood hustlers. But Jordan didn't
want experience. He wanted hunger. He
didn't need thinkers. He needed closers.
Then came the training. Jordan developed
a method called straight line
persuasion. A psychological pressure
cooker designed to turn stammering
rookies into high pressure machines. He
taught them to bulldo hesitation, drown
out doubt, and guide a prospect from
hello to where do I send the check in a
single unbroken line. Soon, the office
took on a rhythm, fast, loud, and
addictive. Phones never stopped ringing.
Orders never stopped flowing. The energy
was electric. The egos were growing. And
so was the money. But Stratton's
brilliance wasn't just in how it sold.
It was in who it sold to. They targeted
the forgotten investors, the
working-class retirees, the desperate
parents, the people Wall Street ignored.
Stratton sold them hope, wrapped in
urgency, dressed in false certainty,
backed by madeup projections. At first,
it was obscure penny stocks, pink sheet
garbage with names like BZZT or YU,
companies that barely existed outside
their own press releases. But once the
money started flowing, the schemes
evolved.
Now, it wasn't just fake companies. It
was real IPOs. They bought up massive
blocks of cheap shares, then turned the
sales floor into a hype machine. Call
after call, promise after promise. They
flooded the market with manufactured
excitement, spiked the stock, and then
dumped everything at the top, leaving
thousands of investors holding the bag.
It was called a pump and dump. But at
Stratton Oakmont, it was called Another
Tuesday. By the early '90s, the firm had
exploded. Stratton wasn't just a
brokerage. It was a carnival. The
office, a blur of screaming phones, air
horns, testosterone, $2,000 suits, and
enough narcotics to kill a rhinoceros.
Jordan built a system where fear and
loyalty were currency. Top performers
were treated like royalty. Bonus checks,
vacations, even watches tossed across
the office like candy. Underperformers
humiliated. cut loose, replaced in
hours, and then came the parties,
strippers in the conference room,
champagne overflowing into fax machines,
lines of coke snorted off compliance
manuals. Nothing was sacred. Not the
furniture, not the company car, not even
the fire extinguisher.
Someone once filled with whipped cream
and tequila. Jordan had officially
become a cult leader in Armani. He
bought a helicopter. He named his yacht
after his wife, Naomi. He owned
mansions, Lamborghinis, and Rolexes. And
through it all, he preached the same
sermon. Success is everything. And if
you're not winning, you're nothing. On
paper, Stratton Oakmont was thriving.
They brought companies public. They
raised hundreds of millions. The firm
was growing faster than anyone could
believe. But under the surface, it was
all smoke and mirrors. Because when you
can't sell the truth, you sell the
dream. and Jordan Belelfford had built
an empire doing exactly that.
By 1994, Stratton Oakmont was on fire,
taking companies public, moving
millions, and pulling in national
attention. But beneath the success, the
structure was starting to rot. The
firm's IPO model was aggressive,
familiar, and increasingly reckless.
Same playbook. Overhype the stock,
oversell the dream, and exit before
reality catches up. But this time, they
weren't invisible anymore. The SEC had
flagged a growing list of suspicious
filings. Complaints were piling up from
investors who bought in at $7 and
watched it crash to 30. Internally, some
brokers were starting to ask questions.
They were pushing stocks with no
revenue, no product, sometimes no
working phone number. Management's
answer, close the deal or get out. And
while the firm grew, so did the
complexity of hiding the money. Millions
were funneled offshore through a web of
shell companies. Some accounts were
under Jordan's aunt's name in the UK.
Others were parked in Geneva under
company names that didn't exist. At one
point, Jordan moved funds using
couriers, including a housekeeper,
smuggling cash stuffed envelopes sewn
into her bra. Jordan called it asset
protection. The FBI called it
laundering.
Inside the firm, things were changing.
Drug use, once a reward, became a
necessity. Qualudes slowed their speech.
Cocaine sped them back up. People passed
out during calls. One broker had a
seizure on the sales floor. Fights broke
out over commissions, women, or just too
much testosterone. At least two
employees had to be escorted out after
violent outbursts. And Jordan, he was
unraveling faster than the firm. His
marriage to his wife was disintegrating.
She'd find pills in the couch cushions,
syringes in the bathroom. He once
crashed his Ferrari into a pillar while
high on Ludws with his three-year-old
daughter in the passenger seat. Then
came the yacht incident. In June 1996,
against the captain's warning, Jordan
insisted they sail from Italy to
Sardinia during a storm. He was drunk,
high, and convinced nothing could touch
him. The Naomi began to take on water in
the middle of the Terraneian Sea. On
board, Jordan, his wife, their daughter,
and over $2 million in jewelry and
narcotics. They had to be rescued by the
Italian Navy. The yacht was destroyed.
Jordan survived, but something inside
him didn't. Back in New York, the walls
were closing in. Journalists from Forbes
and the Wall Street Journal had begun
poking around. Former employees were
talking, but most dangerous of all was
Gregory Coleman, an agent with the FBI's
Financial Crimes Division. Coleman
didn't just see red flags, he smelled
blood. He quietly began piecing together
a timeline. He pulled Stratton's cold
call scripts, subpoenaed wire records,
tracked real estate purchases that
didn't match reported income. He found
that Jordan was withdrawing cash and
patterns $50,000 at a time in cashier's
checks, blared through casinos and art
galleries. Coleman knew what it meant.
So did Jordan eventually. What Jordan
didn't know was that some of his own
brokers had flipped. One had been caught
on a separate fraud charge. Another was
burned by an unpaid bonus. They wore
wires, recorded calls, turned over
folders, and as the heat rose, more
jumped ship, not out of morality, but
self-preservation.
Then came October 1996.
Federal agents raided Stratton Oakmont.
They arrived just after sunrise. Phones
were ripped from desks. Filing cabinets
emptied. Hard drives were copied.
Employees were questioned. Someone tried
to flush documents. Another tried to
walk out with a briefcase full of
shredded contracts. It didn't matter.
The FBI had what it needed. But Jordan
still wasn't done. In early 1997, while
under investigation and explicitly told
not to move funds, he wired $2 million
to Switzerland. The transaction was
traced. The conversation about it had
been recorded. That single transfer
became the thread that unraveled
everything. The chase was over and the
fall had begun.
By late 1998, Belelffort was out of
moves. The FBI had the recordings. The
SEC had the filings. The empire he built
on cold calls and false promises had
finally collapsed. And now it was his
turn. He was facing up to 30 years in
federal prison. Wire fraud, securities
fraud, moneyaundering. The charges alone
could have buried him. So Jordan did
what he always did. He sold. Not stocks,
but information. He flipped. He
cooperated. He wore a wire. And one by
one, the people who once worshiped him
were handed over like receipts. Over 30
employees were indicted. Brokers,
partners, friends. Some of them had
joined Stratton right out of high
school. They learned how to sell from
Jordan. They followed his playbook. And
now they were paying for it. Some served
more time than he did. Jordan, he got 22
months in a minimum security facility.
No fences, no cells. The guards didn't
even carry guns. He played tennis in the
mornings, lifted weights in the
afternoons and at night, he wrote.
That's where he met Tommy Chong, the
comedian from Chich and Chong, who was
serving time for selling bongs online.
Jordan told him the whole story. The
drugs, the yacht, the envelopes of cash,
the lie that became a lifestyle. Tommy
wasn't outraged. He was amused. "Write
it down," he said. So Jordan did. In
2007, he published The Wolf of Wall
Street, a memoir that read more like a
victory lap than a confession. There
were no apologies, no remorse, just
yachts, orgies, fraud, and punchlines.
The public ate it up. He sold the film
rights. He wrote a sequel. And in 2013,
Martin Scorsesei and Leonardo DiCaprio
turned it into a global blockbuster. The
same man who lied to investors was now
entertaining them on the big screen.
Audiences laughed. Critics applauded.
And Jordan Belelfford, convicted felon,
former fraudster, became a pop culture
icon. But the people he scammed, they
didn't get movie deals. They didn't get
closure. Most never got their money
back. A teacher who lost her retirement.
a war veteran who invested his life
savings, a family who reorggaged their
home for the next big thing. They were
left with debt, with nothing. The court
ordered Jordan to pay $110 million in
restitution. To this day, only a
fraction has been paid. The rest
vanished into offshore accounts, real
estate trusts, and legal loopholes. He
claims he's working on it. The victims
are still waiting. But Jordan, he's
doing fine. He's a motivational speaker
now, a sales coach, a podcast host. He
sells success, teaches ethics, books,
stages around the world. He wears the
name the wolf like it's a badge of
honor, not the scar it should be. He
didn't just escape justice, he sold it.
Turned 22 months into a book deal.
Turned fraud into fame. And maybe the
scariest part, we applauded.
I was guilty of being greedy, he once
said, but so is everybody else. Maybe
that's why he got away with it. Because
deep down, we never wanted him punished.
We wanted to be him.
[Music]

text:
One drop of blood. Two hundred tests. No needles, no pain. That was the promise that captivated Silicon Valley. The problem? The machine didn't work. Patients got false diagnoses. And investors threw $700 million at it anyway. This is the story of how a 19-year-old Stanford dropout convinced the world she'd cracked the code on blood testing—and how it all came crashing down.

In this video, we'll pull back the curtain on Theranos, the company that promised a healthcare revolution but delivered one of the biggest frauds in history. We'll explore how a charismatic founder, reckless promises, and a culture of secrecy turned a billion-dollar dream into a nightmare of lies and shattered trust.

0:00 The Dream: How It All Began
4:31 The Illusion: Behind Closed Doors
8:51 The Exposure: Cracks Go Public
12:48 The Collapse: Trial, Verdict, and Aftermath

💥 Holmes didn't start out trying to con the world. She believed her own hype. And for a while, so did everyone else. Watch to the end for a warning about what happens when belief replaces proof, and charisma substitutes for competence.

article false, claimed Keroo was a
misogynist with an agenda. She went on
CNBC and said,
>> "This is what happens when you work to
change things. First, they think you're
crazy. Then they fight you. then you
change the world.
>> But behind the scenes, panic was
spreading fast. Walgreens froze their
partnership and launched an internal
investigation. Safeway, which had spent
over $350 million preparing to integrate
Theronos testing, pulled out completely.
Doctors stopped trusting the results.
Patients came forward with horror
stories about false diagnoses that had
upended their lives. Then the regulators
showed up. In 2016, the Centers for
Medicare and Medicaid Services conducted
an inspection that revealed a complete
disaster. Theronos had failed to meet
basic lab standards. Results were
unreliable across the board. Quality
control was practically non-existent.
The punishment was swift and brutal.
Theronos was banned from operating blood
testing labs. Holmes was stripped of her
license to run a lab for 2 years. The
company was ordered to void 2 years of
blood test results, basically admitting
that thousands of medical decisions had
been made using garbage data. Investors
were furious, doctors were livid,
patients felt betrayed, and homes. She
doubled down, insisting the technology
still worked and promising they'd fix
everything. But the house was already
burning down.
By 2018, Elizabeth Holmes no longer
controlled her own story. The magazine
covers were gone. The TED talks were
over. And in their place came something
much colder. Formal charges from the
SEC. Homes in Bwani were accused of
massive fraud. Deliberately misleading
investors while patients received false
test results. All those years of
promises and billiondoll valuations were
now being called what they really were,
lies. Holmes cut a deal with the SEC.
She didn't admit guilt, but agreed to
step down, pay a $500,000 fine, and
accept a 10-year ban from running any
public company. For a moment, it looked
like she might escape the worst of it.
Then, the Department of Justice filed
criminal charges: wire fraud,
conspiracy, crimes that carried up to 20
years in prison each. This wasn't about
money anymore. This was about freedom.
The trial was delayed by the pandemic,
then by Holmes's pregnancy. When it
finally began in late 2021, it felt like
Silicon Valley itself was on trial. Its
hype, its blind faith and charismatic
founders, its willingness to believe in
magic. The prosecution laid out years of
deception. Former employees testified
about being silenced. Investors
described pitches that were pure
fiction. Lab reports showed evidence of
editing, altering, sometimes outright
forgery. Then Holmes took the stand,
something her lawyers probably wished
she hadn't done. For 7 days, she tried
to rewrite the narrative. She said she
believed in the mission, never meant to
mislead anyone. But then she made it
personal, accusing Sunonny Bwani of
abuse and control.
>> Sunny controlled every aspect of my
life,
>> including your decision to defraud
investors.
>> Well, yes,
>> including your fake deep voice. That
wasn't
>> I mean, that was all natural.
>> Ma'am, we have recordings. The courtroom
was riveted. Some saw courage, others
saw desperation. In January 2022, the
jury delivered their verdict. Guilty on
four counts of defrauding investors. She
was acquitted on charges related to
patient harm, but the damage was done.
Bwani's trial followed. Unlike Holmes,
he didn't testify. The evidence spoke
for itself. Emails, investor
presentations, altered documents. He was
found guilty on all 12 counts and
sentenced to nearly 13 years in prison.
Homes got 11. By then, Theronos was long
dead. The company dissolved in 2018. Its
labs shuttered, its machines scrapped.
Walgreens quietly exited. Investors lost
hundreds of millions. Patients were left
with confusion and in some cases,
trauma. Elizabeth Holmes promised to
revolutionize medicine with a single
drop of blood. What she actually
delivered was broken trust, false hope,
and one of the biggest scandals in
Silicon Valley history. The machines are
silent now, but the story lives on, not
as a tale of innovation, but as a
warning about what happens when belief
replaces proof. When charisma
substitutes for competence, and when one
drop of blood becomes one lie too many.
Holmes didn't start out trying to con
the world. She believed her own hype.
And for a while, so did everyone else.
But in the end, extraordinary claims
require extraordinary evidence. And
Theronos never had any.
[Music]

It's the 1920s. The party's roaring, the stock market is soaring, and everyone from the barber to the shoeshine boy is getting rich. They call it the Roaring Twenties, and people believe the good times will last forever.

It's the Great Depression. You woke up
rich, then went to bed broke. No war, no
warning, just a terrifying crash that
wiped out $200 billion and sent America
spiraling into a decade of hunger and
dust. So, what the hell happened? Let's
rewind to the party before the fall.
Imagine waking up in 1922. The war is
over. The mustaches are ridiculous. And
the economy, it's vibing. Factories are
no longer making tanks. They're making
toasters, vacuum cleaners, and the kind
of refrigerators that say ice boxes are
for peasants. New York's skyline shoots
up like it's on steroids. Jazz music
becomes the Wi-Fi of the 20s. Loud
everywhere. And nobody fully understands
how it works. The economy is booming.
People genuinely believe the good times
will last forever. Even economists said
something like, "Trust me, this decade
absolutely roaring." And the engines of
growth, they're humming. The Model T
rolls off assembly lines faster than
ever, thanks to Henry Ford's moving belt
innovation. What used to take 12 hours
now takes 90 minutes. Cars flood the
streets. Auto plants explode with
demand. Oil, steel, rubber. Every linked
industry gets pulled into the
slipstream. The American economy isn't
just growing, it's revving. As cities
flourish with electricity and luxury,
America falls in love with gadgets like
radios. 10 million homes have radios by
1929. Meaning 10 million homes now hear
both Al Jolson and 30 different soads in
glorious AM fuzz. But while cities are
partying, rural America is struggling to
even get on the dance floor. Farmers
once rich from wartime demand now face
plummeting prices. So they borrow to
modernize. But the shiny new tractors
don't save them. They just help them go
broke slightly faster. Meanwhile, urban
America discovers its new favorite
hobby, buying stuff they can't afford.
Welcome to the era of buy now, pay
later. Want a radio? Finance it. A car?
Finance it. Stock in a company that
makes hats for dogs? Definitely finance
it. Banks, thrilled by this innovation
offer installment plans to anyone with a
pulse. It's the financial equivalent of
saying, "Sure, I'll marry you. We've
been on two dates." But the true heart
of the mania lies in Wall Street. The
stock market becomes Disneyland for
adults. Margin loans let anyone buy $100
of stock with just $10 down. The
remaining $90. Who cares? It's the
future. Stocks only go up, right? Even
the barber knew. Trust me, kid.
Utilities are hot. I made a killing in
socks or stocks. You're still a barber,
though. Yes, but spiritually I'm a
tycoon. You know things are bad when
your barber, your butcher, and your dog
all start giving stock tips. Shoe shine
boys pitch can't miss investments to
bankers. A bellboy tells a Vanderbilt to
dump railroads and go all in on pencils.
Between 1924 and 1929, the Dow Jones
quadruples. Stock prices break free from
gravity. Fundamentals.
Why look at profits when you can look at
vibes? This line is going up and so is
my self-esteem. Companies get creative,
too. They set up holding companies that
own other holding companies that own
absolutely nothing. It's just layers of
nothing and a whole lot of stock hype. A
few people try to sound the alarm.
Economist Roger Babson warns in 1929, "A
crash is coming." Wall Street responds
by buying more stock and telling Roger
to go touch grass. Jazz band starts
playing over him. Dollar bills rain from
the sky. Nobody hears him over the sound
of cash and optimism. Meanwhile, behind
the champagne and jazz, cracks are
forming. Rural debt climbs. Consumer
debt balloons. Economies partying on
Eclipse Edge. And nobody's checking if
the floorboards can hold. But hey, don't
worry. It's 1929. What could possibly go
wrong?
October 29th, 1929. America woke up rich
and went to bed broke. That day would go
down in history as Black Tuesday, the
day the stock market didn't just fall.
It performed a flawless 10-meter dive
into concrete. The Dow plummeted. Ticker
tapes spit out red numbers like they
were possessed. Phones rang non-stop.
Suits screamed. Traders fainted. One guy
reportedly had a heart attack,
recovered, looked at his portfolio, and
had another. $14 billion of wealth
vanished. Gone. Adjusted for inflation.
That's over $200 billion. Not monopoly
money. Real homes, savings, college
funds, hopes, and dreams gone. Sell
everything except my Patagonia vest.
It's all I have left. Outside the stock
exchange, crowds gathered in stunned
silence. Some held hands, some cried,
others just stared at the ground, trying
to understand how an entire economy had
tripped over its own shoelaces. The
roaring 20s hadn't just ended. They had
faceplanted into a brick wall while
carrying everyone's retirement plan. And
that was just the start. The crash
triggered a chain reaction. First came
the margin calls. During the boom,
people had been buying stocks on
borrowed money. Put $10 down, get $100
worth of shares. Great. Until the market
tanks and your broker wants the other
$90 immediately. Investors scrambled.
Many had nothing left to repay. Paper
fortunes vanished overnight. People who
had been rich on Monday were bankrupt by
Thursday. Bankers who had spent the
summer drinking martinis now sat in
their offices staring at balance sheets
like they were written in Greek. And
then came the banks. Oh, the banks.
These grand institutions, pillars of
trust, marble floors, oak desks. Turns
out they were built on worthless paper
and blind optimism. As the stock market
imploded, banks couldn't get their loans
back. So they did the obvious thing.
Collapse. And the people, they ran. Not
jogged, not briskly walked, ran. Bankr
runs broke out like wildfire. Crowds
surged outside local branches, banging
on locked doors, screaming for their
savings. Inside, tellers tried to calm
them down. Everyone, please, your money
is completely safe.
Okay, not completely. Entire families
lost everything. Grandpa's bonds
worthless. Aunt Margaret's savings gone.
Little Timmy's piggy bank still full,
but only because no one had the heart to
tell him he was now the wealthiest
person in the household. The disaster
didn't stop at America's shores. US
banks, panicking, called in their
overseas loans. European economies,
already duct taped together after World
War I, were thrown into a blender.
Germany's fragile recovery collapsed.
Britain wobbled. Global trade, once the
great artery of prosperity, choked and
fell by half in just three years, half.
And yet, amidst the panic came the
denial.
Newspapers printed sunny headlines.
Market adjusts as investors take
profits. Right below, a photo of a man
pawning his wedding ring to buy bread.
Politicians insisted the worst was over.
Bankers in silk vests smiled nervously
into microphones, delivering the
financial version of, "We're totally
fine. Nothing's on fire. President
Herbert Hoover appeared on radio
broadcasts, calm as ever, assuring the
American people that the economy is
fundamentally sound. Meanwhile, millions
sat at empty dinner tables and wondered
which part of that sentence was supposed
to help. And still, the system didn't
stop. It just staggered forward. Broken,
clueless, pretending.
The crash wasn't the bottom. It was just
the beginning. and what waited below.
That's where things get dark.
By 1931, the music was completely gone.
The lights were off. The party was over.
And what came next wasn't silence. It
was the sound of factories grinding to a
halt. Of fathers whispering apologies
they never thought they'd have to say.
Of America exhaling all at once and
realizing it had nothing left to breathe
in. Unemployment soared to 25%. One in
every four Americans who wanted to work
couldn't. Jobs vanished like smoke.
Detroit, once the industrial crown
jewel, watched its auto plants shutter
one by one. Production collapsed by 75%.
The great machines stopped turning. The
lights dimmed. And the men who once
assembled the American dream stood
outside factory gates and waited. For
what? They didn't know. Cities sagged
under the weight of need. Breadlines,
endless and quiet, snaked through
downtowns. Mothers lined up at dawn for
a bowl of thin soup. Children looked on,
too young to understand why breakfast
was a luxury. Teachers reported students
fainting in class, not from boredom, but
from hunger. They hadn't eaten in days.
America wasn't starving metaphorically.
It was starving, literally. Desperation
crept into every room. Banks had failed.
Savings were gone. Dignity was thinning.
The suicide rate surged. Newspapers
stopped printing obituaries. They
couldn't keep up. Behind every statistic
was a name. Behind every name was
someone who had believed once that this
country would take care of them.
Marriage rates collapsed. Birth rates
fell. The future had become something
people avoided talking about. Who could
dream of weddings and children when they
couldn't guarantee dinner? And just when
it seemed things couldn't get worse, the
sky turned black. In the Great Plains,
years of aggressive farming had stripped
the land bare. When the rain stopped,
the soil cracked. Then came the winds.
Dust storms swept across the heartland,
towering, choking. Biblical.
Black blizzards, they were called. And
they didn't just cover the ground. They
blotted out the sun. Crops were buried.
Livestock suffocated. Homes filled with
dust. Families coughed through the night
and woke up coated in the earth that
used to feed them. Oklahoma, Kansas,
Texas, millions fled. They packed
everything they had into broken down
cars and drove west, chasing rumors of
jobs and land that hadn't yet turned to
sand. California or bust, the signs
read. But for many, it was just bust. In
Washington, President Hoover tried to
hold the center. He encouraged
volunteerism, offered modest relief
programs. He even launched the Hoover
Dam, an engineering marvel. But it
couldn't feed the hungry in Chicago or
shelter families in St. Louis. He
refused large-scale federal aid, called
it dangerous, called it unamerican.
But by then, people had stopped
listening. His name became shorthand for
suffering of Hoovervilles, shanty towns
made of scrap and cardboard. Hoover
blankets, newspapers used for warmth,
Hoover flags, empty pockets turned
inside out. His legacy wasn't just
concrete and engineering. It was cold,
hunger, and dust. And then something
cracked. Summer 1932.
Thousands of World War I veterans,
desperate and forgotten, marched to
Washington. They had been promised
bonuses for their service decades from
now. But they needed them now. They
built the tent city outside the capital
and waited peacefully. Congress said no.
Hoover said no. And then the army came.
I fought for this country. So did I.
Tear gas was fired. Camps were burned.
Families fled into the smoke. The
government had turned its weapons on its
own heroes. And for the first time,
Americans watched in disbelief. Not just
at what was happening, but at who they
had become. Radicalism spread. Socialist
rallies. Communist recruitment, not
because people believed in theory, but
because capitalism had left them with
nothing but hunger. Crime surged. Bank
robbers like Dillinger and Bonnie and
Clyde were seen not as villains, but as
folk heroes. people who struck back at
the institutions that had betrayed
everyone else. America wasn't just
broke, it was broken. And yet, even
then, something held. Not belief, not
optimism, but endurance. People didn't
give up. They migrated. They lined up.
They held their families. They survived.
Not because they were certain things
would get better, but because they had
no other choice. But the question
remained, in a country that once
promised endless growth, what was left
when the growth stopped? And who, if
anyone, could lead them out of the
wreckage?
By March 1933, Franklin Delano Roosevelt
stood at the podium for his
inauguration. Millions leaned in. "The
only thing we have to fear is fear
itself," he said. "Not gold, not banks,
not even dust. Fear." It was more than a
speech. It was the first deep breath the
country had taken in years.
Roosevelt didn't wait. Within weeks,
young men in threadbear clothes were
handed shovels, tents, and purpose. The
Civilian Conservation Corps put them to
work. You're here to plant trees and
save the country. In that order? Yes.
The Works Progress Administration soon
followed. Millions hired to build roads,
bridges, schools, post offices. They
didn't just rebuild infrastructure. They
rebuilt pride. People who had once stood
in bread lines now stood on scaffolding,
lifting steel into the sky. In the
Tennessee Valley, FDR launched the TVA.
Dams went up. Lights flicked on. Whole
towns that had lived in darkness began
to glow. Families gathered around
radios, not because they could finally
afford one, but because for the first
time they had electricity to plug one
in. Slowly, unmistakably, life stirred.
GDP rose. Unemployment crept downward.
The dust settled, literally and
figuratively. People dared to imagine a
future again. But FDR didn't stop at
jobs. He wanted to fix the machine, not
just oil it. So, he built rules. The SEC
to keep Wall Street from doing Wall
Street things. The FDIC to protect your
money from disappearing again. Banks
reopened, but this time people weren't
running in to withdraw everything in a
panic. They were depositing quietly,
hopefully.
Then came social security. It didn't
make anyone rich. It didn't need to. It
said, "You matter. We'll remember you.
You won't have to work until you
collapse." It wasn't flashy, but it was
monumental. Even the arts got a job. The
Federal Arts Project paid painters,
photographers, and writers to capture
the soul of a recovering nation. One
photo, migrant mother by Dorothia Lang,
became the face of it all. Her eyes
didn't say, "We're saved." They said,
"We're surviving."
Hollywood chimed in, too. People packed
into theaters to watch The Wizard of Oz,
where a gray world turned to color. In
the middle of a depression, Americans
still dreamed, maybe more than ever.
Cities buzzed again. Restaurants
reopened. Radios played swing music. And
if you squinted just a little, the
skyline looked like it was rising again.
In the distance, factories started
humming. But this time, not just with
consumer goods, helmets, boots,
ammunition. The world was shifting
again. And America, America was starting
to stir, not just for recovery, but for
something bigger. The Great Depression
didn't end with a celebration. It ended
with work, with blistered hands and
tired backs, with legislation, hope, and
a little jazz. With a nation that had
collapsed, choosing piece by piece to
rise again. But as America stood back
up, it didn't realize that something
else was already on the horizon,
something darker, louder, global, and
this time the whole world would feel it.
[Music]

December 2001, America's seventh largest
company files for bankruptcy. $63
billion gone. Thousands of employees
wiped out. Wall Street shocked. But not
because it happened. Because no one
could explain how. This is the story of
Enron. The company that sold nothing,
made billions, and then imploded while
everyone clapped. Imagine a company that
made its fortune by moving gas through
pipes. Not the explosive kind, the
boring kind. That was Enron in 1985.
Just your average Houston pipeline firm
formed from a merger no one outside a
tax attorney's office cared about. But
then came Ken Lei. He had a PhD in
economics, a deep tan, and one big idea,
deregulation.
If the government stopped telling energy
companies what to charge, Enron could go
from utility company to energy trader.
Suddenly gas wasn't just pumped, it was
bought, sold, hedged, and speculated on
like Wall Street, but smellier.
Lei brought in Jeff Skielling, a
fast-talking Mackenzie consultant who
believed deeply in markets,
spreadsheets, and himself.
Skiilling's pitch, Enron wasn't just a
pipeline business. It was a tech
company. We don't sell energy, he said.
We sell the future of energy. And Wall
Street loved it. The real game changer
came with Enron online, a digital
marketplace for trading energy
contracts. It made gas trading look like
ordering pizza. Click a button, move
millions. Suddenly, Enron wasn't just
some Texas gas firm. It was Silicon
Valley with a cowboy hat. Reporters
swooned. Fortune magazine crowned it
most innovative company in America for 6
years straight. Inside Enron HQ, the
vibe was intense. Skilling told
employees they were the smartest guys in
the room. Translation: If you weren't
performing, you were gone. Bonuses were
big, backstabbing was casual, and every
quarter was a battle to impress
investors.
You closed five deals, cut costs by $20
million, boosted quarterly revenue by
double digits, and landed a contract
that guarantees margins through 2009.
Yes, sir. All ahead of schedule.
Hm, impressive. If we were running a
normal company, Enron called itself a
market maker, a tech innovator, a brain
trust. From the outside, it looked like
the future. But ask a simple question.
Wait, what do they actually do? And
you'd get a shrug, a whiteboard, and 40
minutes of buzzwords. But the stock
price kept rising. So no one asked
again. And while the spotlight shone
brighter and brighter behind the scenes,
something was quietly, dangerously
cracking.
By the late '90s, Enron was a legend.
The stock skyrocketed from $7 in 1997 to
over $90 by 2000. That's over a,000%
gain in 3 years. If you bought Enron
instead of groceries, you were a genius.
The media called it a miracle.
Executives called it a party. But behind
the champagne and slide decks, the math
wasn't mathing. See, Enron had made big
promises. Constant growth, big numbers,
no bad quarters. But energy markets
aren't Tik Tok. They don't go viral
every week. So, they changed the rules.
Enter Marktomarket accounting, also
known as we're counting chickens that
haven't even hatched and may not even be
chickens. Here's how it worked. Enron
signs a 10-year energy contract. Instead
of waiting for actual cash to roll in,
they count all 10 years of projected
profit immediately.
Wait, can you do that? We are doing it.
So, on paper, it looked like Enron was a
cash machine. But many of those deals
were barely profitable. Some hadn't even
started yet. Others were based on
projections that made astrology look
conservative. Internally, it was chaos.
But as long as the image held, no one
dared blink. And when the numbers didn't
add up, enter Andy Fasto, Enron's chief
financial officer. And his main job was,
well, let's call it financial
storytelling. He created dozens of
outside entities called special purpose
entities or SPEs.
Technically separate from Enron, but in
practice, totally controlled by it.
Here's the scam. Enron would take its
worst assets, deals that were failing,
assets that were losing value, and sell
them to these SPEs. On paper, it looked
like Enron was offloading risk and
bringing in cash. In reality, Enron was
funding both sides of the deal. It was
like selling your broken car to your
dog, giving him your credit card to pay
for it, and then telling your wife,
"Look, honey, I made a sale." He had fun
naming these entities like LJM1,
LJM2, and Raptor because nothing says
totally legit companies like randomly
generated names. I'm not breaking the
rules. I'm using them creatively.
While Fasto juggled liabilities like
Flaming Swords, Enron's top executives
were cashing out. millions in bonuses,
stock options, villas, private jets,
regular Enron employees told to pour
their retirement savings into Enron
stock. Their 401k plan was basically
hail Enron. Every major Wall Street
analysts still gave Enron glowing
reviews, a buy rating. Many of them came
from firms doing business with Enron.
Meil Lynch, for instance, made millions
managing Enron's stock offerings while
publicly praising its financials.
Objectivity was optional. Revenue was
not. The truth was buried under layers
of jargon and spreadsheets designed by
people who treated ethics like a
software plug-in. Optional, confusing,
and easy to ignore. And the company
encouraged that confusion. Enron's
internal motto might as well have been.
If you can't explain it, you're probably
doing it right. By 2000, Enron's image
was bulletproof until someone finally
asked, "Wait, where's the actual money?"
August 2001, Enron Tower. Jeff
Skielling, CEO of the hottest company in
America, walks into his office, places
his resignation letter on the desk, and
leaves just like that. No scandal, no
press conference, just a casual, "Peace
out. I'm done being brilliant." Wait,
what? No worries. He wants to spend more
time with his millions. I mean, his
family reality red flag the size of
Texas. That same month, the SEC launched
an investigation into Enron's offbalance
sheet entities, which in corporate speak
means, we smell smoke but haven't found
the bodies yet. So Ken Lei, the original
Gaslight Alchemist, Enron's founder,
returns as CEO and smiles like your
grandpa after accidentally deleting your
homework and says, "Hi everyone. It's
just another Monday, business as usual."

Ordinary people poured their savings

vaults. Businesses crumbled. Jobs

a staggering
25%. Red lines stretched for blocks. In

to nearly
$12. Gas stations in the United States

over the world's most powerful
economies.

everyone. In the early 2000s, banks and
lenders fueled an unprecedented housing
boom, handing out mortgages to anyone
who asked, even those with shaky credit.
Home prices soared, and Wall Street saw
an opportunity. Instead of questioning
the house of cards they were building,
financial institutions doubled down.
Banks bundled risky subprime loans into
complex financial products called
mortgagebacked securities or MBS and
collateralized debt obligations or
CDOS. These were then sold to investors
around the world stamped with AAA
ratings by credit agencies that either
didn't understand or didn't care how
fragile they really were. For years, the
system seemed unstoppable.
Investors profited. Banks thrived.
Homeowners believed prices would never
fall. But cracks began to show in 2006
when housing prices peaked. As values
dropped, homeowners found themselves
owing more than their homes were worth.
Mortgage defaults surged. Then came
2008, the year the world unraveled.
Leman Brothers, a giant investment bank,
collapsed overnight, sending shock waves
through global markets. The financial
system, built on bad debt and reckless
speculation, froze. Banks stopped
lending. Stock markets nosedived.
Trillions of dollars vanished.
Governments scrambled to prevent total
economic collapse. The US government
poured $700 billion into failing banks
through the troubled asset relief
program, TARP. Central banks slashed
interest rates to new zero. Stimulus
packages flooded the economy in a
desperate attempt to restore confidence.
But for millions, the damage was done.
Homes foreclosed. Jobs disappeared.
Savings evaporated. The crisis plunged
the world into a deep recession,
exposing the greed, poor oversight, and
systemic fragility that had fueled the
meltdown. In the aftermath, governments
imposed tighter regulations, including
the DoddFrank Act, aimed at preventing
another
catastrophe, the CO9 pandemic. At the
start of 2020, the stock market was
unstoppable. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones
were soaring to record highs, fueled by
a strong economy and investor optimism.
But in the shadows, an unseen threat was
spreading. One that would bring markets
to their knees faster than ever before.
In late 2019, news of a mysterious virus
emerged from Wuhan, China. At first, few
paid attention. The markets shrugged off
the headlines. But as February 2020
arrived, the virus spread beyond China
to Italy, Iran, and the rest of the
world. What seemed like a distant health
crisis suddenly became a global
emergency. Then came March, the month
the markets crashed. Panic erupted as
governments locked down entire
economies. Businesses shuttered
overnight. Supply chains froze.
Investors fearing a worldwide recession
rushed for the exits. Within weeks,
stock markets crumbled. The Dow Jones
suffered its three worst single day
point drops in history. March 9th, March
12th, and March 16th, falling nearly 13%
in a single session. These days became
known as Black Monday, Black Thursday,
and Black Monday again. Just when it
seemed things couldn't get worse, an oil
war between Saudi Arabia and Russia sent
oil prices into freefall, adding more
fuel to the fire. It was chaos. But
governments and central banks fought
back. The US Federal Reserve slashed
interest rates to zero and unleashed
massive stimulus programs. Congress
passed the CARES Act, a historic $2.2 $2
trillion rescue package that sent direct
payments to citizens and prompted up
businesses. Around the world,
policymakers scrambled to contain the
economic fallout. Despite the
devastation, something extraordinary
happened. By April, whispers of vaccine
development and the rise of the
stay-at-home economy led by tech giants
like Amazon and Zoom sparked a historic
rebound. Stocks climbed at a record
pace. By August 2020, the S&P 500 had
fully erased its losses, marking the
shortest bare market in history. But
beneath Wall Street's recovery, Main
Street was suffering. Small businesses
collapsed. Unemployment soared. The
crisis exposed a deep disconnect between
financial markets and the real economy.
A divide that still lingers today. The
CO 19 crash wasn't just a financial
meltdown. It was a reminder of how fast
fear can spread, how crucial government
intervention can be, and how
unpredictable the global economy truly
is. Because in 2020, the markets didn't
just fall. They plummeted, rebounded,
and left the world forever changed.
History has shown us again and again
that no economy is immune. Crashes
happen fast, recoveries are slow, and
the lessons are often forgotten. So, the
question is, what will trigger the next
collapse? Make sure you're prepared. Hit
subscribe and join us as we break down
the past to predict the future

subtitles.plaintext:
You're born in 1932 in the Dutch East
Indies and you're not Dutch. That's
already a problem. You're also a girl,
so whatever chances you had, cut them in
half. Still, life isn't a nightmare. You
don't starve. Your house has no
electricity, no running water. It smells
like sweat, damp earth, and bodies that
never really get clean. Your father
works in the rice fields he doesn't own,
never will. Your mother sews until her
fingers crack, selling stitches for
coins that barely last the week. You're
Indonesian, which isn't even a country
yet. Just a scatter of islands owned by
someone else. The Dutch control
everything. The government, the trade,
even the language you're allowed to
speak. This is your world, and it's
already decided who matters in it. Not
you. At least not for good reasons. By
seven, you're hauling water from the
well, buckets heavier than you are. By
10, you learn the rules. Keep your head
down around the Dutch officials. And be
sure to speak only Dutch in public. Most
girls in your village never learn to
read. They marry at 14. But you're
[music] different. There's [bell] a
Dutch school a few miles away. You beg
your parents to go. Eventually, they
agree to find a way. They scrape all the
money they have to make it happen. You
work hard studying and get accepted. You
walk four miles every day, rain or heat,
no excuses. [music]
That's where you meet Arif, a boy from
the next village. His father runs a
small shop. He shares his lunch. He
makes you [music] laugh. By 13, you
realize you like him. Time goes by. 1942
arrives.
The Dutch disappear. Japanese soldiers
replace them. New flags, new language.
They talk about Asia for Asians. About
opportunity.
>> Everything Dutch was banned.
>> Only Japanese and your native language
are allowed. And strangely, schools stay
open. Your teacher is Indonesian now.
She looks like you. Sounds like you. She
tells you something no one has ever said
before.
Girls, you have a future now. You're 15
years old and for the first time, things
are going well. You're on top of your
class. You have books, a school uniform
you're proud of, a leather journal where
you write poetry about change. You want
to be a teacher.
Arif still walks with you sometimes. He
waits near his father's shop and slips
you extra mango when no one is looking.
You sit on the steps and share it with
sticky fingers. He makes you laugh. You
imagine a future with him. University
first, then marriage. One morning, your
teacher clears her throat. Scholarships
to Tokyo. Higher education for the
brightest.
Nursing, [music] teaching,
administration.
When she says your name, your heart
almost jumps out of your chest. Tokyo, a
real university. Your father cries when
you tell him. Not quiet tears, proud
ones.
Our daughter, he keeps saying, "Chosen."
For the first time, you wonder, maybe
Japan isn't as bad as people say. Your
mother sews you new clothes. Your father
buys you a leather traveling bag.
Neighbors bring you food. That evening,
Arif meets you behind your house. I'll
wait, he says with tears in his eyes.
However long it takes, 3 years, 5, I
don't care. His voice breaks. You
believe him. But you soon find out
things don't turn out the way you think.
You pack carefully your books, your
journal, one family photograph. Your
parents give you a hug. Write to us,
they say, every week. Tell us you're
safe. Tell us you're eating well. You
promise them. You board the ship with 13
other educated girls. All of you are
excited for what's to come. But the ship
doesn't go to Tokyo. It goes to Burma. A
fenced compound, barbed wire, guard
towers, armed soldiers. All the girls
are gathered in a group. A Japanese
soldier speaks calmly like he's reading
a list. You're here to provide comfort
to the Imperial Japanese Army. You will
serve as soldiers. You will not refuse.
Escape means death.
The words don't register all at once.
They land like blows one after another.
There is [music] no scholarship. Tokyo
was never real.
Your parents didn't know. Your teacher
didn't know. The lie was so convincing
that even adults who loved you handed
you over thinking they were giving you
[music] a future.
Instead, they sent you straight into
hell.
You're assigned a number eight. Your
room is barely big enough to lie down in
a mat, a wall, nothing else. Your
leather bag, the books, the journal, the
life you packed so carefully gets tossed
into the corner like trash.
That night, you open your journal. Your
hand shakes so badly you can barely hold
a pen. You manage one sentence.
They lied about everything. You were
then treated by army medics. They
examined your body and sent you back to
your dorm. As you walked back, you saw
many rooms. You could see everything
from outside.
Your services that were being provided.
And then it was your turn. They took you
from your dorms and then into a room.
The first soldier comes in. You try to
explain that there's been a mistake,
that you're a student, that you're
supposed to be in Tokyo. He doesn't
understand your language. You speak to
him in Japanese. He doesn't care. You
resist it. He reacts. Your dress tears.
You struggle.
Then he does what he came to do.
Your body stops feeling like it belongs
to you. pain, confusion, pressure, all
of it blurring together until you're
somewhere else entirely, watching it
happen to someone you don't recognize.
When it's over, he fixes [music] his
uniform and leaves.
You lay there, your body still
breathing,
but the girl who wanted to teach
literature is gone.
After they were done, you were [music]
sent back to the dorms. You notice two
other girls crying. You already know
what they went through.
The routine sets in fast. You wake up
before dawn. Clean the dorm with the
other girls. Floors, mats, buckets. No
one speaks. If there is blood, you scrub
it until it's gone. You line up for
inspection.
A military doctor checks you for
disease. Cold hands, no words, just
making sure you're fit for use.
Then you're sent back to your room. A
soldier enters. The door closes. That is
the day. Some soldiers are young. They
avoid your eyes. Some speak. Some stay
silent. A few apologize afterward.
It changes nothing.
Some show photographs. wives, children.
One soldier cries about his wife, about
whether he will make it home alive. He
thanks you for listening and [music]
then he told you to turn around. They
come one after another from morning
until night. You still write in your
journal, not for comfort, to keep
record, to prove this is real. March
15th, 13 men, one had a scar. He talked
about how the war is a stalemate.
March 16th, [music]
9, I got sick. I cleaned it up. March
17th.
I hate them. During one of your medical
appointments, the doctors say a word.
Pregnant. Your heart drops. The doctors
speak to each [music] other fast, quiet.
They don't know you understand Japanese.
You catch one word,
experimentation.
Then a number, 731.
You don't know what it means. They don't
give you time to ask. They strap you
down. There is no medicine. You bite
your [music] lip until your mouth tastes
like iron.
Later, you write in your journal. It was
removed. I start work again in 3 days.
Some of the girls get moved. New ones
arrive. Others leave in bags. Bags they
put themselves in.
Their places are filled. Korean,
Chinese, Filipino. So much for Asia. For
Asians.
You catch your reflection in a mirror.
You don't recognize the face looking
back. Bruises that never heal. joints
that ache all the time. You teach the
new girls what you've learned. Many
can't read. Most are from the
countryside. You tell them the rules.
Don't fight unless you can win. Save
your strength.
One of the Filipino girls thanks you.
Her Japanese is broken.
Please accept this. She says the guards
didn't take it. It's all I have left
from home.
She holds a mango in both hands, her
head bowed.
Your eyes burn.
You take it. You share it with her.
Juice runs down your hands. Sticky,
sweet.
You never see her again.
Rumors spread among the dorms that Japan
was surrendering.
You know the Japanese would rather die
than surrender.
Office papers burn behind the
administration building, eliminating
evidence.
You hear yelling and gunshots from
another building. It continues
throughout the night.
You and the others huddle together in
the dark, waiting to learn if you will
be executed or freed.
Allied soldiers arrive next morning.
Americans, Australians. They find you
and 37 other women still alive. skeletal
disease. Some barely conscious. One
American soldier gets sick. Another just
stands there crying.
They give you food, water, blankets,
medicine. They ask you questions you can
barely answer. What happened here? How
long?
How many men? You tell them. [music]
They write reports, take photographs.
You are labeled liberated, but your
[music] body doesn't feel free. When
they tell you that you can go home, you
realize something too [music] late. You
don't know what home means anymore.
The journey home was long. Processing
camps, [music]
stacks of paperwork, waiting rooms that
smell like sweat and [music] bleach.
When you tell people the truth, they
look away.
An older Indonesian woman pulls you
aside. [music]
She speaks to you in Dutch.
Say you worked in a factory, she
whispers. [music] It will be easier. You
do. You reach Java weeks later. Your
house looks the same. The roof, the
door. Your mother opens it and
immediately starts crying. She sees the
[music] scars and your frail bones. She
pulls you inside. She doesn't ask
questions. [music]
She looks at your arms, your collar
bones, your face.
You are supposed to be at college.
Your father stands in the doorway. His
eyes get watery. They don't ask what
happened. They don't need [music] to.
Something is wrong. That much they could
see. The thing you did next is what you
regret [music] the most.
You tell them what happened. All of it.
Your mother breaks. Her crying [music]
turns wild. She collapses to the floor.
You try to hold her. [music]
Your father doesn't move. His eyes stay
on the ground. Then he turns [music] and
walks out. You get up to follow him,
worried, afraid. [music]
Your mother cries out, "Stay here. Leave
him be. That night, [music] your mother
brings food every hour. Your father sits
outside your door. No one sleeps.
Days pass. The village watches. People
whisper. Your parents say nothing. Your
father stops eating, stops speaking.
He works the field longer than before.
Comes home exhausted, quiet.
One morning he doesn't wake up. The
doctors say his heart failed. Your
mother doesn't argue. You understand
what killed him. Not the truth. [music]
The space where the truth should have
been.
After the funeral, Arif comes by. He
stands [music] outside, waves slowly to
you, his face careful, soft. You go to
meet him. He's holding a basket of
mangoes, more than anyone needs.
I'm sorry about your dad, he says. He
shifts the basket in his hands, doesn't
offer it yet. Let me know how we can
help. We can't, you say. Your voice
shakes.
I can't be that person anymore.
He finally holds the basket out to you.
You don't take it.
What happened? He asks.
You shake your head. It isn't the truth.
He knows that. I don't need to know, he
says. I just needed to see you. He sets
the basket down between you. I'll leave
these, he says. He takes a step back and
walks away.
You retreat inside.
The mangoes sit in the dust until the
sun goes down.
Time passes. You eventually leave town.
You find work as a seamstress. The girl
who once wanted to teach literature now
sews buttons, men's hems, turns old
things into something usable again.
You never marry. You never let anyone
touch you. The life you might have had,
children, a family, you can't imagine
it. You can't bring a child into a world
where you would be her mother.
>> [laughter]
>> She would be ashamed of you. You would
never tell anyone what the Japanese did
to you, especially after what happened
to your father.
Arif calls sometimes, mostly to check on
you, to tell you about your mother. She
stayed behind in your hometown. Years go
by, and every so often you see a
newspaper story. A Korean woman speaks
out, then a Chinese woman. They call
them comfort women. Eventually, the
story explodes.
International headlines, protests,
demands. The Japanese government denies
everything.
You think about adding your name, about
proving Indonesian girls were taken,
too. But you don't.
Nothing will bring back the girl who
wanted to teach literature.
The police knock on an apartment door. A
wellness check. The apartment is clean,
orderly. They search the rooms. They
find what they're looking for. A person,
deceased, female, 70s, alone.
How long has she been gone? One officer
asks.
At least 4 days, the other says. A
[clears throat] man from her hometown
called it in. He adds. Good thing he
did. While they wait, they check the
rest of the apartment. One room feels
wrong. There's only a table and a chair.
On the table, a leather travel bag,
brass knuckles, cracked and worn.
Inside, school books from 1943.
A journal.
It starts as poetry,
then it becomes something else.
Descriptions of things no one was meant
to survive.
Then blank pages.
At the bottom of the bag, carefully
folded, a scholarship application.
Tokyo University. Stamped approved.
We know that story was rough to hear,
but it is important that these stories
get told. If you did enjoy the video and
liked hearing about this somewhat
forgotten portion of history, you might
like what's coming up
