subtitles.plaintext:
You're born in the thick forests of the
land and you're screwed. You just don't
know it yet. It's around the year 1600s,
long before anyone called this place
America. And the air smells like pine,
smoke, and river water. The forest gives
food, fire, and family. But it also
takes when it wants. Life is never easy.
The men hunt deer. The women carry
water. The children gather sticks for
the fire. That's how it's always been.
Your first bed is deer skin by the fire.
Your mother hums to you each night. She
gives you a small white shell bead. Keep
this close, she says. It will bring you
luck. You believe her because her words
are sacred.
By 10, you know how to work. By 12, you
know how to dig a grave. When the snow
comes early, two cousins die. Your
people call it a hard season. You think
they're insane.
Then one year, the hunters return with
strange news. They saw strangers at the
edge of the forest. Men with pale faces
and hair like corn silk. Men covered in
metal that shined like the sun. They say
these men came on giant boats. They say
they're building wooden walls near the
river. Your people weren't sure what to
believe.
One morning, you see the truth for
yourself. A group of strangers walks
into your village. They bring shiny
beads, bells, and food that smells
strange. Your people welcome them. They
smile back, but their smiles don't reach
their eyes. Not long after they arrive,
the coughing starts. First one person,
then 10, then whole families. Elders
call it by names you've never heard.
Cursed illnesses, or smallpox as we know
it. Sickness that spreads faster than
fire. The healers can't stop it. By
spring, half the village is gone. Your
father dies in the night, choking on his
own blood. You wake to find him cold
beside the fire, eyes still open like
[music] he's waiting for someone to
close them. Your mother cuts your hair
shoulder length and dresses you like a
boy. She says the pale men take girls.
You don't understand why. You soon find
out later, though. The strangers come
back with more men. They demand land.
They say your people are on their
territory now. Your people laugh. How
can land belong to anyone? The strangers
don't laugh. They burn three tents to
prove they're serious. Your uncle tries
to fight back. They shoot him with
weapons that crack like thunder. He
falls and doesn't get up. A battle
breaks out. During the small battle, the
chief takes the women, kids, and elderly
to the caves. For weeks, everyone stays
hidden, surviving on insects and on some
occasions, deer and rabbits. But the
food in the area runs out. There wasn't
much to begin with. One morning, you
venture on your own to help forage for
food. You don't tell anyone. While
picking berries, your mother finds you.
She scolds you for going out. While on
the way back, someone grabs your hair. a
fellow native like yourself, but not
from your tribe. Behind him, the pale
white men, their faces smiling, mouth
salivating as if you two were a meal.
The translator tells you what they want.
Show us where the others hide or we will
your mother. They hold a blade to her
throat. You look at your mother's face.
She shakes her head. No, you love her
more than anything.
You point toward the caves.
Three men drag her toward the bushes.
The rest of them head to the cave. They
yank you in the opposite direction, hand
clamped over your mouth. You hear her
screams cut through the trees. Then you
hear worse, the silence after. You never
see her again.
You arrive at the settlement. They bring
you back to a building with many rooms.
It smells like sweat [music] and fear.
Inside, you see other girls. Girls from
other tribes. Their eyes look empty. You
learn quickly what happens here. The
settlers use them. [music] At night, you
hear the cries through the walls. You're
not sure what [music] awaits your fate.
One day, a slave trader opens the door.
He says with an angry face, "You're
lucky our boss likes you."
>> A man walks from behind the slave
trader. He wears all black with a gold
cross on his neck. He takes you into his
massive home. He tells you to cook and
clean. When you speak your own words,
he says your language is the devil's
tongue. You weren't the only girl there.
It was an orphanage. Some nights the
father, well, that's what you were told
to call him, would take some of the
girls into his chambers. You're not sure
what happened, but you didn't ask.
Talking to the other kids in your native
language, well, that could result in
severe punishment. You learn quickly to
be useful and invisible at the same
time. You learn their language. You walk
like a shadow. You hide the shellbead in
your clothing. It's the only thing
that's still yours.
Weeks turn into years. The town becomes
a thriving community run by the pale
white people. [music] And the town
builds something new, a school. They say
it's for you. They say it's for your
soul. The building smells of chalk and
soap, but what happened inside was quite
rotten. The walls are painted white, the
color of mercy, but there is none here.
The women who run it wear black veils
and crosses. They call themselves
sisters. They say they will save you.
The first thing they do is cut your
hair, give you a new name. They tell you
your name is gone, [music]
your words are gone, your gods are gone.
At night, they make you kneel on raw
grain until your knees turn purple at.
If you cry, they smile and say, "It's
the devil leaving your body." You learn
not to [music] cry. One night, the head
priest visits the dormitories. Every
girl in the room holds her breath,
praying he walks past [music] her bed.
His footsteps echo on the stone. He
stops in front of your bed. Come here. I
will bless you.
He takes you to his room. He smells of
wine and wax. Throughout the night, he
whispers prayers while he hurts you. You
stop believing [music] in heaven.
One girl disappears after he visits her.
The next day, her bed is empty, and no
one asks why. You all know why. In the
morning, the nuns make you scrub the
floors until the stone turns red. They
tell you to be grateful. That pain
brings you closer to God. You begin to
forget your mother's face. You begin to
forget your own voice. You hide in
silence because [music] silence is
safer.
Years pass. You're 18 now. They say
you're ready, ready to serve, ready to
obey. They send you back to the
settlement, the same place that once
stole you. They give you to a Christian
home. You scrub their floors and do
outside work. You spoke their language
well, but you hardly spoke. You try to
be a shadow like you've always been, but
the master had other plans. He was no
different from the priest. The wife
finds out. She makes the master trade
you off. The militia needed someone to
talk to the tribes, someone to make
trades, someone to translate. For the
first time since you were taken, you
become useful. You're not invisible.
It almost feels good. Even though you
were betraying your own kind, it didn't
matter. You no longer identify with it
anyway. They would never accept you. A
fellow militia settler starts coming
around. He's different from the others,
you think. He says his name is Evan.
[music] He asks your name, your real
name. You tell him. He brings you bread.
He smiles when he sees you. You think
maybe this is what safety feels like.
You think maybe you can belong to both
worlds. He says he'll take care of you.
You believe him.
One night he brings you to his cabin. He
says he loves you. You don't know if you
love him back, but you know what happens
to girls who say no.
Months pass. You wake up one morning and
feel something's wrong. Your body aches.
Then the sores appear. First one, then
more. The healer woman takes one look
and turns away. She whispers a word
you've never heard before, but you know
it as syphilis. Another sickness the
settlers brought. The sickness with no
cure. You go to find Evan, the settler
who said he loved you. You run to his
cabin. You pray that he's there and he
is. You run into Evan's arms. You cry.
He holds you. [snorts] The next day, you
wake up. You get up to make breakfast
even though your body aches. But your
lover is gone. Only a letter. You never
see him again. The sickness spreads
through your body like fire. Your skin
breaks open. Pus oozes. Wounds cover you
from head to toe, even on your tongue.
Your bones ache. Your mind starts to
slip. The other girls in town now avoid
you. They know what it means. You don't
go back to Evan's house. The church
won't let you inside anymore. They say
you're infected by sin. The charity
house won't let you in either. You
wander aimlessly around the town. They
kick you out. You walk into the forest.
[snorts] You keep walking until you find
a peaceful river. You lay beside it. You
think about your mother. You wonder if
she'd even recognize you now. You wonder
if she's still alive to care. [music]
You reach into your pocket, the shell
bead you've kept hidden for all these
years. You [music] try to hold it,
hoping to pray for luck, but your hands
shake too much to hold it. It falls to
the grass. You don't have the strength
to pick it up.
You close your eyes and think about the
forest. The fires, the laughter, your
mother's song. The sound of the river
washes away your thoughts.
In the dead of night, you hear a sound.
You peer into the darkness with what
little strength you have. You see
something walking away. A spirit. A
fellow native still wearing their
traditional clothes, not yet caught by
settlers. You try to speak your native
language, but you're too weak to speak.
You smell something sweet.
Berries. The same berries you ate when
you were young. You take a bite. Sweet.
Delicious. Memories of your childhood
fill your mind.
By morning, you're gone. No one claims
your [music] body. No one finds it
except for the animals. No marker, no
name, no prayer. Just another native who
died in the woods alone.
And in town, another girl arrives at the
orphanage.
>> Hundreds and hundreds of federal Indian
boarding [music] schools across the
country. Nearly 1,000 documented native
child deaths. Well, the real number is
likely to be much, much higher. But the
federal government has never never
formally apologized until today. I
formally apologize
as president of the United States of
America.
>> So, yeah, not America's best chapter.
Hopefully, that moment made you feel a

Anyways, believe it or not, someone had

You're born in a wagon tent. Not a
house, not a village, just a wagon
rolling across the open plains of Saita.
The wind never really stops out here.
Neither does the movement. You're a boy,
and unfortunately, you're beautiful,
which sounds nice until you realize
you're also poor and not Greek. Yeah,
that combination is going to ruin your
life.
Your people are nomads. They don't farm
the land. They follow it. Where the
sheep go, you go. Where the goats and
cattle graze, the wagons follow behind.
One massive moving herd stretching
across the plains.
Food is never guaranteed, but your
people know animals better than anyone.
Your diet is mostly meat, milk, and
whatever they can hunt. deer, rabbit,
even eagles and wolves sometimes, but
mostly it's a lot of milk. Your mother's
milk, sheep milk, goat milk, and horse
milk. Whether you like it or not, you
drink it constantly.
When you're five, you spend most of your
time with your mother in the wagon. She
practices archery, men's clothing, and
watches the herds from a distance.
Sometimes your [music] father lifts you
onto a horse and lets you ride with the
men. They practice archery while moving,
shooting from horseback like it's
nothing. One afternoon, your tribe
settles near a river. The wagons form a
loose circle. Fires are lit using dried
animal dong. Another strange smell fills
the air. First, fermented horse milk,
sharp and sour. Second, a thick earthy
smoke as herbs are burned nearby. It's
safe to say your people definitely know
how to party. While the adults drink and
sing, the children play nearby, but you
stay close to your mother. The other
boys notice things. Your face is softer
than theirs. Your hair is braided neatly
at your shoulders. You don't wrestle as
hard. They laugh. Your father doesn't.
He looks at you for a long moment. He
doesn't say anything, just disappointed.
And even though you don't understand why
yet, something inside you already knows.
Out here, softness is dangerous.
You don't see it coming. That's the
first thing you remember about the day
everything ends.
The morning starts like every other one.
Smoke from dung fires drifting low
across the grass. You and your mother
are sleeping. The men are farther out,
watching the herd. Out of nowhere,
shouting erupts and horses stampede into
your village. Not your tribe's [music]
horses. These ones move fast. They were
taller and leaner. You didn't know what
was going on, but you knew these men
rode horses to take, not to live. Men
shout, but not in your language. Some
people fight, [music]
they don't last long. Others run, they
don't get far. [screaming]
Your father is nowhere to be seen. You
and your mother jump out of the wagon,
but there's nowhere to run. The land is
flat and treeless. You're grabbed from
behind before you even know which
direction to flee. You kick. It does
nothing. You see your mother. She's
screaming your name, pushing toward you.
Then she's pulled back by multiple men.
That's the last time you ever see her.
They don't hurt you. That's important.
Children are valuable. Your wrists are
tied. So are the other children. Some
are crying. Some are silent. You learn
very quickly which one hurts less.
You march for hours. No wagons, no
fires, no time to stop, just walking.
That night, you're fed just enough to
keep moving. When you see a bug, you
grab it quickly and shove it in your
mouth before anyone sees. You swear
you'll stay alive, [music] and one day
you'll get revenge. The men talk around
the fire, different accents, different
words. You catch a few familiar words,
maybe a dialect close to yours. You
don't understand what they're saying,
but you understand the tone. They're
negotiating.
Over the next few days, the group gets
smaller. Some of the kids disappear at
night. Others get added. You don't know
where you're going. You only know you're
moving south toward the coast.
Eventually, you smell the sea. You've
never smelled anything like it before.
Salt, rot, something metallic.
That's when you see the ship. It was
your first time seeing a structure that
big. But this isn't the time for
sightseeing. You're pushed down into the
hull. Chains clink. Wood caks. The light
disappears.
Everyone sits in complete darkness.
Above you, men pull the oars. You can
hear them grunting, shouting, counting
the rhythm. Below you, you sit in the
dark. And just like that, your nomadic
life on the plains of Syia is over.
You're not sure how many nights go by.
No stars, no way to tell time. The ship
moves constantly, rocking back and
forth. It almost reminds you of your
tiny wagon back on the planes. Almost.
Cold water sloshes across the floor. Not
enough to drown, just enough to soak
your feet. Nothing ever dries.
Every now and then, someone near you
gets seasick. And when that happens,
well, it stays down here with all of
you. So do the buckets meant to be used
as toilets. They're supposed to be
emptied. They aren't. They overflow.
Food comes down every few days. Hard
bread is tossed in your direction. You
grab it quickly, not because you're
hungry, but because if you don't,
someone else will. You get one sip. The
water tastes like rusty metal. The smell
becomes everything. After a while, you
don't even notice it anymore.
Sometimes, someone above opens a hatch.
Light spills in, blinding and brief.
Something or someone is carried out. You
tell yourself they must be badly hurt.
They're never brought back. The ship
slams into the dock. Voices shout from
above. Light pours into the hole for the
first time in days, and it burns your
eyes. Someone yanks you upright. Your
legs don't work right anymore. They
shake. You stumble. You're dragged up
onto the deck. The air smells different
here. Not grass, not animals.
Oil, fish, smoke. Too many people packed
too close together. You hear shouting
everywhere. Fast, sharp words you don't
understand.
>> This isn't the planes. This is a port.
You're herded off the ship with the
others. Some kids are older than you,
some younger. All of you look the same
now. Dirty, thin, quiet. Anyone who
cried on the ship already learned not
to. Men wait at the dock. Not soldiers,
not raiders. These men wear clean
clothes, sandals, cloaks, gold rings
around their fingers. They almost look
kind, except they're smiling. That's
worse.
You're marched through narrow streets,
stone everywhere, walls too close.
People stare at you like you're
something strange or useful. You don't
know which yet. Eventually, you're
brought to an open square. It's loud,
crowded, and full of people pretending
not to stare.
This is the market. Not for food, for
you. Stripped down. No explanation. Just
hands pulling, cutting away whatever
you're wearing. Cold air hits your skin.
You try to cover yourself. Someone slaps
your hands away. Your eyes start to
water.
You're lined up shoulderto-shoulder. A
man walks down the line slowly. He lifts
chins. turn faces side to side, presses
fingers into arms and legs, checking,
judging.
You realize something terrible very
quickly. They're calculating value.
A hand tilts your face toward the light.
Someone squints. He studies you. Another
voice says something you finally
understand.
Pretty.
A man in a white robe steps forward.
He's older, clean shaven. He inspects
you with the same cold assessment as the
others, but his touch is gentler.
Numbers are shouted, hands raise, people
nod, coins clink.
You don't understand how bidding works,
but you understand when it's over. The
same man grabs your arm and wraps you in
a robe. You're pulled out of the line.
The rest fade into the background.
For a second, you wonder if that's good.
Your new master leads you through the
streets of Athens. The city is loud.
Merchants shouting, children laughing,
philosophers debating in the shade. He
hands you a sweet roll. You've never
seen bread without green chunks in it.
You devour it, and for a moment, you
forget everything else that's happened.
The house you're taken to is large.
Marble floors, painted walls, a
courtyard with water trickling gently in
the center. You've never seen anything
like it. You've also never felt smaller.
The master hands you off to the
headservant at the doorway and walks
away. An older Greek man stands waiting.
He barely looks at you. Then he sigh.
[sighs]
Filthy barbarian. He says you'll be
bathed, fed, dressed. He pauses.
And trained. That night they scrub you
until your skin is raw, oil water, your
hair is cut, your nails trimmed. They
dress you in a soft tunic. Too soft. You
barely recognize yourself when you catch
your reflection in polished bronze.
You don't look like a nomad anymore. You
don't look like yourself. You look
valuable. The next morning, the
headservant leads you to the master's
chambers. The master finally speaks to
you. His name is Alexander, a citizen, a
philosopher, a man who throws lavish
parties for other men just like him. He
tells you that you're lucky. Lucky to be
in his house, lucky to serve a man of
culture and learning. You won't be
trained for the fields, he explains, but
for something higher. You'll learn Greek
music, how to pour wine without spilling
a single drop.
You are not like the others, he says,
resting a hand on your shoulder.
You have potential.
You nod. He smiles.
It's the smile of a man who's just
bought a very expensive vase.
Training starts the next day. Another
servant is assigned to you. He's
Persian, mid-aged, and tired in a way
that sleep doesn't fix. His back is
slightly bent. His hands move
automatically like they've done this a
thousand times already.
He shows you the ropes. How to stand,
how to bow, how to pour wine without
letting the jug touch the cup, how to
smile when spoken to, and how to
disappear when you're not needed. He
corrects you without anger. Just habit.
Never speak unless asked, he says. Never
look them in the eye and never ever say
no.
You ask him why. His lifeless eyes look
at you for a long moment. Then he turns
away. You learn.
Days pass as you learn Greek faster than
you thought possible. Not because you
want to, but because survival depends on
it. You learn their words, their
customs, their gods.
Then one day, he's gone. No warning, no
explanation. His mat is empty. His cup
is gone. You don't ask where he went. In
this house, questions are dangerous.
He had become something like an older
brother to you, kinder than the
headservant, less eager to remind you
that you were a barbarian, that you were
not Greek.
One night, the headservant tells you,
"It's time.
Bathe yourself, he says.
I'll return to retrieve you. He turns
away. He doesn't look back when he
speaks.
Listen carefully, he says.
In this house, you survive by being
quiet and by being useful.
He pauses.
Serve him well and don't make a fuss.
The door closes.
The headservant returns. You follow him
through the house. Your feet make no
sound on the marble. You pass rooms
you're not meant to enter. Doors that
stay closed.
He stops outside a set of doors, places
a hand on your shoulder, and walks away.
You open the doors and walk in. Your
master is inside, seated, relaxed. He
looks up when you enter. A smile reaches
his face.
Come closer, he says. You do.
You've been trained well, he says. You
nod.
You'll stay here tonight, he continues.
You'll attend my gatherings from now on.
You belong to my quarters.
You smile and nod. You remember the
instructions and you obey.
After you realize the worst part, it
didn't happen all at once. It happened
piece by piece.
A little less you every time.
When it's over, Alexander rises [music]
as if nothing happened. He leaves you
where you are. Servants [music] bring
you a plate full of sweet rolls. Your
stomach turns. You let them [music] go
cold.
Nothing appears broken, but you are no
longer who you [music] were when you
entered. You don't return to the
servants quarters that night. Your
[music] place has changed. Where you
sleep, where you stand, how others look
at you. The next morning, the older
servant won't [music] meet your eyes.
Because you are no longer just a
servant. You have the master's ear.
[music] You'll soon find out who has the
other one.
Time goes by. You're a young man now.
[music] You've grown taller and you're
still beautiful. At least that's what
they tell you.
Music, pouring wine, singing when asked.
You know how to stand, how to smile, how
[music] to disappear.
You believe your place is safe.
Then one day, Alexander brings someone
home, a boy. He's Persian, much younger
than you, holding a sweet roll in both
hands like it might vanish.
Alexander introduces him to the
household with the same gentle smile he
once gave you.
This is Darius, he says. He will be
trained as well.
Your stomach twists because you
recognize the look. It's the same way
Alexander used to look at you.
You try to be kind to him. You teach him
Greek, show him how to pour wine, how to
stand, how to smile. You don't tell him
what comes next.
One night after a particularly long
gathering, Alexander calls you to his
private chamber.
You've served me well, he says. Better
than I expected.
You nod, unsure where this is going.
I've been thinking, he continues.
[music]
When you reach your 20th year, I will
free you.
Your heart stops.
You may stay here, he adds, not as a
servant but as a companion.
He pauses, as a friend. The years that
follow are the best of your life.
[music]
You're still a servant technically, but
the promise of freedom changes
everything.
You're allowed to read scrolls to study
philosophy. You walk through the city
with a little more dignity. Alexander
stops visiting your quarters until one
day he invites you to host a private
family gathering. Normally you entertain
philosophers, men with similar tastes.
This time is different.
Alexander meets you in the courtyard. He
looks pleased. Then you notice it. A
faint tension in his posture, almost
nervous. That's new.
Do they? He says, "You will help receive
my family."
The word family hits you hard. You don't
react.
For a moment, you smell the planes
again. Grass, dung, smoke, horse sweat,
and then it's gone. The gate opens. A
woman steps through first. Greek,
well-dressed, not beautiful, but
composed.
She moves like someone who's never had
to learn where she belongs.
My wife, Alexander says. She inclines
her head toward you. Polite. Her eyes
don't linger. They don't need to. Behind
her comes their daughter, 18. Her gaze
is sharper than her mother's. She
notices you noticing her. Then she looks
away.
Last comes the boy, [laughter]
8 years old. He runs ahead without
permission, laughing, dragging a wooden
toy across the stone. Alexander smiles
at him. It's a smile you've never seen
directed at you.
Father, the daughter says, touching his
arm. You step back instinctively and
become a shadow. You pour wine, serve
food, stand exactly where you're told.
Who is he? The boy asks, pointing at
you. Alexander answers without
hesitation.
A member of the household.
Nothing more.
The wife thanks you. [sighs and gasps]
Her voice is calm. The days after their
arrival, the house settles into a new
routine. You're still needed, but not
where you were before. You stand farther
from Alexander now. It's the daughter
who breaks the pattern.
One afternoon, you're [music] adjusting
a lamp in the courtyard when she stops
nearby.
You eat? She asks.
You freeze for half a breath. Then nod.
She glances toward the house to make
sure no one is listening. Greek? She
asks. You nod again. That seems to
surprise her.
My tutor says, "I ask too many
questions." She says, "He says
philosophy isn't meant for women." You
answer carefully. A line from a
legendary Greek poet. She listens. Not
like a guest, not like her father, like
someone actually interested in you.
After that happens, it happens again and
again. Short exchanges, quiet ones,
always in [music] passing, never
lingering.
She asks about the city, about the men
who argue for hours on virtue, love, and
the roles of dominant and submissive.
You let her know your thoughts and
ideas, [music]
but never enough to invite trouble.
One day, she says something that
surprises you.
I envy you.
You laugh. The first time in years.
You've heard the debates, she continues.
You've walked places I'm never allowed
to enter. She pauses and looks down.
I'll be married by winter. She says it
like a fact, like there's no other
option. [music] You don't respond.
Silence feels safer.
From then on, there's an understanding.
She never speaks to you in front of
others and you never initiate the
conversations. After all, you were
trained not to.
Sometimes she leaves a scroll open on
the bench, notes for you [music] near
the edge.
You'll answer in small letters.
For the first time in years, someone
sees you as more than a roll. [music]
This feeling feels
>> good.
One morning, you notice what's missing
before anyone tells you. Her bench in
the courtyard is empty. No scroll, no
letters, just clean stone. At breakfast,
her place is gone. Not moved, removed.
The table looks smaller without her. No
one announces anything. No farewells, no
explanations.
You hear it later from a servant who
doesn't realize you're listening. She
left before sunrise. Married [music]
well far from the city. That's all. You
wait [music] for a message. You hope to
see her appear in the hallways.
Something, anything.
Nothing comes. [music]
That afternoon, the master sends for
you. Not to his chambers, but to the
study room. He doesn't sit when you
enter. He remains standing, hands folded
behind his back. "You've served the
household well," he says. "Circumstances
have changed."
He doesn't mention the promise. He
doesn't need to. With my family now
settled, certain arrangements are no
longer appropriate.
"You'll be placed elsewhere," he says.
A respectable household, suitable work.
He meets your eyes for the first time in
days.
This is for the best.
You nod. That's what you've been trained
to do. That night, you were moved back
into the servants quarters. The next
morning, someone [music] else pours the
wine. You recognize his hands. Younger,
still hopeful.
He stands where you once [music] stood.
He smiles the way you used to smile. No
one introduces him. They never did with
you either. As you leave the courtyard
for the last time, you glance once
[music] toward the bench. It's still
empty, clean, as if nothing ever
happened there [music] at all.
Time keeps moving. It always does. The
new house is smaller. [music]
You're still useful, still trained,
still careful, but no one looks at you
the way they once [music] did. Your face
starts to look older. Your voice
deepens. [music] The softness fades, and
people notice.
One day, you notice something familiar.
A new servant arrives. Young, foreign,
standing too straight, trying too hard
not to be noticed.
You recognize the posture immediately.
You wore it once. You're asked to show
him the rules. How to stand, where to
look, when to speak. You teach him the
same things that were taught to you. Not
because you want to, because this is how
survival works.
He asks you one question.
Does it get easy?
You don't answer. There's no instruction
for that. You are moved again and again.
No one ever strikes you. No one ever
raises their voices. They don't have to.
You were good at what you did. One
afternoon, you catch your reflection in
a bowl of water. Older now, ordinary,
unremarkable.
You think of the courtyard, the bench,
the little notes written near the edge.
You wonder if she ever thinks of them.
Then you stop because that [music] life
was never yours to remember.
You live long enough to be forgotten.
That's the final mercy. And somewhere in
the city, Alexander's son grows up. He
inherits the name, the house, the
future. Someone else pours the wine now.
Someone else stands where you once
stood. someone else believes just for a
while that their position is [music]
safe. And if anyone else tells your
story, it won't sound [music] tragic.
They'll say you did well for a
barbarian. Because history doesn't
record what happens to people like you,
only that you were useful until you
weren't. If you think this was bad,
there are others who had it worse. Their
story is next.

subtitles.plaintext:
You're born in the slums of London, the
1800s to be exact. Not to wealth, not
even to warmth. Your crib, a coal crate,
a gift from your father before he died
in a coal factory. You arrive in a
single room flat that smells like coal
smoke and boiled cabbage wedged between
six other children. Half of them die
before age 8. Work accidents, disease,
starvation. Your mother's a widow, which
is already a disaster in Victorian
England. She works three jobs. A lawn
dress by day, a factory hand by night,
and a third you're not supposed to know
about. The bills have to be paid
somehow. Your father was a coal miner.
He died along with two of your brothers
in a mining accident. It was
unfortunate. They were buried in a mass
grave because your family couldn't
afford private burials. You grow up
believing two things. Hunger never
sleeps, and work never feeds you enough.
Breakfast is yesterday's moldy bread.
Your mother leaves before dawn to work.
Your grandmother stays behind to watch
the younger ones. It's almost as if
people have kids just to work. Some
life, right? The bathroom is outside. No
running water, no plumbing. By 5, you're
running errands for pennies to help feed
your family. By 6, you're helping care
for your baby brothers while your mom
works. Your mother works at the wash
house. Her hands are always red and
cracked from the chemicals. One night,
you overhear her arguing with your
grandmother about a man who cuts up
women in the East End. They say the
night isn't safe for certain people. You
wonder if your mom is one of them. Your
mother leaves anyway. By 7, you can tell
which men are safe by how fast they look
away. The streets are crowded. Drunks,
beggars, men standing with nowhere to
go. Some are dangerous, some are
desperate. You learn to tell the
difference fast. The air stinks of soot
and sweat. The gutters run black from
the black coal soot that fills the air
like a heavy black cloud. The streets
teach you faster than any school ever
could. Not that you could afford school
anyway. Lesson one, don't talk to
strangers. Lesson two, don't trust the
police. Lesson three, don't stare at the
upper class. Sometimes between the noise
and the smoke, you dream small,
>> a full meal,
>> a new pair of shoes, maybe a dress
without stains. Maybe one day, one
afternoon, you find a silver button in
the gutter, dull, bent, worthless. You
still keep it, hidden under your pillow.
It's the only thing in the world that's
truly yours.
When the rent comes due and the coins
don't, the landlord pounds the door
until the walls shake. You know the rent
is due, he says with a smirk. Your
mother offers him jin and a smile that
doesn't reach her eyes. You don't
understand the trade yet, but you
understand shame. You're 13 now. Life is
harder. Your grandmother's gone, and now
you watch the younger kids. You starve
every other day so your brothers can
eat. Your mother says the workhouse is
the last resort, but she knows what
happens to kids there. That's why your
brothers aren't there anymore. One day,
she says she's found you a job, proper
work, decent pay, meals every day. She
says you'll be safer where you're going
with tears in her eyes. You believe her
because you have to. You tell her it
will be okay. You're not sure why she
cries. To you, it's just another job.
That night, a woman arrives with a
carriage. Your mother hugs you so hard
it hurts. They exchange quiet words and
the sound of coins. You climb into the
cart. You don't know it yet, but you've
just been sold. Your childhood ends
here. You arrive at her house in White
Chapel. Big for the street, small for
hope. A red lamp glows in the window.
Beds too close together. sheets that
never dry. She calls herself Aunt
Maggie. You're her little helper now.
She gives you three rules. Be nice to
gentlemen. Don't cry where they can see.
Always smile. Easy, right? The next day,
training starts. Cold water, powder,
rouge on your cheeks, curtsy, poor jin.
Laugh. When they laugh, they call it
work. You call it pretending. Years go
by and Aunt Maggie says it's time for
your first real client. He paid extra
because you're new. You go into a room
you've cleaned a hundred times, but this
time you're not the one cleaning it. The
man smells of alcohol and opium smoke.
He insists you try the pipe. Says it
will calm you. You decline.
>> He insists again. You give in. The room
blurs. It's your first time. It feels
strange. Wrong and almost gentle. He
touches your cheek. Soft, he says, then
laughs. Says you remind him of his
daughter. That's supposed to be
comforting. It isn't. After he leaves,
you throw up in a bucket. He left extra
coins on the table. Aunt Maggie smiles
and calls you her big helper now.
Congratulations,
you're employed.
Nights blur. Gas lamps hiss. Opium smoke
thickens the rooms. Men come and go. You
stop counting them. You keep your silver
button hidden in a drawer. It's the only
thing that's still yours. One girl
disappears. They say she ran off.
Another is found in an alley, throat
cut. Nobody talks about it. Everyone
keeps working. By 18, you're considered
experienced. That's Victorian for broken
but useful. The doctor visits once a
month with leeches and judgment. He
calls you little lady. You call him
nothing. Then one night, something
strange happens. A man asks to see you
twice, not for what the others pay for,
just to talk. He's a dock worker, hands
like rope, eyes tied from honest work.
He brings you tea instead of jin. He
says his name is Samuel. You don't
believe him, but you don't question it.
For once, you talk about yourself, not
the house, not the clients, the girl you
used to be. You tell him about your
mother, your brothers, your father's
coal mine. You even tell him about the
silver button you found when you were
small. He smiles. Keep it close, he
says. That's luck, that is. You laugh.
The first time in years. Weeks pass. He
keeps coming back. Always tea, sometimes
soup. He says he's saving enough to buy
a cottage outside the city. A little
room, a garden, a door that locks from
the inside. Then one night he asks you
to come with him. You stare at him like
he's mad. And then you say yes. You both
start saving every extra shilling, every
tip, every coin you can hide from Aunt
Maggie. He promises he'll meet you by
the river when he's ready. You give him
your silver button to keep so you'll
know I mean it. You say for the first
time, you let yourself believe in
something better.
The night comes. The fog's thick, heavy,
almost alive. You wait by the river with
your small bag of coins. You wait an
hour, then two, then until dawn. He
doesn't come. You ask around the docks.
The men won't look you in the eye. Then
you see the crowd by the pier. Police
kneel beside a shape on the
cobblestones.
A body rope burned hands. A bloodied
shirt. It's Samuel. They say he was
mugged for his wages. The police pry
open his cold hand. And there it is.
Your silver button still shining under
the soot. You take it back. You don't
cry. You just close your fist around it
until it cuts your palm. The city hums
around you like nothing happened. You
walk home in silence. You don't dream
anymore. You go back to Aunt Maggie's.
She doesn't ask where you were. You
don't tell her. The next morning, she's
shouting again, and the men are lined up
like nothing happened. Life doesn't stop
here. It just repeats. Weeks pass. The
city feels colder now. The rooms smell
more like sickness than sin. You start
drinking what the men drink. The pipe
helps, too. It helps blur the faces.
Aunt Maggie coughs blood into her
handkerchief one morning. She says it's
just the weather. It isn't. By winter,
she's gone. No funeral, no notice, just
another empty chair by the fire. The
house changes hands. The new madam
doesn't know your name. She calls
everyone girl. Rent goes up, wages go
down. They sell the furniture, then the
drapes, then the girls. You keep working
because what else is there? The police
raid again. You run out the back door
barefoot. The fog swallows you whole.
You keep running until the house is just
another light in the smoke. And just
like that, you're on your own. You rent
a room above a gin shop in
Spittlefields. No roof worth the name,
no lock that works. You still go out at
night. The streets are your new house
now. You work corners near the river.
The same river that took Samuel.
Sometimes you think you see him in the
fog. But it's just another man, another
bargain. You have money now, but your
body starts to fail you. You catch
something maybe from the pipe, maybe
from a man, maybe from London itself.
The doctor calls it a women's disease.
He tells you to drink mercury. You do
what he says. Your hair falls out. Your
teeth ache. You spend your nights
coughing more than talking. The men stop
coming and so does the money. You sell
your shoes for bread. You porn your
dress for jin. You keep one thing, the
silver button. You hold it when you're
cold. You hold it when you can't
breathe. You hold it when you remember
what it felt like to be somebody's
daughter. One night, you sit by the
river again. Same spot, same fog. You
look down at the water and it looks
back. You think about your mother, your
brothers, the room with the coal smoke.
You think about Samuel's hands. You
think about the button and how small it
really is.
By morning, the sun rises over an empty
bank. A passer by finds a woman slumped
against the wall. Cold. Still in her
hand, a silver button, polished, clean,
beautiful. No name, no family, just
another girl the city forgot.
[Music]

text:
Why it sucks to be born a Biblical woman (In Ancient Israel)
Think your life sucks? Try being a woman in ancient Israel. From betrayal to survival, discover the brutal reality of what these women endured behind closed doors  and why their stories were never meant to be told.

#history #biblical #ancientisrael

subtitles.plaintext:
Warning. Viewer discretion is advised.
>> You're born around 1,200 B.CE in the
rocky hills of ancient Israel. Not a
son, a daughter, which means another
mouth to feed when the bread already
runs thin. Your hut leaks when it rains
and bakes when it doesn't. Breakfast is
moldy barley bread so coarse it cuts
your gums. Your father works a patch of
rocky ground that yields less grain each
year. Your mother counts lentils while
your baby brother cries from hunger. By
12, your body changes and your future
changes with it. In this world, that
means you're a woman. It also means
you've become a calculation.
The rains have failed, the goats are
thin, and your father keeps staring at
you like you're both his child and his
last grain measure. He knows the law.
Everyone does. A father can sell a
daughter into service when the family is
drowning. They quote scripture to make
it feel clean. It doesn't feel clean.
One morning, your father doesn't meet
your eyes. A wealthy landowner has made
an offer. Not for a servant, not for a
wife, for a concubine.
Coins clink on the table. Your mother
weeps. Your father's boughs so low he
could lick the dirt. You climb into an
ox cart with a scratchy blanket and
moldy bread for the ride. You're not
sure what's going on, but you never see
your family again.
Your childhood ends here. The ox cart
rattles for hours over stone hills and
dust roads. You pass vineyards clinging
to terraces, olive groves heavy with
dust, shepherd boys whistling to their
flocks.
The smell of pressed olives and goat
dung drifts from roadside villages. You
travel for two days till you reach
Jerusalem.
By evening, you're carried to a city of
stone walls and sprawling estates.
Storehouses bulge with grain. Olive
presses stain the courtyards.
Servants hurry past without looking at
you. But the wife looks. She stares at
you. She doesn't blink. Then she walks
away.
You're given a bed in a side room, a
dress that isn't new, and a list of
rules. Speak softly. Eat what you're
given. Do not contradict the wife. And
remember why you're here, sons. Not a
wife, but above a slave, something in
between. Your first days blur into
routine. Grinding grain until your
shoulders ache. Carrying wellwater jars
that bite into your hands. folding
cloaks and stacking oil jars while the
steward checks every item. Your birthday
comes by. You're 13 now, but no one
notices except for the master. He gives
you a sly smile and walks away. The wife
notices, her face blank. She walks away
as well. At Sabbath, you stand behind
the wife as she blesses the bread. Her
hands on top, yours below. The message
is clear. She is first. You are not.
Servants don't speak to you unless
ordered. The wife speaks only to correct
you. The master barely speaks at all.
That first night comes sooner than you
expect. The servants don't explain much.
They just light oil lamps and drape the
master's chamber with heavy curtains
that smell of smoke and goat farts. The
wife pretends not to notice, but she
lingers long enough to remind everyone
who's still in charge. Then she leaves
you standing there like a servant who's
been dismissed.
The master doesn't waste time. There are
no vows, no blessings, no sweet talk.
You're standing there with a thin robe,
shaking. The master touches your face.
He smiles. Your heart beats fast, but
not for joy. You're about to faint just
standing there, but then you remember
the only instructions you got from the
older maid. Stay quiet. Don't embarrass
the household.
That's it. One moment you're a daughter,
the next you're property.
Congratulations.
You're officially a concubine now.
After it's over, you lie in bed shaking
and leaking. The older servants come to
comfort you, but it doesn't help. You
feel empty. A memory of you and your
younger brother comes to mind. It
comforts you a little. You remember your
mother's bread and bean soup. You fall
asleep. Days turn into weeks. One moon
bleeds late. The next doesn't come. The
steward's wife notices first. The house
shifts. The master increases your
portions. The wife lets you stand closer
behind her. Servants bow deeper.
You're not a person. You're a promise.
You hear that pregnancy is dangerous. It
can raise your status or it can kill
you. The labor drags through the night.
You scream into mats while incense
stings your eyes. Other women whisper
prayers outside the door. At dawn,
another cry joins yours.
A boy.
For a moment, you think you matter. You
don't. You're useful. and useful is
never safe.
Seasons pass. You learn how gossip
works. At the well, women lower their
voices when you walk past. In the
storooms, a servant hides a cracked jar
and blames you for it. Every mistake
belongs to the concubine.
Then, a new girl arrives on an ox cart
with the same blanket and wide eyes.
You're told to teach her the rules. You
see yourself in her face. You realize
you were never the solution. You were
just the season before hers. Not long
after, the wife grows heavy with a
child. A boy. The house erupts. Your son
kisses his halfb brother's forehead.
Everyone cheers. You force a smile, but
inside it feels like choking. No matter
what you do, you'll always be second.
The years blur. Your son grows strong in
the fields, quick with numbers, careful
with words. He is praised when he
succeeds, blamed through you when he
fails. The steward starts using him for
errands. The master nods at him in
approval. The wife smiles politely, but
never warmly. Her son's future is
written in law. Yours shrinks by the
season. The law says it's fair. The law
always favors the wife's son, never
yours. Then the master dies in his
sleep. The elders gather. Witnesses
crowd the courtyard. The inheritance is
read aloud. The wife's son takes the
lion's share. Your son takes the scraps.
A field at the edge. A fraction of the
flocks. The elers's words sound polite,
but to you they taste like ash. Your boy
lowers his eyes. The wife's son stands
tall, carried forward on pride. Everyone
sees the difference. No one questions
it. You keep your room smaller now. You
pour wine for guests who don't say your
name. You teach younger girls how to bow
without looking up. You fade into the
background. Time moves on without you.
New concubines arrive. Younger,
prettier, hungrier. You become the woman
people pass in the courtyard without
noticing. Your son becomes a man with
responsibilities but not authority. He
knows exactly where he stands. Everyone
does.
Sometimes you catch your reflection in a
polished bowl. The girl your father sold
is gone. What's left is someone with no
name. When you die, they'll say the
house was blessed with sons and full
storehouses.
They won't say your name. They never
did. That is why it sucks to be born a
concubine in ancient Israel. Not a wife
with honor, not a servant with escape,
just property. Useful until you're not.

subtitles.plaintext:
Level one, the runner. You're 13 years
old. You live in Fresno. It's deep Norte
territory. Red is everywhere. On the
corners, on the fences, on the backs of
jackets. The older guys post up outside
the liquor store on Belmont. They wear
red. They have cash. They have phones.
They have respect. Your family has
nothing. Your dad is gone. Your uncle
got deported. Your mom works nights at
the cannery. But those guys on the
corner, nobody messes with them. You
start showing up. You don't ask
questions. You just hang around. They
notice you. They call you little homie.
One day, someone hands you a phone.
Watch the block. Text a 14 if you see
black and whites. That's it. You make
nothing. But you're in the circle now.
You're useful. You're seen. That's
enough for now. Level two, the peewee.
You're 14. You've been watching corners
for 8 months. You know the schedules.
You know the faces. You know who's dirty
and who's not. One of the older guys
pulls you aside. His name is Puppet. He
says you're ready. You nod. You know
what comes next. You've heard about it.
Six members form a circle in the back of
someone's yard. You stand in the middle.
The count starts. One. A fist catches
your cheek. Two. A boot hits your ribs.
Four. You're down. Six. You taste
copper. You don't cry. You don't run.
You take every second. When it stops,
Puppet pulls you up. He puts a red rag
in your hand. You've got a name now.
They call you Huero. Or Downer. Or Lobo.
That name is yours forever. You're Norte
for life now. Level three. The soldier.
You're 16.
You wear red every day.
You rep 14. The number 14. N is the 14th
letter. That's Nuestra Familia.
That's your family now.
Your job is simple. You move product.
The Veteranos control a drug corridor
between two neighborhoods. You're the
middleman. Someone passes you a package
behind a dumpster off Tulare.
You walk it six blocks to a house with a
red door. You knock three times. You
hand it over. You leave. You get 300 a
week. That's more than your mom clears
in 4 days. You also put in work when the
clique needs muscle. Scraps from the
south have been pushing into the
neighborhood. That's disrespect. You and
four others roll on them. No questions.
You handle it. That's your job. You keep
your mouth shut after. Always. Level
four, the Veterano. You're 20. You've
been locked up once already. 11 months
in county for assault. The detective sat
across from you for 6 hours. You said
nothing. Not one word. You came home to
a party. Handshakes. Respect. You earned
your stripes. Now you're a Veterano. You
don't run packages anymore. Younger
soldiers handle that. They kick money up
to you. You take your cut. You pass the
rest up the chain. Your job is the
block. You control two streets near
Highway 99. You decide who sells. You
decide who gets taxed. You also
discipline the younger guys.
If a Pee-wee is running his mouth, you
correct him. Sometimes that's a talk.
Sometimes it's a beating. You make about
1,200 a week. You have a used Impala.
Red interior. You're building something.
Level five, the shot caller. You're 25.
You run a set now. 30 members answer to
you. You control an entire neighborhood.
The older guys inside promoted you. A
letter came through channels from
Pelican Bay.
You're the shot caller now. Your word is
final on the streets. The Veteranos
bring you their problems. Rival set
tagged over your mural on King's Canyon.
One of your soldiers got jumped at a bus
stop. A dealer is skimming. You make
decisions. You give orders. You also
collect tribute. Every set in your
territory kicks money up. You take your
percentage, then you pass the rest to
the regimental commander. You're
clearing 4,000 to 7,000 a week, but the
heat is constant. The gang task force
has photos of you. Your car gets
followed. You sleep different places
every few nights. You trust nobody
fully, not even your own blood. Level
six, the regimental commander. You're
28. You operate across multiple sets
now. Four shot callers report to you.
You coordinate drug distribution across
three zip codes. The supply comes
through connections tied back to
Sinaloa. Meth, mostly, some heroin. You
don't touch it. You manage the flow. You
set the prices. You make sure tribute
moves cleanly up the chain. You also
manage conflict. When two sets beef over
territory lines, you settle it. Your
decision stands. You also handle
external threats. Sureños have been
bleeding north out of Bakersfield.
Scraps pushing into Norte land. You
coordinate the response across all your
sets. You don't show up personally. You
send the order down. It gets handled.
You're making 15,000 a week. You have a
house in a quiet suburb. Your neighbors
think you flip properties. You haven't
been arrested in 4 years. You're
careful. You're strategic. You're
dangerous. Level seven, the regimental
general. You're inside now. Pelican Bay
State Prison, security housing unit. But
your power didn't shrink when those
doors closed. It grew. You run an entire
street regiment from your cell. Your
commanders on the outside answer
directly to you. Orders travel through
lawyers, through coded letters, through
visitors who memorize messages and carry
nothing written. When you say expand
into a new town, your commanders expand.
When you say a certain soldier is a
liability, that soldier disappears
within days. You report to the Nuestra
Familia generals above you. The Cat 3
members. The hierarchy inside Pelican
Bay is its own world. You control your
yard. You control the flow of drugs
inside the prison. Guards are on
payroll. Phones come in through
contraband networks. You run the economy
of your block. You're a general. A cage
doesn't change that. Level eight, the
Nuestra Familia. You are not just
Norteño anymore. You have been vetted,
tested, proven. You've taken an oath, a
blood oath. You are now a full member of
Nuestra Familia itself. This is
different from running with the Norte.
This is the organization behind the
organization. You are bound for life.
The penalty for death. There are no
exceptions. The generals above you
control regiments across all of Northern
California. Fresno, Sacramento, San
Jose, Salinas. You sit in a federal
institution now, Florence, Colorado.
They moved the top leadership there
after Operation Black Widow. 22
indictments, RICO charges, two members
facing death penalty for ordering
murders, but the organization kept
moving. It always keeps moving. Your
orders still travel. Your structure is
still intact. You're inside a cage
inside a cage and you still have power.
Level nine, the general. You are a
mythology now. You built regiments. You
shaped territories. You kept the Norte
structure alive through raids, through
takedowns, through betrayals. There is
one general left standing at the top in
Pelican Bay. Everything flows through
him. Every tribute, every order, every
execution, every expansion. He doesn't
exist on social media. He doesn't have a
public face. He is a name spoken
carefully. You don't reach this level.
Most soldiers never see beyond level
three. Most are dead or serving long
sentences before they get close. The
generals are the architecture. They are
the reason the Norteño survived every
federal operation that came for them.
Their orders travel from a concrete cell
in Crescent City or in Florence all the
way down to a 13-year-old on a corner in
Modesto. The chain never breaks. Level
10, the fall. You're 32.
You've been in for 17 years total, shot
twice, arrested five times. You've seen
partners killed. You've seen partners
flip. One of your own soldiers testified
in federal court. You never saw it
coming.
The RICO case took 2 years to build.
When they came, they came with
everything. Wiretaps, surveillance
footage, informants you trusted. The DA
offered you a deal. You said nothing.
You went to trial. The jury came back
guilty on six counts. The judge gave you
25 years, no parole.
You're in Corcoran now, but the set
didn't mourn long. Someone stepped into
your spot the same week you were
sentenced. Your replacement is 24 years
old. He's hungry. He's exactly what you
were at that age. The tribute still
moves. The orders still flow. Nothing
paused for you. Level 11, the end.
You're 35.
You've been inside for 3 years. You get
a letter from your sister. Your mom is
sick. You can't go see her.
You can't do anything except sit with
it.
You think about the day you first picked
up that phone on the corner in Fresno.
You were 13.
You thought you were joining something
real. You were.
It was real.
It just had one direction.
Forward and down.
There's no exit. Blood in.
Blood out.
You knew that at 14 and you know it at
35
The difference is now you feel the
weight of it.
You have 22 more years in this cell.
You think about the kids in your old
neighborhood right now, hanging around
the same corners, watching the same
older guys, learning the same lessons.
You were that kid once.
A new runner is standing on Belmont
Avenue in Fresno right now. He's 13. He
has a phone in his hand. He's watching
the block. He's waiting for someone to
call him something other than little
homie.
The cycle continues.

subtitles.plaintext:
Level one, Halcón. You stand on a corner
in Chilpancingo. You don't carry a gun,
you carry a phone. Your job is to watch.
A police truck rolls past. You text
three letters. That's it. That's your
whole job. You are a lookout. The older
men call you Halcón. Hawk. You see
everything. You report everything. You
earn maybe 200 pesos a day. That's less
than $12. You sleep at home if you're
lucky. Some nights you sleep on a
mattress in a safe house with four other
guys. You don't ask questions. You watch
the street and you keep your phone
charged. Nobody outside the group knows
your name. To the police, you're just a
teenager on a corner. To the group,
you're a small piece of a large machine.
But you're inside now. That matters. You
proved you can keep your mouth shut.
That's the first rule. It's the only
rule that really counts.
The training for this job takes two
weeks. Someone older shows you the
signals. Military checkpoints get one
pattern. Police vehicles get another.
Army convoys get a third. You learn the
surrounding streets. You learn which
routes are fast, which ones have
cameras, which ones have neighbors who
watch too much. You're given a phone
with a new number each month. You
memorize nothing. You destroy every
message after reading. A man comes by
once a week to check on you. He doesn't
say much. He watches how you're holding
the phone, how you're standing, whether
your eyes are focused. He's looking for
fear. Fear makes mistakes. Mistakes make
problems. You learn to keep your face
flat, neutral. The work is tedious.
Hours on the same corner, rain,
afternoon heat, night chill. You watch
vendors close their shops, mothers
picking up children from school, couples
walking home together. You watch and you
report and you tell yourself this is
temporary. This is the entry point.
Everyone starts here.
Level two, foot soldier. You're not
watching anymore. You're moving. You
carry packages from one house to
another. You don't know what's inside.
You don't ask. You go where they tell
you. You show up when they call. You
might drive someone somewhere. You might
stand outside a building for hours with
your hands in your pockets, a radio in
your jacket, waiting. The work is boring
until it isn't. One afternoon, a rival
crew rolls through your block, three men
on motorcycles. They slow down. They
look at you. You look back. Nothing
happens this time. But, you know what
that look means. You go home and you
don't sleep. You're earning real money
now, maybe a thousand pesos a week. You
send some to your mother. She doesn't
ask where it comes from. You don't tell
her.
The men above you are watching how you
move, how you handle pressure, how you
follow orders. You don't complain. You
show up. You wait. You do the job. This
level lasts between six months and two
years, depending on your speed and
reliability. You're being tested for
traits the organization needs. Can you
keep calm in a crisis? Can you follow
orders without question? Do you get
nervous when federales pass? Do you talk
too much when you drink? They send you
to handle deliveries in different
neighborhoods to see how you navigate
unfamiliar territory.
They watch whether you get lost or
confused. They observe how you interact
with business owners and other gang
members. Some foot soldiers never
advance further. Some plateau here and
stay useful at this level their entire
working life. Those are the steady ones,
the reliable ones, the ones who don't
want power and don't want to die. But,
if you show the right combination of
nerve and intelligence, you get noticed.
You get pulled aside. You get told
there's another opportunity. Level
three, enforcer. Someone didn't pay. A
shop owner in Iguala owes three months.
Your boss calls. Two other guys come
with you.
You walk into the store in the middle of
the afternoon. The owner sees your
faces. His hands start shaking. You
don't raise your voice. You don't have
to. You tell him he has 48 hours. You
walk out. Most of the time, that's
enough. Sometimes it isn't. When it
isn't, you come back and you make a
point. You don't like this part, you do
it anyway. You've been arrested once,
spent 2 weeks in a cell in Morelos. You
said nothing. You stared at the wall.
They released you. When you walked out,
someone was already waiting. An
envelope.
That was your reward for keeping quiet.
You understood then what loyalty means
inside the group. It means everything.
The enforcer's job isn't just about
collecting debts. You're also about
image, projection. You move through the
city in a way that makes people
understand the hierarchy. You wear
certain brands. You travel in certain
vehicles. You go to certain bars. You're
a walking message. This territory
belongs to someone. Those debts will be
collected. That line will not be
crossed. You learn to fight properly.
Not street fighting. Not the kind you
learned as a kid. Real fighting. Someone
takes you to a gym outside the city
where off-duty soldiers train fighters.
You learn combinations, pressure points.
You learn how to hurt someone without
leaving marks that police photographers
can document. You also learn to use
tools. A baseball bat wrapped in
electrical tape. A length of pipe. You
learn how much force different jobs
require. Sometimes bruises are the
point. Sometimes you need actual damage.
Broken bones tell a story. Broken bones
stay broken for months. Every time the
owner of that shop moves his arm, he
thinks about you. He thinks about what
happens if he doesn't pay next time.
That's efficiency. That's the machine
working.
Level four. Plaza operator. You run a
block now. Maybe three. In Tetecala or
Jojutla or one of the smaller towns
outside the city.
You control who moves product through
your streets. You collect the weekly
payments from the businesses in your
area. You manage seven men below you.
You're the one they call at midnight
when something goes wrong. A soldier got
stopped at a checkpoint. Someone's
talking too much in a bar. You handle
it. You're on the phone constantly. Two
phones. One for the business, one for
family. You never use the wrong one.
Your name starts appearing on lists
inside the state attorney's office. You
know this because you pay someone inside
to tell you. That's part of the job now.
You build relationships. You stay
useful. You send money up the chain
every week. Every peso accounted for.
You keep a small cut. Nobody questions
it as long as the numbers are right.
You're not visible from the outside.
That's by design.
You stay small. You stay quiet. You keep
the machine running.
Your territory generates steady income,
extortion from businesses, tax on
product moving through, money laundering
operations disguised as legitimate
commerce. You open relationships with
local officials, a municipal police
commander, a judge's assistant, someone
in the tax office who can make paperwork
disappear. These relationships cost
money, but they're investments. They're
insurance. When a federal operation
comes close, you know hours in advance.
You get word that a certain neighborhood
is being watched. You move your
operations. You rotate your schedule.
You change which safe houses you use.
You're learning that this level of the
organization is about information flow
as much as it is about controlling
territory. You're learning that money
and information are almost the same
thing. Money buys information.
Information protects your money. The
balance between those two keeps you
alive. Level five. Regional commander.
You're sitting in a room with 12 men.
All of them answer to you. One of them
is a municipal police officer. Another
runs a construction company that moves
cash through payroll. You've been
operating in Guerrero for six years. You
know every road through the mountains.
You know which federales are bought and
which aren't. You control supply routes
through the Sierra. The terrain works
for you. No federal convoy reaches those
hills without you knowing hours in
advance. Your reach covers four
municipalities, Guerrero, Morelos, parts
of Puebla. You report to one man above
you, a name most people have never
heard. You send him his percentage. He
leaves you alone to work.
Three times this past year, rival groups
tried your territory. Los Ardillos
pushed from the south. Guerreros Unidos
tested a road near Tixtla. You pushed
back. Hard. You don't lose ground. You
can't.
Losing ground means losing men. Losing
men means losing the confidence of the
man above you.
That's the one thing you cannot afford.
You have a phone with over 11,000 voice
messages stored on it. Names of
officials, meeting times, payment
records. You never let that phone leave
your sight. The authorities know your
alias. They don't know your face. Not
yet.
You rotate between three different
houses on different days. You never
sleep in the same place two nights in a
row. You have a family in a town two
hours north. You see them once a month.
Your kids don't know what you do. Your
wife stopped asking years ago.
One morning a man you trust calls with
news. A federal operation swept into
Chilpancingo overnight. 12 arrests.
Three of them are your people. You don't
panic. You move. You call your contact
inside the state government. You burn
two phones. You're in a truck heading
toward the mountains before noon.
The Sierra closes around you. You
disappear into the terrain like you were
never there.
The federal rally set up checkpoints on
the highway. You're already past them.
You eat cold food in a safe house with
no windows and you wait. You make calls.
You assess the damage.
Three weeks later you're back in
position. Your territory is still yours.
The men still answer to you. But the
operation cost you. Two safe routes are
gone. A storage point near Amacuzac is
finished. You start rebuilding piece by
piece. New routes, new contacts. You
replace what was lost and you keep
moving. You never stop moving.

Level one, the recruit. You don't get a
gun, you get a mop. You show up before
sunrise.
The older men are still asleep.
You clean around them.
You don't make noise. You don't make eye
contact. You wash cars. You run errands.
You carry bags. You are a ghost with
chores. The F E S doesn't know your name
yet. They know your face. That's enough
for now.
You sleep on a cot in the back room. You
share it with four other recruits.
You're hungry most nights. The food
comes last to you.
You don't complain. Complaining is
weakness. Weakness gets you removed. You
watch everything. You listen to every
conversation you're allowed near. You
study how the older men move, how they
speak, how they carry themselves. You
are learning. That is your only job. You
make no money. You cost money. Every
week you prove you're worth keeping
around. Some recruits don't last a
month. They get impatient. They ask for
too much too soon. You don't ask for
anything.
You just show up every single day.
The vetting happens slowly. They need to
know you won't talk. They need to know
you won't steal. They need to know you
won't panic when the police come. You
understand none of this is explicitly
tested. It's all observation. A man will
walk past you and drop an envelope with
10,000 euros on a table. He'll leave the
room. You'll stay at your mop. You won't
look at it. You won't touch it. Later
that day, the envelope is gone and no
one mentions it. This is the test. You
passed because you never acknowledged
its existence. Another recruit, a kid
who lasted 2 weeks, saw that envelope
and his eyes went wide. He was gone by
evening. They drove him to the edge of
the city and dropped him off with a
warning. He was lucky. He wasn't a
threat because he was stupid, not
because he was smart. The family doesn't
kill stupid recruits. Stupid recruits
just disappear into normal life and no
one cares.
But smart recruits who can't keep their
eyes still, those ones are dangerous.
You learn to look at nothing. You learn
to see everything. These are not
contradictory skills. You learn them
simultaneously. Your first 3 months, you
don't speak unless spoken to. Your
fourth month, someone asks you a
question and you answer in six words or
fewer.
By month six, you've graduated to full
sentences, but only in response to
direct questions.
You never volunteer information. You
never offer opinions.
You have become a tool. Tools don't have
opinions. Tools get used or they get put
away.
Level two, street soldier.
You have a territory now. It's small,
maybe two blocks, maybe a market square,
but it's yours to protect. Your job is
simple. You collect. A shop owner owes
the family 50 euros a week. You go to
the door. You knock. You smile. You
remind him. Most of them pay without a
word. Some of them test you.
You handle it. You don't escalate unless
you have to, but you know how.
You watch for rival crews moving into
your area. You report everything up the
chain. Your crew leader checks in twice
a week. He doesn't help. He inspects. If
your numbers are low, it's your fault.
You carry a phone. You never use it for
anything personal. You never say
anything direct over a call. You speak
in code. You learned the code. It took 3
weeks to memorize. You start earning.
Not much, but something.
You have a little cash for the first
time. You buy better shoes. You want to
buy a jacket. Your crew leader tells you
to wait. Don't look like money yet.
You're still too visible. The police
know your face by now. That's normal.
Every soldier gets flagged. You're on a
list somewhere. You accept that. This is
where men either grow or break. The
territory is yours to protect, which
means it's also yours to defend. You've
seen what happens when someone pushes. A
soldier two districts over didn't push
back hard enough when a rival crew moved
on his block. They found him in the
river three days later. The message was
sent and received. You are not that
soldier. You are quick, but measured.
You notice a new face in the market
asking about protection money before you
move. You report it immediately.
Your crew leader brings in two more men.
The rival crew's recruitment attempt
stops. No violence was necessary. You
kept your territory without bloodshed.
This is the kind of thinking that gets
noticed. You also learn which business
owners are informants.
The baker on 7th Street always tips
police when anything happens nearby.
You know this because you watch the
patterns. Two hours after a minor
incident, a police car appears. It
happens every time. You report this,
too.
The family decides what to do about it.
You learn not to care about the outcome.
Caring is a liability. You develop a
routine. Same streets, same times, same
people. Predictability keeps things
peaceful. Surprises create problems.
You're becoming reliable. Reliability is
the currency that matters at this level.
Level three, the Mick. Friend. That's
what the title means. It sounds soft. It
isn't. You are the bridge between the
street crews and the men above them.
You know everything happening on the
ground. You also know enough about the
top to be dangerous. That is why they
trust you carefully. You coordinate. A
crew in the northern district has a
problem with a supplier. You fix it. A
payment dispute between two soldiers
turns ugly. You sit them down. You
resolve it before it reaches the boss.
You keep the peace. Your job is to make
sure small fires never reach the bosses'
ears as large ones. You attend meetings
you don't speak at. You take notes in
your head.
You never write anything down. Your
apartment is clean. No cash at home. No
weapons at home. Nothing that connects
you to anything. You have a legitimate
job on paper, import and export. You
actually do some of the work, maybe 30%.
The rest is covered. The police have
looked at your business twice.
Both times, everything checked out. You
are careful. Careful is how you got
here.
Your name has never appeared in a
report, not once.
You intend to keep it that way.
The Mick role is about translation.
You speak the language of the street and
the language of power. Street soldiers
understand respect and territory. The
bosses understand logistics and money
and long-term sustainability.
You help each turn into the other's
framework. A soldier wants revenge
against another crew. You explain why
the boss would rather acquire their
territory through business than gunfire.
A boss wants to expand operations into a
new city.
You explain why the local soldiers might
resist and what incentives would change
their thinking.
You become essential by being the person
who understands everyone. This makes you
a threat if you ever become unreliable.
The previous Mick disappeared 4 years
ago. No one discusses what happened to
him. You've heard rumors. You don't ask
questions. You assume he made a mistake
and paid for it. You are determined not
to make that mistake. Your wife thinks
you work long hours in import and
export. She's not wrong. You also know
that the day you become compromised, her
knowledge of this life becomes dangerous
to her.
You have made arrangements with your
Krytar. Certain men know certain things
about her location, her routines, her
safety. These men understand that any
harm to her would mean reprisals against
them personally.
This is how you protect her without
telling her. Love and the organization
exist in different spaces. You've
learned to keep them separate.
Level four, Krytar, underboss.
You run a region. It covers four cities.
Hundreds of men answer to you, but not
directly. You never meet most of them.
You don't want to.
Distance is protection. You communicate
through the mic beneath you. You receive
reports. You make decisions.
A major shipment is coming through the
port at Durrës.
You approve the route. You approve the
drivers. You approve the cut going to
the dock workers. Everything passes
through your hands without touching
them. You sit in a restaurant you own
legally. You drink coffee. You read the
financial reports your accountant brings
you.
Your accountant believes he works for a
logistics company. He is partially
right. A rival family in the south has
been pushing into your territory. You
don't react fast. Fast reactions make
mistakes. You watch them for 2 weeks.
You learn their pattern. Then you send
three men to buy the building where they
operate. You don't threaten anyone. You
buy their landlord. You raise their
rent. You make their operation
uncomfortable in ways they can't trace
back to you. They move. You expand into
what they left. You gain territory
without a single phone call anyone could
record. You are never in the same
location twice in 1 week. Your driver
changes every month. Your phones change
every 2 weeks. You have four right now.
You know which is which without looking.
That stopped being something you had to
think about years ago. It just became
automatic. The Kryetar position is where
you stop being a man and become an
institution. You have a title now that
means you're accountable for entire
regions.
When a shipment fails to arrive at its
destination, your head is on the line.
When a police investigation gets too
close to your operations, your decisions
determine whether men go to prison.
You've already had two men arrested in
your region. They took the fall quietly,
as expected. They'll serve 4 years and
come out to find their families taken
care of. This is the contract. It's
unspoken, but absolute. You've learned
to think in terms of scenarios.
What if the Dutch family decides to move
their operations into your territory?
What if the police finally flip one of
your mics? What if a soldier gets
ambitious? For each scenario, you have a
contingency. Some contingencies are
business solutions. Some are more
permanent. You don't make the permanent
decisions lightly, but you make them
when necessary. You've authorized three
such decisions in your tenure. All three
proved correct. All three prevented
larger problems. You've also stopped
three operations that you were pressured
to authorize, and they would have been
mistakes.
This balance is why the boss keeps you
where you are.
You think beyond the immediate
situation. You think about consequences.
Level five. The cry. The boss. You are
the FIs. You are the family. You don't
run the streets. You don't count the
money. You don't make the calls. You
make the decisions that make all of that
possible.
You sit at the head of a table. 12 men
sit below you. They stand when you
enter.
They don't sit until you do.
You look at each of them, and you
already know everything about their
week. Your consigliere reports to you
through channels you designed yourself.
You have known these men for 20 years.
Some of them since childhood. You still
don't fully trust any of them. That is
not cruelty. That is the reason you're
still alive.
Your family controls cocaine
distribution across three countries. You
have agreements with the cartel in
Ecuador. You have people in Rotterdam,
in London, in Naples. None of them know
your name.
They know a phone number. They know a
code word. They know a bank account in
Cyprus. That is enough.
The police in four countries have files
on you. Thick ones. They have never
touched you.
There are too many layers between you
and anything provable. You live in a
house with walls that cost more than
most men earn in a decade. Cameras cover
every angle of the property. Two men are
outside your door right now. They'll be
there when you fall asleep. They'll be
there when you wake up. You haven't
walked into a grocery store in 11 years.
You haven't taken a commercial flight in
eight. Every movement is planned a week
in advance. Every route is checked.
Every room is swept before you enter it.
You have everything a man could want.
You also have no freedom. You knew this
was the arrangement. You accepted it a
long time ago. There is no retirement
for a man in your position. No quiet
farm somewhere. No peace at the end. The
throne doesn't empty until the man
sitting on it is gone.
You understood that before you ever took
the seat.
