subtitles.plaintext:
You hatch in the dirt already glowing,
and the first thing your light does is
give you away. You are 3 days old. You
are smaller than a grain of rice,
and you are already hunting. Something
soft moves in the dark beside you, a
snail, many times your size, and you
don't hesitate because you were never
built to. You climb onto it, sink your
jaws in, and inject the fluid that turns
it soft and still from the inside. Then
you drink what's left of it while it can
still feel you doing it. This is what
you are. Not a spark of magic drifting
over a summer field, a killer in the
ground with a light on its back. That
glow every child up there thinks is
magic, down here, it means one thing,
poison, stay away. You don't know any of
that yet. You don't know anything yet.
You only know you're hungry, and there's
another one moving in the dark just
ahead. Skip forward. You will live like
this for almost 2 years. 2 years in the
dirt. 2 years of hunting things bigger
than you in the dark, of hiding your
poison behind a warning light, of never
once seeing the sky. Some nights you'll
hunt in packs, several of you draining
one snail together, most nights you hunt
alone. Nobody up there knows this part
exists. To them, you are a few magical
weeks in June. They have no idea those
weeks are the very end of your life, or
what you had to be down here in the dark
to earn them. 2 years for what's coming,
you get about 12 days. Skip forward. You
climb out of the soil rebuilt, winged,
delicate, a lantern burning at the end
of your body, and the first time you
light up, it astonishes even you.
A cold green-gold fire blinking on out
of nothing, no heat, no burn, nearly
every scrap of energy in you turns
straight into light. It is the most
efficient light anything on Earth has
ever made, and engineers have spent
decades failing to copy it, and it's
coming from you. You lift into the warm
night, and the whole field answers a
hundred lights blinking on around you.
And for one moment, it feels like the
dark was made to be filled with exactly
this. This is the part everyone loves.
Right now, up here, you are the most
beautiful thing anyone will ever see.
People stop their cars for you. Children
chase you across fields with jars. And
that light they love, the same light
that screamed poison,
stay away when you were a killer in the
dirt is about to become the exact thing
that gets you killed. You have 12 days.
You will never eat again. There's no
time and no reason.
From the second your wings dried, you
started burning down. Everything you are
now exists for one single purpose, and
you haven't done it yet. So, you begin
to speak the only language you have. You
flash.
One pulse, half a second long, thrown
out as you dip through a small curve in
the air, a rhythm that belongs only to
your kind, that no other firefly uses.
Then you wait. 2 seconds. You are asking
the dark a question. Is anyone there? Is
anyone like me? If a female of your kind
is watching from the grass, she answers
one flash at exactly the right delay.
Your code, her code, a conversation of
light across the dark until you find
each other. You flash. You wait. Night
one, you flash. You wait. Nothing. Night
two, a thousand lights in the field and
not one of them is for you. Night three,
your glow is dimmer now. You can feel
it. You're spending light you will never
get back and no one has answered. Every
night you rise. Every night you ask the
dark the same question.
Every night the answer is no, and the
days you have left drop by one.
10 left, then nine. You flash. You wait.
Then below you, an answer. The right
pattern.
The right delay. You turn and drop
toward it, flashing as you go. And
you're almost there, close enough to see
the glow, steady in the grass, when
something is wrong.
The shape behind the light is too big,
the legs are too long, it isn't waiting
the way a mate waits.
It's braced. You break off a wingbeat
later than you should, and haul yourself
back up into the dark, and the light
below you goes dark, too patient,
already waiting for the next one.
You don't understand what just happened.
You only know your whole body screamed
at you to run. Some don't run in time.
Nobody sees them go. The field keeps
glowing.
You climb higher, and you flash again,
because flashing is all you have, and
the days keep falling. Eight left. Look
at the field now. It looks like the sky
fell into the grass, the most peaceful
thing in the world. It isn't peaceful.
Every light out there is a question or
an answer, and not all the answers are
honest. Scattered through that grass are
lights speaking your exact language who
are not your kind at all. They have
learned your code.
They know precisely how long to wait.
They are answering you in your own words
in the dark, where you can never see
what's holding the light, and you have
no way to tell.
A real mate and the thing hunting you
send the same flash. Your entire life
comes down to guessing which glow is
love, and which one is the last mistake
you'll ever make.
A week gone now. You keep flashing.
There is nothing else you were built to
do. Here is what you are, at your best,
the most efficient light maker on the
planet.
A creature so finely built that
thousands of your kind can rise on a
single night and fill an entire valley
with a language made of light. Two years
you survived underground as a hunter,
and you climbed out to burn beautifully
for 12 days. All of it aimed at one
moment in the dark, and none of it, not
the light, not the language,
not the two years of waiting, lets you
tell the truth from the trap. Then one
night, an answer comes back so perfectly
that something in you goes still. The
right flash, the right delay, Again,
when you ask again, patient, certain.
After a week of throwing your light into
the dark and getting nothing back,
someone is finally speaking to you in
your own language exactly every single
time. This is it. This is what the 2
years underground were for, and the
burning down, and every unanswered
flash.
You fold toward her light through the
dark, flashing as you come, and you land
in the grass beside the glow you crossed
the whole life to reach. You made it.
Against everything, you found her. She
is not your kind. She is a different
firefly entirely, and she has spent your
whole courtship copying the love code of
your species flash for flash,
delay for delay, because she cannot make
her own poison, and yours is the only
place to get it. She let you fly all the
way down.
And the moment you land, she takes you.
You flash not the mating pattern now,
just light, just panic, and it changes
nothing.
She holds you and begins to eat you
alive, and as she does, she draws the
poison out of your body into hers, so
that when she lays her eggs, they'll
carry your defense.
The light you spent your entire life
sending into the dark worked exactly the
way it was built to. It brought
something to you. It just wasn't love.
And here is the last of it.
In your final moment, you are not
afraid. You answered a perfect signal.
You reached her, and something in you is
certain right to the end that you won.
The field keeps glowing above you.
Nobody notices one light go out. There
were hundreds, and yet, once in a few
forests left on Earth, your kind does
something no one has ever fully
explained.
Thousands of you, strangers, flashing in
perfect unison,
a whole hillside going dark and bright,
dark and bright, together, like one
enormous thing breathing light. Nobody
teaches them. Nobody leads them.
They just find the same rhythm in the
dark. For a few nights every summer, it
is the most beautiful thing on the
entire planet. And every year, there are
fewer lights in it because your light is
going quiet. The lamps and the streets
and the screens are so bright now that
you can't find each other in the glare.
Your flashes lost in a sky that never
gets fully dark anymore.
Whole meadows that used to burn every
June stay empty now.
A child today may grow up having never
once seen what every child before them
took for granted. Somewhere in the
ground tonight, an egg is glowing
faintly in the dark.
In 2 years, it will climb out, dry its
wings, and rise into whatever field is
left. It will flash into the night.
It will wait for an answer. It won't be
able to tell which lights are love. None
of you ever can. You spent your whole
life chasing a light that lied to you.
At least it was quick. There's a
creature everyone calls lucky, the one
children make wishes on, the one painted
on cradles for good fortune.
And one warm afternoon, something is
going to land on its back, slide inside
it, and eat it alive so slowly that it
keeps walking around in the sun for
weeks
not knowing it's already dead. And then,
it doesn't even get to die. It gets
turned into a guard for the thing that
killed it. Go find out why it sucks to
be born as a ladybug.
It's on your screen now.

subtitles.plaintext:
You break out of your egg, and the first
thing you do is eat the egg next to you,
it was never going to hatch.
Your mother laid it that way, empty,
unfertilized, a first meal left behind
for whichever of you came out hungriest.
You don't know that. You don't know
anything yet. You only know it's soft
and you are empty, so you open your
mouth. You are smaller than a grain of
rice. You are black and wet and covered
in spikes.
You look nothing like the thing people
love. And somewhere in this same garden,
something already knows you're here. It
is small and black and very patient. It
will wait almost your entire life. You
will never see it coming. None of that
exists yet. Right now, there is only the
egg and the hunger and the next one
after that. Skip forward. You have shed
your skin four times and you have found
the only thing you are for, killing. The
aphids cover every stem, soft, green,
slow,
endless, and you move through them
eating one after another after another.
You will kill about 5,000 of them before
you are done. This is why farmers buy
your kind by the boxful and pour them
into their fields like ammunition. They
think you're a blessing. You're a
slaughter they can aim.
You don't decide to hunt. There is an
aphid, so you eat it. There is another
one behind it. Find the next one. Then,
the ground moves and the aphids aren't
yours. Ants farm them.
They stroke the aphids for the sugar
they leak and they guard them like
cattle. And when you push in to feed,
the ants find you. They bite. They haul
at your legs. They pour over you in
numbers you cannot fight and you are
dragged backward off the stem and
dropped over the edge of the leaf. You
didn't lose because you were weak.
You lost because there were 400 of them
and one of you. You write yourself in
the dirt and climb back up because the
hunger doesn't care that you lost. Find
the next one. A jumping spider has been
on this leaf longer than you have. You
don't see it. You've walked past it
twice. The third time, it takes you. You
don't fight nothing. Your size out-pulls
the spider. You do the only two things
your body knows. You go limp,
completely, like something already dead.
And you bleed foul yellow poison out of
every joint in your legs, over its
fangs, into its mouth.
For 1 second, the spider hesitates,
tasting something wrong. 1 second is
enough. Its grip opens, and you drop off
the leaf, through the air, into the soil
below, and you lie there, upside down,
not moving, poison leaking down your
legs, while it watches from above and
decides you are not worth it. That
bitter poison and the bright red shell
everyone finds so cheerful and the seven
neat black spots, none of it was ever
decoration.
It's a warning label. It says, "I will
make you sick." Everything pretty about
you is a threat you wrote in your own
blood. Some ladybugs don't get the
second. Nobody finds them. Nobody
notices.
You got it. You right yourself and
climb. Find the next one. You seal
yourself to the underside of a leaf and
you dissolve. What was black and spiked
breaks down almost to liquid and
rebuilds itself.
And when you crack the case open, you
are pale and soft and wrong-looking and
over few hours, the red bleeds in and
the spots surface one by one until you
are finally the creature on the greeting
cards. You look brand new. You are
exactly what you always were, still
hungry, still killing. Find the next
one. Then, the cold comes, and it wants
to kill you more efficiently than any
spider. You cannot survive a winter
alone, so you follow a scent laid down
by ladybugs you have never met into a
crack in a wall, and you pack in with
thousands of them, a single shivering
mass in the dark, and you wait out
months you might not live through.
Midwinter, a warm week arrives, a false
spring. It wakes some of them. They
crawl out into the sun, burning the last
reserves they were saving, and 3 days
later the cold slams back down and takes
every one of them. You feel the same
warmth pulling at you, your whole body
screaming to move toward it. Holding
still is the hardest thing you will ever
do. By morning, the ones who couldn't
are frozen on the wall outside. And
pressed against you the entire time is a
bigger cousin arrived from the other
side of the world wearing almost your
exact colors.
It carries something inside it, a
parasite that does nothing to it and
rots you from within. You don't have to
fight it, you only have to touch it. You
spent the whole winter touching it. The
patient thing came through the winter,
too. It's in the garden right now,
warming its wings in the same sun you
are. It can afford to wait. You have one
summer left. It only needs an afternoon.
Skip forward. You come out of the winter
anyway, thinner, slower, alive one of
the few. And for the first time, nothing
is chasing you. You find a mate.
Everything you have ever done was for
this.
The eaten siblings, the poison, the
ants, the spider, the winter, the
parasite you somehow didn't catch all of
it, was the road to a warm leaf in
spring and a few seconds that finally
make you what the child believes you
are, lucky. You lay your eggs on the
underside of a leaf.
Some fertile, some not a first meal,
left behind the way it was left for you.
You have done the whole thing right.
Here is what you are at your best, a
hunter that clears a whole rose bush of
5,000 pests, armored in a poison most
predators have learned by heart, marked
in a warning the entire garden obeys.
For something the size of a lentil,
almost nothing on Earth is built better
at staying alive. None of it is going to
matter because the patient thing has
finally found you. It is not a bird. It
is not the cold. It doesn't want to eat
you.
It is a wasp, black, smaller than you
are, and it lands on your back so
lightly you never feel the weight. It
slides a needle between the plates of
your shell and it's gone before you
understand anything happened. A
pinprick, nothing. You keep walking, you
keep eating, find the next one. But
there is an egg inside you now, and it
hatches. And the thing that comes out
begins to feed. It is careful.
It eats your fat, your reserves, the
soft insides you can lose, and it leaves
your legs working and your heart going
because it needs you alive.
For 3 weeks it hollows you out while you
walk around in the sun not knowing you
are already something's food. Then it
chews through your belly, climbs out
between your legs, and spins its cocoon
there
inside the cage of you. And here is
where the luckiest creature on Earth
learns the last thing. You don't die.
Something the wasp left behind locks
your body over its child. Your legs will
not answer you.
You cannot walk. You cannot eat. You
cannot leave. When a beetle or a bird
drifts near the cocoon, your body
twitches hard, wild, enough to drive it
off. You are guarding it. You cannot
stop guarding it. For a week, maybe two,
you crouch over the thing that ate you
and shield it with the last working
parts of your body. Then the wasp climbs
out beneath you, dries its wings,
and flies off to find the next ladybug.
And about one time in four, you are
still alive when it's over. You get to
keep living in the body it emptied.
There is no name for what you are now.
There is only the leaf and the sun and a
hunger you no longer have the insides to
the
Skip forward. It is a warm afternoon and
a child finds one of your children
walking across her fingertip. Red.
Perfect. Seven black spots. She closes
her eyes and wishes for good luck. Your
daughter sits there shining, carrying
every single thing you carried. The eggs
she'll eat, the poison in her legs,
the winter ahead, and the wasp already
somewhere in the garden, patient,
waiting for her to grow up. The child
opens her eyes, lets her lift off her
finger, and watches her go.
And feels lucky. She will never know.
None of them ever do. Maybe that's the
one mercy in it, that the whole world
loves you and not one of them will ever
have to learn what the colors cost. You
were a killer the whole world mistook
for something gentle. There's another
one out there that nobody mistakes for
anything.
The deadliest hunter in the sky, it
catches almost everything it chases, 95
times out of a hundred, and eats it
alive in the air, still moving. It looks
like summer itself drifting over a pond.
But before ever touch the sky,
it spent years buried in the dark water
below it, waiting, starving, wearing a
face that shoots open to grab whatever
gets close.
Every beautiful thing about it was built
in a nightmare you never see. Go find
out why it sucks to be born as a
dragonfly. It's on your screen now.

subtitles.plaintext:
You split out of your egg casing
underwater and the first thing your body
does is swim upward. Not because you
decided to, your muscles do it
automatically. You don't have a brain
capable of decisions yet. You have a
head, a thorax, a segmented abdomen, and
a breathing siphon at your tail that you
need to press against the water surface
every few seconds or you drown. This is
day one. You are 1 mm long. You live in
stagnant water, a pond, a puddle, a
water-filled crack in a wall, a bottle
cap sitting in the rain. You spend your
first day learning one motion. Swim up,
breathe, sink, repeat. There is nothing
else to do yet. There is nothing else
you can do yet. On the second day, you
find food. You are not a predator. You
filter microorganisms and algae from the
water using a pair of mouth brushes that
rotate constantly sweeping particles
inward.
You don't choose what you eat. You eat
whatever the current brings. You eat all
day. You are going to spend 10 days
doing this. Around you, the water is not
safe. Dragonfly nymphs sit motionless in
the silt below waiting for larva to
drift into range. They don't chase. They
don't need to.
They wait and then they strike and their
strike takes 11 milliseconds. Water
striders patrol the surface above you.
Small fish hold position at the edge of
the weed line.
Every few hours, something disappears
from the cluster that hatched with you.
You were 200 when you started. You are
fewer now. You molt on day three. Your
exoskeleton splits along the back and
you pull yourself out of it. You are
briefly exposed, soft, pale, slower than
usual while the new skin hardens.
This is when the dragonfly nymphs take
the most. The molting ones can't move
fast enough. You harden in time. You
molt again on day five, again on day
seven,
again on day nine. Each time, you are a
little larger. Each time, skip forward.
Day 10. Your body stops eating and
starts changing. The larva stage is
over.
You enter the pupa stage, a comma-shaped
casing that floats at the surface,
breathing through two tubes at the top
of its head. You are inside it. You are
not moving. You are not eating.
You are dissolving. Not metaphorically.
Your larval body breaks itself down into
a soup of cells. And those cells rebuild
into something completely different.
Wings where there were none.
Legs that fold into a different
configuration. A head that reorganizes
around a new set of structures. You will
be unrecognizable to anything that saw
you a week ago.
This takes two days. On day 12, the
pupal casing splits open at the surface.
You have to stand on the water to let
your wings dry. Not hover over it. Stand
on it.
The surface tension holds you for 30
seconds while your wings extend and
harden. You cannot fly yet. You cannot
leave yet. Birds scan the surface. Fish
watch from below.
You are standing on top of the water,
completely exposed, and there's nothing
you can do except wait for your wings to
work. They work. You lift off. Skip
forward.
You are a fully formed adult male
mosquito. You are 4 mm long. Your body
weighs less than a milligram.
Your wings beat 500 times per second,
generating a tone in the range of 450 to
600 Hz, the sound that every human
within earshot has learned to dread.
You know the one. The thin whine that
finds your ear the second the lights go
out and vanishes the instant you sit up
and turn on the lamp. That's not a
threat. That's just wings.
500 beats a second inches from your
face. You have compound eyes that give
you nearly 360°
vision. You have antennae covered in
thousands of fine hairs, each one tuned
to detect sound, air pressure changes,
chemical signals. You are built to find
one thing. You will spend your entire
adult life trying to find it. But first,
there is something you need to
understand about yourself. You cannot
bite. The proboscis, the long,
needle-like structure at the front of
your face, the one every human
recognizes, the one they fear, is yours.
You have it.
But yours is not the same as the
female's. Hers has six interlocking
stylets. Two for cutting, two for
anchoring, one that injects saliva, one
that draws blood. Hers is sharp enough
to penetrate skin with 1/1000 the force
it would take a needle. Hers carries
proteins that stop blood from clotting,
suppress the immune response,
thin the walls of capillaries so the
blood flows freely. Yours is too soft to
cut anything. You were not built with
the cutting stylets. You were not given
the saliva enzymes.
You have the housing of a weapon with
none of the mechanism inside it. The
only thing your proboscis is capable of
doing is drinking from a flower, nectar,
fruit juice, sugar water.
The same thing a bee does. You have
never drawn blood. You cannot draw
blood. You are biologically incapable of
it. Every human who has ever been bitten
by a mosquito was bitten by a female.
Most people refuse to believe that the
first time they hear it. Go ahead, try
to remember a single male biting you.
You never have, you never will. There is
no mouth on this planet less capable of
it than yours. Only females need blood.
It provides the protein required to
develop eggs. Males never need it, were
never built for it, and spend their
entire lives drinking from plants. You
are a mosquito. You drink from flowers.
Nobody knows this about you. Skip
forward. At dusk, you find the swarm. It
is above a gap in the tree line, a
visual landmark the males use to anchor
the swarm location. Hundreds of you are
already there, hovering in a column,
beating your wings in the fading light.
The sound is dense, layered, a wall of
wing beats at slightly different
frequencies, all overlapping. Every male
in this swarm hatched from the same pond
system within the last few days. Every
one of you has the same purpose. You
join the column, you rise and fall in a
rhythmic pattern, not flying forward,
not flying away, just hovering and
dipping and rising. The pattern that
signals fitness to a female. The males
who hover steadily, whose wings beat
with the most consistent frequency, are
the ones females are more likely to
select. Your antennae are tuned to
detect 400 hertz. That is the wing beat
frequency of a female. Every sensory
system you have is pointed at a single
question. Is that 400 hertz signal in
the air yet? It isn't. You wait. Around
you, other males are waiting, too. Some
have been here since last night. Males
live between six and 10 days as adults.
A few of the ones in this swarm will be
dead before dawn. Their energy reserves
run out and they simply stop flying.
There is no warning. They are there and
then they are not. A bat makes a pass
through the swarm. It is a pipistrelle,
small, fast, capable of catching insects
in complete darkness using echolocation
that updates 200 times per second. It
takes two males on the first pass and
three on the second. It does not aim. It
flies through the densest part of the
swarm and takes what its mouth catches.
It will make eight more passes tonight.
The swarm reforms around the gaps. You
are still in it. The 400 hertz signal
enters the swarm at 8:43 p.m. She is
larger than any of the males. She enters
from below flying upward through the
edge of the column. Immediately the
males closest to her drop toward her
adjusting their wing beat to harmonize
with hers a behavior that happens faster
than conscious thought faster than
choice contact in the air. It takes
under 30 seconds. She will only do this
once in her lifetime. If she mates with
you, she will not mate again. She mates
with you. She pulls away before you have
fully registered what happened. She
descends out of the swarm and is gone.
You are still hovering in the column.
You have done the only thing your adult
body was designed to do. Skip forward.
The next morning she is hunting. She
uses carbon dioxide the breath you
exhale to locate a host from 50 m away.
She uses body heat to narrow the range.
She uses the chemical compounds on your
skin to confirm the target. She lands on
a human forearm, presses her proboscis
against the skin, and cuts through in
under a second. Her saliva enters the
wound before the blood starts flowing.
It numbs the site. It suppresses the
immune response. It thins the blood. She
drinks. If she's carrying malaria
Plasmodium parasites picked up from a
previous host, they travel into the
bloodstream now.
If she's carrying dengue, yellow fever,
West Nile virus, they travel now.
Mosquitoes are responsible for nearly
700,000 human deaths every year more
than any other animal on Earth. More
than sharks, crocodiles, snakes, lions,
and hippos combined. There is one
country on Earth your kind has never
managed to conquer. Not because it's too
cold, the Arctic is full of you. Iceland
simply has none and scientists still
aren't fully sure why. She will bite
three or four more hosts before she
dies. You are on a flower 2 km away. You
found a patch of flowering plants near a
stream this morning and you have been
here since sunrise, moving between
blossoms, drinking nectar through your
soft proboscis. This is your life
between dusk swarms.
Flower to flower, sugar to sugar, you
are not looking for blood, you are not
carrying disease to anyone. You are a
mosquito on a flower in the morning sun
doing the same thing a bee would do
and you have no idea that somewhere your
species is being blamed for the worst
death toll in the animal kingdom. You
don't know what biting is. Skip forward.
Day six. A swift, a small bird that
catches insects entirely in flight,
never landing except to nest, takes you
from the air at 7:14 p.m. It has been
hunting the swarm for three evenings.
Swifts can consume 3,000 insects in a
single day during breeding season. To a
swift, a swarm of male mosquitoes is a
food source, not a threat. They don't
check what kind of mosquito it is.
They don't distinguish between the
females that bite and the males that
don't. You are all the same size, the
same shape, the same wing sound. You
were flying toward the 400 Hz frequency.
You had found it. Somewhere on the
ground below the swarm, a human is
slapping at a mosquito on their arm.
It's a female. It's always a female, but
the human doesn't know that and has
never stopped to think about it. To
them, there is only one kind of
mosquito, the kind you swat. You spent
six days on this earth. You drank
nectar. You flew at dusk. You never bit
anyone, not once, not ever,
not capable of it. Nobody will remember
you any differently. But six days is
still six days. You drank, you flew at
dusk, you had a mouth.
There's a creature that never gets even
that. Two years underwater, then it
climbs into the air, sealed shut, no
mouth at all. It can't eat, it can't
drink.
It gets one day to find a mate and then
it's over, having never tasted a single
thing.
Go watch why it sucks to be born as a
mayfly. It's on your screen now.

text:
Why it sucks to be born as a Mayfly

🤝 Sponsorships: zoozleworld@gmail.com

You are born with no mouth. You will never eat. You have one day — sometimes five minutes — to live, mate, and die. This is what it's like to be born a mayfly: nature's shortest, cruelest life

Inspired by Dinzo and Bound
.
.
.
.
.
.

00.56-THE IMPOSSIBLE BIRTH
02.17-THE PROMISE/ TWO YEARS IN THE DARK
03.25-THE RIVER WANTS YOU DEAD
04.41-WHAT YOUR BODY WAS BUILDING
05.02-THE HATCH
06.10-THE FIRST FLIGHT
08.10-THE SWARM
09.29-THE FEMALE
10.01-RUNNING OUT OF TIME
10.50-THE END
11.42-LOOP CLOSE

#whyitsucks  #mayfly  #yourlifeas

subtitles.plaintext:
You have a mouth. You can eat, drink,
call out when something goes wrong. The
mayfly does not have that. You are a
mayfly. You have just emerged from a
river. Your wings are already dry.
You can already fly. Your body is fully
formed. Two tails streaming behind you.
Four wings catching the afternoon light.
Enormous compound eyes that can see in
almost every direction at once. But your
mouth is sealed shut. Not damaged, not
broken, sealed by design.
Your body never built the internal
structures needed to eat. No stomach, no
working digestive system, no ability to
take in food of any kind. You were
assembled this way on purpose because
evolution decided you would never need
to eat. The adult form of a mayfly
exists for one thing and one thing only,
and eating is not part of it. You have
roughly 24 hours to live. Skip forward.
You spent almost 2 years getting here.
Not 24 hours, 2 years. You hatched from
an egg the size of a grain of sand at
the bottom of this same river. In the
dark, among the silt and algae and slow
current of the riverbed. You had no eyes
that could detect shapes yet, no sense
of direction, no understanding of up or
down except what the current told you.
You were a nymph, a larval form with
gills along your abdomen, six legs,
three tails, and a fully functioning
mouth. That mouth worked. You ate algae
scraped from rocks. You filtered
microorganisms from the water moving
through your gills. You ate plant
detritus drifting down from the surface
above. Eating was the only thing you did
every day for nearly 730 days. You
molted your exoskeleton up to 45
separate times during those 2 years.
This is more molts than almost any other
insect. Each time your body outgrew its
shell, the shell split along the back
and you pulled yourself out of it soft,
pale, slow. Your new skin taking hours
to harden.
During every molt, you could barely
move. Your legs didn't work properly.
Your reaction time dropped to almost
nothing.
You sat on the riverbed waiting for your
new exoskeleton to harden and hoped
nothing found you in the meantime.
Things found you. Trout patrol the
mid-depth of this river in loose
formations, holding position in the
current, watching the water below them
for movement. When a nymph molts, it
moves wrong, sluggish, uncoordinated,
briefly pale against the dark riverbed.
Trout have learned to watch for exactly
this. They do not need to hunt
aggressively.
They simply wait, and the molt cycle
delivers prey to them on a regular
schedule throughout the year.
Water beetles hunt the shallows.
Stonefly larva bigger than you will eat
smaller nymphs without hesitation.
Hellgrammite larva, which grow to nearly
8 cm, can take a mayfly nymph whole.
Crayfish pick through the algae mats
where you feed.
The riverbed, which looks from above
like a quiet and undisturbed place, is a
continuous predation event in every
direction. Of the hundreds of eggs laid
with yours, most did not survive 2
years.
They were eaten during molts. They were
caught by current shifts that swept them
into faster water where they couldn't
hold on. They were picked off by the
trout holding just above them in the
water column.
Attrition is constant, and it never
stops. You survived all 45 molts.
You lived in the dark for 2 years. Not
metaphorically, the riverbed is dark.
During daylight hours, diffuse light
filters down through the water, enough
to create a vague sense of up, but not
enough to navigate by. You never saw the
sky. You never saw open air.
You never experienced anything except
current, silt, algae, rocks, and the
bodies of things eating each other in
the dark around you. You felt the
seasons through water temperature, cold
enough in winter to slow your metabolism
almost to a stop, warm enough in summer
to accelerate it. The seasons happened
to you. You did not observe them. In the
final weeks of your second year as a
nymph, your body began to change without
your choosing it. Wing pads thickened
along your thorax, your compound eyes,
which had been adequate for life on the
riverbed, enlarged dramatically, your
head restructuring around them to
accommodate the size they needed to be
for flight. Your body began diverting
food intake away from growth and into
fat storage. You were not getting
bigger. You were being loaded. Whatever
was coming next required fuel, and the
only way to carry fuel into it was to
build it into your tissues beforehand
because you would have no way to refuel
once you got there. Then, one evening,
the water temperature crossed a specific
threshold, not very different from the
temperature the night before, a fraction
of a degree, but enough. You felt it in
your body as a signal you had never felt
before. It was not a decision. It was a
trigger. Every mayfly in this stretch of
river felt the same thing at the same
moment. The hatch began. Skip forward.
You rose through the water column. For
the first time in your life, you swam
upward instead of holding position
against the current.
The surface of the river appeared above
you, a shimmering ceiling you had never
approached. You pushed through it, and
immediately your nymphal skin split
along your back, and you were standing
on the surface of the water in open air,
wings unfolding and inflating for the
first time.
The sky above you enormous and full of
light you had never experienced at this
intensity. You had approximately 30
seconds to get off the water. Swallows
had been patrolling the river surface
since before dawn. They had seen the
first emerging mayflies and communicated
the hatch to others.
By By time you surfaced, there were
dozens of them. Low, fast, skimming the
water with open mouths, taking emerging
mayflies directly off the surface film
before their wings could work. A
swallow's reaction time is fast enough
to intercept insects midair. On the
surface, wings not yet dry, you were not
midair. You were stationary.
You were exactly what a swallow is built
to take.
Your wings dried. You lifted off and
joined the cloud rising above the river.
What it looks like from a distance is a
snowstorm, but moving upward, a column
of white wings rising from the water
into the afternoon light. Millions of
insects ascending at once,
dense enough to be visible from 100 m
away. Fishermen drive long distances to
watch a mayfly hatch. Photographers
position themselves on riverbanks for
hours to capture it. It is one of the
most documented natural phenomena in
freshwater ecology, described
consistently as breathtaking,
otherworldly, one of the most beautiful
things in nature. From inside it, you
are one of millions of identical bodies
burning a fuel supply that began
depleting the moment you left the water,
racing a clock that started the moment
your wings dried, and you have a sealed
mouth and no way to add even one calorie
to the reserves you were born with.
Every wingbeat costs something you
cannot get back. You fly upward. Males
ascend higher,
females stay lower, near the surface,
near the water. You are a male.
You rise into the swarm, not a chaotic
cloud, but a structured column. Each
male performing the same rhythmic
pattern, rising and dipping and rising
again. The motion continuous, driven by
muscle memory so deep it requires no
conscious input. You do not choose to do
this. Your body executes it
automatically from the moment you reach
swarm altitude. The pattern signals
health and energy reserve.
The males who sustain it most
consistently are the ones whose fat
reserves are holding. The males whose
reserves are failing fly the pattern
with decreasing precision, shallower
dips, slower rises, a degradation
readable to a female from meters away.
You can hear the swarm before you see it
clearly.
The collective wingbeat of hundreds of
thousands of males creates a hum at a
specific frequency, audible even over
the sound of the river below.
Inside the column, it is loud enough to
feel. You take your position and begin
the pattern. The males around you are
burning fuel at the same rate you are.
Some arrive before you and have been
flying longer.
You can see the ones whose reserves are
nearly gone. They drift lower, their
pattern dissolving into irregular
wingbeats, until they drop below the
critical altitude and fall toward the
surface.
When they touch the water, they cannot
get back up. The surface tension holds
them. They become food for the trout
rising from below, who have shifted from
the nymphs on the riverbed to the spent
adults on the surface, because the hatch
has made surface feeding more efficient
than bottom feeding for the first time
all year.
The river below the swarm looks like it
is
boiling.
Fish are surfacing dozens of times per
minute. Birds are working every edge.
The hatch is the most dangerous moment
of the mayfly's entire life cycle, and
it is also the only moment the mayfly
exists with wings. Skip forward. A
female enters the swarm from below. She
rises through the column slowly, larger
than the males around her,
flying with a different pattern, not the
rhythmic display of the males, but a
steady upward movement that announces
what she is to every male she passes.
The males closest to her drop
immediately, adjusting their approach,
competing for position not through
aggression, but through proximity. There
are hundreds of males for every female
in this column. The competition is
entirely positional. Whoever is closest
at the right moment is the one who makes
contact. You are close enough. Mating
happens in midair. It takes between a
few seconds and a couple of minutes.
She pulls away while it is still
completing, dropping back toward the
surface with a direction and purpose you
do not share.
She has eggs to deposit, up to 8,000 of
them, and a specific section of the
river surface to find for optimal
placement. She will be dead within a few
hours of laying them. You are still in
the swarm. You have done the only thing
your adult body was assembled to do. The
2 years of molting and surviving and
loading fat in the dark riverbed, all of
it pointed at those few seconds of
contact in the air above the river.
There is nothing left in your life cycle
that requires you. The system has what
it needed from you. Your fat reserves
run out over the next hour. You can feel
it in your flight muscles. Before
anything else, the power output
dropping, the swarm's rhythm becoming
harder to sustain, the column below you
coming closer as you lose the altitude
you need to maintain. You are still
sending signals to your wings, your
wings are still responding. But the fuel
driving them is nearly gone and there is
no way to add more. Your mouth is
sealed, there is nothing to eat, there
never was. You drift lower, you touch
the surface, the current takes you. From
a bridge upstream, a person who drove 2
hours to watch this hatch is taking
photographs.
The surface is covered in spent adults,
wings flat on the water, bodies drifting
in the current, the massive emergence
reducing itself to a carpet of the dead
stretching as far downstream as the eye
can follow. They will post the
photographs with a caption about the
beauty of nature. The image will get
thousands of likes.
People will comment that it looks
incredible. You drift under the bridge.
Somewhere upstream, 8,000 eggs are
sinking to the riverbed. In the dark,
among the silt and algae and slow
current, they settle into the rocks. In
a few days, they will hatch. Small, pale
nymphs will push out of their casings,
gills already working, legs already
gripping the rock, mouths already open.
They will eat, they will molt, they will
do what you did for 2 years in the dark.
And on an evening when the water
temperature crosses a threshold, they
will rise to the surface for the first
time. They will step out of their
nymphal skin into open air.
They will have 24 hours. They will have
no mouth. The hummingbird gets 9 years
and 18 crossings of the Gulf of Mexico.
The fire ant gets a colony, a flood, a
trail that never stops.
You got 24 hours above the water and a
sealed mouth you were born with. Every
mayfly that has ever lived has gotten
exactly this much. Not one has ever
gotten more.
There is another animal that also can't
eat. It doesn't hatch in a river, it
doesn't live for a day, it lives for a
week, and every human on Earth has spent
their entire life hating it for
something it is physically incapable of
doing. Next video.

text:
Why it sucks to be born as Silkworm

🤝 Sponsorships: zoozleworld@gmail.com

.
.
.
.
Inspired by Dinzo and Bound

#whyitsucks #silkworms #silkworm

subtitles.plaintext:
You hatch the size of an eyelash, and
you are already the only one of your
kind that has ever existed, not
metaphorically, literally.
There's not a single silkworm on Earth
that does not live in a building, on a
tray, in front of a human. Your species
has been extinct in the wild for 5,000
years. The wild version of you died out
around the time people invented writing.
What's left is you.
A pale grub on a tray,
in a room of trays, in a building you
will never leave.
A person is already waiting not to hurt
you, to feed you. A fresh mulberry leaf
is placed where you can reach it. You
find it with your face. You start
chewing.
Because that is the only thing you know
how to do, and the only thing you will
ever do well. There are 300 of you on
this tray, a thousand trays in this
room, rooms like it on three continents,
and every one of you is the same animal,
exactly the same.
5,000 years of careful breeding made
sure of that.
You were not found. You were time's
made.
Just wait until you find out what for.
In 4 weeks, you will do something almost
no other animal on Earth can do. Out of
a small gland in your head, you will
produce a single thread of liquid silk,
almost a kilometer long, unbroken, finer
than a hair, and stronger by weight than
steel.
You will wrap it around yourself in a
figure-eight motion no one taught you,
for 3 days straight, until you have
built a perfect shell. It is one of the
most extraordinary feats of construction
any living thing performs. And that
shell is the exact reason you have to
die before you ever come out of it. The
moth you would
have become the one your body is trying
to build right now inside that perfect
shell, will never get to leave it.
Because if it did, it would ruin the
thread. And the thread is the only
reason your species still exists.
So, somebody gently drops your cocoon
into a pot of boiling water on day 28 of
your life while you are still inside it.
While you are still becoming. Just wait
for it. You eat for 4 weeks. That is
your entire life. In those 4 weeks, your
body grows 10,000 times. Imagine a human
baby reaching the weight of a humpback
whale before its first birthday. That's
the kind of thing happening inside you
on a leaf in a tray while you don't even
notice. Your skin gets too tight four
times.
Each time, your body splits the old
shell open and you step out of it
bigger. A small white animal made almost
entirely of unspun silk. You are not
eating to grow. You are eating to fill.
You are not the only silkworm on this
tray. You have never noticed the others.
Your eyes barely work, but they are
there and not all of them are like you.
Some hatch 2 days late. Some are eating
slower. Some have a slight
discoloration, a small irregularity in
how they molted.
A body that for reasons no one will
write down isn't quite shaped like
yours. A hand passes over the tray. It
picks them up. You don't see this
happen. The hand never touches you.
Whatever it is that makes you correct,
you have it. Your size is right. Your
color is right. Your timing is right.
You are exactly the shape the building
expects. The ones who weren't go into a
bucket and out the door and they don't
come back. You eat your leaf. It isn't
cruelty. It's the math.
A silkworm too small to make a full
cocoon costs more in leaves than its
silk is worth.
So, it doesn't get to make the cocoon at
all.
To spin the thread that kills you, you
first have to earn the right to spin.
And you don't know you've been earning
it. You don't know the others ever
existed. You just keep eating because
the leaf is there. On day 28, something
inside your body tells you to climb. You
don't know why. You climb anyway. You
lift your head and something in you,
some gland you have been filling for 4
weeks without knowing, opens. A thread
of liquid silver comes out of your
mouth. It hits the air. It hardens.
It catches on the wood in front of you.
It works.
You don't know what times it times is.
You just know that your body has finally
done the thing it was built to do and it
has worked on the first try. You begin
to turn slowly, patiently, a figure
eight over and over.
Your head moves through space the way a
person draws a horizon and where it
moves, the thread follows. Every few
seconds, another loop. Every few
minutes, another layer. You will not
stop for 72 hours, 3 days. Head turning,
thread emerging, one unbroken filament
from one tiny mouth
until you have wrapped almost 2 and 1/2
thousand feet of silk around your own
body and the world outside the shell
goes dark. You are now alone inside the
most exquisite thing you will ever make.
It is perfect.
It is also the last thing you will ever
do. Inside the cocoon, your body has
started to come apart.
This is supposed to happen. You're
turning into a moth. The body that
climbed up here is dissolving. Every
internal organ rearranging into
something with wings, antennae, eyes
that work. It will take 2 weeks.
You feel none of it. There is no animal
on this planet more defenseless than a
silkworm in its third day inside the
cocoon. You have no shell of your own.
Your nerves haven't finished forming.
You can't move. You can't sense.
You aren't a larva anymore and you
aren't a moth, yet you You a soft,
half-finished thing in a shell you built
for protection.
And at exactly this moment,
the shell leaves the ground. You don't
feel it. You can't. A hand picks up the
cocoon you built around yourself, sets
it carefully in a basket, and carries it
down a hallway you will never see. The
handling is gentle.
Whoever is carrying you is being careful
not to damage the silk.
They are not being careful about you.
Inside the shell, you are still trying
to become a moth.
You do not know you have been moved. You
do not know what room you are in now.
You do not know the room has a vat in
the corner with the lid off and steam
coming out of it. You have 1 day left.
You don't know that, either. The water
has been boiling for an hour. Your
cocoon is lowered in with the others.
Inside the shell, the temperature climbs
in seconds, and the substance that glues
your silk filament together, sericin,
begins to dissolve into the water. This
is the only way the kilometer of thread
you spent 3 days making can be unwound
in one continuous piece. If you had been
allowed to finish becoming a moth, your
first act would have been to spit an
enzyme onto the inside of your shell,
dissolve a hole, and crawl through.
That enzyme would have cut the thread
into hundreds of useless pieces, so they
don't let you finish. The thread comes
out in one piece. You don't. If you had
been one of the few they kept, the
breeders here, is what you would have
become. A small white moth the size of a
postage stamp. You would have tried to
fly. You would have failed.
5,000 years of breeding made your body
too heavy and your wings too small. You
would have flapped on the tray,
searching, never lifting off.
You would not have eaten. Your kind has
lost its mouth.
There is no food on this planet you
could have swallowed. You would have
lived 4 days, mated, and died on the
tray in the dark without ever once
leaving the building,
without ever once flying. That is the
version of your life that somewhere on
this planet, somebody is right now
arguing should be saved. We already took
it.
We took it 5,000 years ago, slowly, one
chosen pair at a time, until the animal
you were became the animal you are, a
creature that can only be born inside a
building, only feed off a single leaf,
only spin one shape, and only die one
way.
The boiling isn't the cruel part of your
life. The times shape times of your life
is the cruel part. The boiling is just
the day it ends. Every pound of silk on
Earth, every shirt, every tie, every
wedding dress, every pillow case
required between 2,000 and 3,000 cocoons
to make. Every one of those cocoons was
a small white animal in boiling water
on day 28 of its life.
The silk industry produces about 70
million pounds of raw silk a year. That
is roughly 10 billion cocoons.
10 billion
every year. There is no nature
documentary about you.
No children's book has your face on the
cover. You will not appear in a David
Attenborough special. You are too small
to mourn, too useful to spare, and the
building you were born in is one of
millions. But you were the animal that
spun something almost no creature on
Earth can spin, and no one ever saw your
face.
On a tray in a building somewhere in the
world right now, a new egg is hatching.
The grub the size of an eyelash pulls
itself free of the shell. It cannot fly.
Its grandparents couldn't either.
It cannot eat anything but the leaf in
front of it. It does not exist anywhere
outside this room.
It does not know any of that. The hand
places a leaf where the grub can reach
it. The grub finds it with its face. It
takes its first bite. Life as a silkworm
might be rough, but there's another
animal out there that has it way worse.
Trust me, it's wild. Check out the video
and see for yourself.

text:
Why it sucks to be born as Anglerish. 

🤝 Sponsorships: zoozleworld@gmail.com

You're born a mile beneath the ocean, in total darkness, smaller than a grain of rice — and your body is already shutting down. Your stomach is shrinking. You were never built to survive.

You were built to find her. And the moment you do, you bite in, you never let go… and you start to dissolve. Your eyes fade. Your fins wither. Your blood becomes hers — until there's almost nothing left of you but a lump fused to her side.

You get everything you were born for. It costs you yourself.

This is why it sucks to be born as an anglerfish.

🐟 If this got you, you'll never forget these two:
▶ Why It Sucks To Be Born As a Hummingbird:    • Why It Sucks To Be Born As a Hummingbird  
▶ Why It Sucks To Be Born As a Fire Ant:    • Why It Sucks To Be Born As a Fire Ant  

🔔 New animal every Tuesday. Subscribe so you don't miss who's next:    / @zoozleworld   

—————————————
In this video we break down the brutal real life of the deep-sea anglerfish: born into crushing darkness with a body already failing, the impossible search for a mate in an endless black ocean, the rivals racing for the same female, the predators waiting in the dark — and the final horror, where the tiny male fuses into the female's body, dissolves his own eyes, fins and organs, and her immune system surrenders to let it happen. Nature's strangest love story is really a disappearing act.

#whyitsucks #anglerfish #deepsea #ocean #animals #nature #wildlife #facts

subtitles.plaintext:
You are born into the darkest place on
Earth and nothing here will ever come to
help you. A mile beneath the waves, the
sunlight gave up long ago.
There is no blue, no gray, no up, no
down, only black. Pressing on every side
hard enough to crush a submarine and
cold enough to stop your blood if your
blood were warm. You are smaller than a
grain of rice and already you are
hungry. The hunger is not a feeling. It
is a countdown. Down here, food does not
arrive. There are no schools of fish, no
drifting feasts. Lord,
there is the occasional scrap that fell
from a world you will never see and
there is nothing else. You drift through
miles of empty water and meet no one for
days. Worse, your own body is betraying
you. Your stomach is shrinking, your gut
is shutting down organ by organ as if it
already knows you were never built to
eat your way to old age. You were built
for one thing and it isn't survival.
Because somewhere out there in all that
black, there is one thing that can save
you. Find it and you never go hungry
again.
Find it and everything you were born for
finally makes sense. But here is the
part nobody tells you at birth. The
thing that saves you is the same thing
that ends you.
The moment you find it, you Times stop
existing. You won't understand that yet.
You will. Keep swimming. But you do have
one gift. One. You are almost nothing,
no glowing lure, no great jaws, no size
to speak of. The monster everyone
pictures when they hear your name, that
isn't you.
That's Times her. What you have instead
is a face built to find her. Enormous
eyes straining for a light that may not
exist.
Nostrils so huge they swallow your whole
head because she leaves a trail in the
water, a scent threaded through the dark
and you can read it. And right now,
faint as a whisper,
you catch it. A trace, a direction, hope
for the first time in your tiny life.
Hope is cruel down here because the
ocean is vast and you are a speck and
the trail is thin. And she could be 100
m away or 1,000.
The deep is so empty that most males who
are born will never find a single female
in their entire lives. They drift. They
follow ghosts of a scent and they die
alone in the dark still searching. The
clock is still running, your gut is
still closing. Every hour you spend
chasing the wrong current is an hour of
fuel you cannot replace. You are racing
a starvation you were designed to lose.
The trail grows stronger. You are closer
now. And then you understand something
that turns the water colder than it
already is. You are not the only one
following it. Every thread of her scent
in the dark is a signal and you are not
the only starving male who caught.
Somewhere beside you in the black,
others are swimming the same desperate
line toward the same female. Brothers
you will never see racing you toward a
finish none of you understand because
she does not choose just one. She can
take several.
Females have been found with as many as
eight males fused to their bodies, eight
little hopefuls who all won, all latched
on, all gave up everything for the same
prize. So, it isn't only a search
anymore. It's a race and losing it
doesn't mean you get to live.
It means you die out here alone still
chasing a scent that something else
reached first. And you are not the only
thing moving in the dark. The abyss has
its own hunters' mouths that open wider
than their own bodies. Teeth like glass,
things that wait motionless for anything
foolish enough to swim in a straight
line. You are a slow, exhausted,
bite-size snack with your nose buried in
a scent trail and no idea what's beside
you. One wrong drift. One shape in the
black that wasn't there a second ago.
Most of your brothers don't end their
story fused to anyone.
They end it as someone else's scrap,
somewhere in the cold, and the trail
they were following just goes quiet. And
then the scent stops being a trail. It
becomes everything thick, close, all
around you. After a whole life of
chasing a whisper, you are finally
standing in it. She is right here, and
that's when you see her glow.
A real light, steady, hanging in the
black like the only star in a dead sky.
You follow the scent, the final stretch,
and she takes shape around that light.
Enormous beside you, dozens of times
your size,
a great dark body with that single
luminous lure swaying over a mouthful of
teeth. Terrifying. Beautiful. The only
other living thing for miles. This is
it. This is the moment your whole
impossible life was for. Every empty
day, every missed scrap, every rival you
outran in the dark, all of it was the
road to her. You made it.
Against everything, you found her, and
you got there first. This is your
triumph. So, you do the only thing you
were ever built to do. You bite in, and
you do not let go. Then something begins
to happen that you cannot stop. Where
your mouth meets her, both of you start
to come undone.
Your lips dissolve into her skin, your
bloodstream reaches for hers and finds
it. You stop being a fish beside her and
start becoming a part of her. And here's
the part that should be impossible. In
almost any other animal, her body would
fight you.
Foreign flesh fusing into hers should
set off an immune system that attacks
and destroys it the same way a human
body rejects a transplanted organ. But,
it doesn't. To make this union work at
all, the angler fish gave up part of its
immune system entirely. The very
defenses that recognize an intruder and
tear it apart. They traded away a piece
of what protects them from disease, just
so a stranger could melt in and stay.
You don't get to marvel at it. You're
already dissolving into her. You don't
need your eyes anymore, so they fade and
go dark. You don't need to swim, so your
fins wither away.
You don't need to eat, so the gut that
was already failing simply finishes the
job and disappears.
One by one, the pieces of you that made
you times you times switch off, because
she is your blood, your food, your
everything now. Until there is almost
nothing left of the creature that
crossed an ocean of darkness to get
here. Just a small lump fused to her
side, kept alive, kept ready a sack of
what you were, hanging off the body of
the only thing you ever found. You got
everything you were born to want, it
cost you yourself, and you won't be the
only one. She can carry more than one of
you, several little fused lumps along
her body, each one a male who won, each
one a story exactly like yours that
ended the same way.
To her, you are not a partner. You are a
permanent attachment, an organ she
happens to have collected. You will
never swim again, you will never see
again.
You will never again be a single
creature with a life of your own. You
will hang there in the dark, doing the
one job that's left for as long as she
lives. And she can live for years. Years
of you hanging in the black, blind,
fused, silent, woken only when her body
needs you, releasing what she came to
collect, then going still again.
Biologists even have a name for what
you've become, not a mate, a sexual
parasite. You are the most successful
failure in the ocean. You completed your
one mission perfectly, and the reward
was to be erased. That is the prize.
That is what waited for you at the end
of the hardest search in the animal
kingdom. You were born in the dark,
hunted in the dark, starving in the
dark, and the happy ending was to
disappear into someone else forever. So,
no, it does not suck a little to be born
an anglerfish. It sucks all the way
down. But, the anglerfish only has to
disappear once.
There's a creature out there so fragile
it has to die a little every single
night and drag itself back to life every
morning just to make it to sunrise. You
think the dark was bleak?
Go see what it's like to be born as a
hummingbird. It's on your screen right
now.

text:
Why it sucks to be born as army ant 

You're born blind. You will never see anything in your entire life. And the moment you hatch, something closes its jaws around you and drops you into a line of half a million ants that never stops moving.

You don't know where the line is going. No ant does. You just follow the one in front of you — forever. And if that line ever bends into a circle… you'll walk it until you drop dead, completely certain you're going somewhere.

This is why it sucks to be born as an army ant.

🐜 If this got you, you'll never forget these two:
▶ Why It Sucks To Be Born As a Fire Ant: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PASTE_ID
▶ Why It Sucks To Be Born As a Hummingbird: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PASTE_ID

🔔 New animal every Tuesday. Subscribe so you don't miss who's next:    / @zoozleworld  

—————————————
In this video we break down the brutal real life of the army ant: born blind for life, carried into the column before it can stand, the death spiral that makes thousands march in a circle until they die, soldiers with jaws so big they can't even feed themselves, the nest built entirely out of living bodies, the birds that hunt the swarm — and a colony that doesn't notice or grieve a single one of the half-million that die for it.

Nature built the most powerful swarm on Earth out of half a million blind slaves who never chose any of it.

#armyant #ants #animals #nature #wildlife #insects #facts

subtitles.plaintext:
You hatch in the dark and something
already has you in its mouth. Not
biting, not hunting,
just carrying. Jaws close around your
body before you can even stand and they
lift you and they move fast and you let
them because you have no idea what's
holding you and no way to find out.
You're blind. Not blind from the dark,
blind for life. You wait for your eyes
to start working and they never will
because you weren't built with the kind
that see. Everything you will ever know
arrives as smell and touch. The scent of
the body ahead of you, the weight of the
body behind. The jaws set you down into
a moving line and you do the only thing
your body knows how to do. You find the
ant in front of you, you follow it, you
don't know where it's going. You will
never know where it's going.
Not one ant in this line knows and the
line is half a million long. You've
heard of your kind, the swarm that
strips everything in its path, the
nightmare that eats anything too slow to
run, the monster.
That's the colony. That's not you.
You are one ant in a body of 500,000.
You have no name. You have no home. You
have one job and the job is to never
stop walking. And somewhere in that
simple rule, a death you can't see is
already waiting for you. It started the
moment those jaws set you down. It won't
stop until you drop. Here is the deal
you were born into. Together, the colony
is one of the most powerful predators on
Earth. Blind, brainless on its own, but
moving as one, it can strip six tennis
courts of forest of every living thing
in a day. And your one rule, follow the
ant ahead, never stop, never break the
line, is the only reason that body
works.
It's the perfect system. It's why you
can't be beaten. It's also the exact
thing that can kill you because if that
trail ever loops back on itself, you
will follow it in a circle until you
drop dead and never once realize you
stopped going anywhere.
Your greatest strength has a death built
into it. And here's the part that will
get you. And the way this ends, you'll
walk straight into the thing that kills
you and you'll be completely certain
you're doing everything right. Just wait
for it. The march starts before the sun
is up. You don't decide to march. The
ant in front of you moves, so you move.
The ant behind you moves because you
did. The trail knows where to go, a
smell laid down by the ants ahead, and
your only job is to not lose it. A log
appears in your path. The column doesn't
go around it, it flows over it, up one
side and down the other. Rocks, roots, a
dead branch, the river of you simply
pours across all of it. You move 20 m an
hour.
Every hour, all day, and everything in
front of you runs. A cricket bursts out
of the leaf litter. A spider abandons
its web. They're not running from one
ant. One ant is nothing.
They're running from the front of you, a
wall of half a million blind mouths that
eats anything too slow. Go back for a
second to before you could walk. You
were a larva in the dark and ants you
never saw came and fed you.
You didn't choose what they brought or
how much and that feeding by strangers
in the black decided everything you
would ever be. Fed a little,
you stay small, a worker the size of a
grain of rice, built to carry babies and
to be a brick in the wall at night.
Fed more, you become a soldier with a
head so huge you can barely lift it and
jaws like hooked blades. Sounds like the
better deal. It isn't. Those jaws are so
big the soldier can't feed itself.
It has to be hand-fed by the smaller
workers. It's whole life built into a
weapon so completely it can no longer do
the one thing every animal needs to do.
Whatever they fed you, you didn't choose
it. You woke up already being it.
Something hits the column. You don't see
it. You can't. The first you know of it
is the ground shaking through your legs
and the scent of the ants around you
spiking with alarm all at once. There
are birds that have built their whole
lives around you. They don't fear the
swarm, they follow it day after day
dropping down to snatch the insects you
flush out of the leaves.
And when the pickings are thin, they
take you. A shadow you will never see
drops out of a sky you have never seen
and the ant in front of you a second ago
is simply gone. You keep walking. You
have to.
The trail says keep going and the trail
is the only thing you have.
The same blindness that keeps you locked
to the trail is the reason you'll never
see the thing that eats you. When the
light fades, the colony stops marching,
but there is no nest waiting. There has
never been a nest. So you build one.
Out of yourselves. You and hundreds of
thousands of others hook your legs and
jaws together and become the walls, the
floors, the tunnels, a structure a meter
across. Queen and babies deep in the
warm center made entirely of living ants
holding still for hours in the dark. If
you're on the outside, you're the wall.
You hang there in the cold all night
gripping while the inside stays warm. In
the morning the house comes apart, every
brick stands up, and the brick walks
away. You were the architecture.
Now you're back in the line. That is
your actual life. This is the colony at
the height of its power. And for once,
you are part of something winning. A
roach the size of 50 of you tries to
run. It doesn't matter. The front folds
around it. You can't see it, but you
feel the other surge, and you surge with
them, and your jaws find something hard,
and you bite down, and you do not let go
while 100 others do the same. In
seconds, the thing that was 50 times
your size stops moving. The soldiers cut
it apart. The carriers haul the pieces
back toward the babies.
Nothing too slow survives the front of
you.
Half a million blind individuals, no
leader, no plan, moving like one
enormous animal across the forest floor.
This is the monster you were scared of.
The nightmare swarm.
And now you know what? It's actually
made of half a million blind slaves who
never chose any of it, following a
smell, unable to stop. It works. It
actually works. And it works because not
one of you ever stops to ask where the
line is going, which is the most
dangerous thing about you. It only takes
one wrong turn. You're near the edge of
the column when the ant leading your
little branch hits something, a stone, a
gap, a break in the trail, and turns
around.
And the moment it turns, it picks up the
freshest, strongest scent nearby, the
scent of the ants behind it,
which is you. So, it starts following
you, and you're following the ant ahead
of you.
And that ant is following the one ahead
of it, and the line, which has always
been straight, quietly bends into a
circle and closes. Nobody notices. None
of you can see.
All any of you knows is that the trail
is strong, and the trail says keep
going. So, you keep going. This is the
death spiral. You are now walking in a
perfect circle, and so is everyone
around you. And the longer you do it,
the worse it gets because every lap, you
all lay down more scent, and the
stronger the smell of the circle
becomes, the more certain every ant is
that this is the trail, that this is the
way, that you are going somewhere.
You are going nowhere. You have never
gone anywhere.
You are blind and you are following a
circle of your own making and you cannot
tell the difference between this and the
march that fed a colony of a million.
For hours, sometimes for days,
the blind keep palpating the smooth
trail and the bodies of the ants ahead
of them, never once perceiving that they
are making no progress, only wasting
everything they have. One by one you
start to drop.
And the ones still walking step over the
ones who fell and keep circling because
the trail says keep going. Your greatest
strength, the thing that made you
unbeatable,
it just turned you into a wheel of the
dying.
That was the promise. And here's the
part that should bother you, if you had
anything in you that could be bothered.
The colony doesn't notice. A few hundred
of you spun off and died in a circle and
to a body of half a million,
that's nothing. The march doesn't slow.
The queen keeps laying. The bivouac
builds itself again at dusk out of other
bodies. You were never an individual.
You were a cell.
And a body does not grieve a cell. You
hatched blind. You were the wall and the
weapon and the wheel. And you never once
saw the thing you gave everything for.
You die where you fell.
Nothing comes back for you. There are
over 200 kinds of army ant, some 20
million strong, and they have been
marching across this planet blind,
homeless,
eating everything in their path for a
hundred million years. Every one of them
lived the life you just lived. And not
one was ever missed. Deep in the warm
center of a bivouac tonight, a new one
of you is hatching. It can't see. It
reaches for the nearest body and holds
on.
Something picks it up in its jaws and
sets it down in a line that is already
moving. It doesn't know where the line
goes. It will follow it anyway.
It always does. Life as an army ant
might be rough, but there's another
animal out there that has it way worse.
Trust me, it's wild. Check out the video
and see for yourself.

You're born the most beautiful bird on earth. And that is going to be a problem.

That tail — longer than your whole body — takes six months to grow. She'll look at it for three seconds, then walk to the male next to you. The same tail that's supposed to win her is the reason the leopard sees you first. And every single year, your own body tears the whole thing off and drops it in the dirt.
This is why it sucks to be born as a peacock.

Nature gave the peacock the most famous beauty on the planet — and made it one of the hardest lives to survive.

subtitles.plaintext:
You are born the most beautiful bird on
Earth. This is going to be a problem.
Not today. Not this year. Not for a
while. Right now, you are a peachick,
brown, the size of a fist. You look like
a slightly off version of your mother,
and that is the only reason you are
alive. Nothing in this forest looks at
you twice. You eat insects. You follow
her through the undergrowth. Nothing
chases you. Nothing notices you. Nothing
wants you. Enjoy it.
In 2 years, your body starts building
the thing that will take over the rest
of your life.
And from the moment it starts, you will
spend every waking hour of every spring
trying to be seen by one specific kind
of audience, and you will fail in front
of her over and over for years. By year
four, your train will be fully
developed. 150 feathers. 300 g. 1 and
1/2 m of bronze and green and iridescent
blue. Each feather ending in an eye
spot, a perfect circle of color that
exists for one reason and one reason
only. You are going to fan that train in
front of a peahen.
You are going to vibrate it until every
feather shimmers and the rustling fills
the air. You are going to position
yourself so the morning light hits the
eye spots at exactly the angle that
makes them blaze. She is going to walk
to the male with slightly more
iridescent eye spots than you. You are
going to stand there
with your tail fanned in an empty lek,
and the worst part isn't the empty lek.
It isn't the 6 months you spent growing
the train. It's what happens in August
after you have failed for the entire
season, when your body, on its own,
decides to take the whole thing back.
Just wait for it. Skip forward. You are
2 years old. The train has started.
Small right now, shorter than it will
be, fewer feathers, the eye spots not
yet at full iridescence.
But the compulsion to display has
arrived and you don't know how to
evaluate your own train against the
others yet, so you fan it anyway. You
spread what you have. You vibrate it.
The rustling sounds the same as it will
when the train is full.
The peahens continue foraging. Not once.
Not on the days when you position it
perfectly. Not on the mornings when the
light is right. Every morning, whether
anyone approaches or not, whether the
dominant male is watching or not,
whether it is working or not, the
display happens because the display must
happen.
The compulsion does not ask whether it
is worth it. This is your life for the
next 2 years
building the train and displaying it in
a lek while the peahens, on average,
visit three different males before
choosing one and choose based on the
iridescence of the eye spots, the
density of the lower train,
the vigor of the vibration, all things
that are not yet fully yours. 3 years
old, the train is bigger. Still not
full.
Still not enough. The dominant male in
your lek copulated 11 times last season.
You copulated zero. You did do one
thing.
A younger male, 2 years old, smaller
train, no threat, wandered into your
display area. You turned, fanned the
full train, and walked toward him. He
left immediately.
You claimed approximately 4 square
meters of muddy ground at the edge of a
forest in India. That is your territory.
You display in it every morning. Nobody
comes.
But no one else is in it, either.
Year four. The train is complete. Year
four, the full train fans open for the
first time. 150 feathers.
You feel the weight of them different
from the seasons before the full spread,
the full rustle, every eye spot catching
the morning light. You have been
building toward this for 2 years and now
it is here and it is objectively
extraordinary. A peahen approaches.
She is looking at the lower section of
your train. Not the eye spots, not the
iridescent crown you spent 6 months on,
the lower train. For about 3 seconds.
Not the chest, the lower train
for roughly 3 seconds. She walks to the
male 12 m away. His eye spots are
fractionally more iridescent. You cannot
measure this. She can. If a peahen
walked past your tail, the lek is a
territorial arrangement that is not
designed in your favor. Males claim
display areas and defend them. The most
dominant males claim the center. Peahens
entering the lek drift toward the
center.
Research on lek behavior shows that in a
group of 10 males, the top one or two
males will account for the majority of
matings.
The males at the edge of the lek display
just as hard, fan just as fully, vibrate
just as vigorously, and copulate
significantly less.
Sometimes zero. You are at the edge of
the lek. Not because your tail is bad,
because the male in the center has a
fractionally better tail and peahens,
applying evolutionary logic that has
worked for millions of years, prefer to
mate with a fractional best available.
Their offspring will inherit those
genes. It is a rational system. It is a
rational system in which you are
standing at the edge of a field with 150
feathers fanned in the morning light
displaying to no one. There are good
mornings. You learn the light. The eye
spots iridescent peaks when the sun is
at a specific angle roughly 45° relative
to your position, and you learn to
rotate your display to hold that angle
as the sun moves. You learn when the
peahens move through the lek and you are
ready before they arrive.
You learn to hold the vibration longer,
to fan the lower train wider, to produce
the specific wing spread and bow at the
right moment. A peahen approaches and
stays. She watches the lower train.
She watches the eye spot iridescence.
She is still there after 30 seconds,
which is longer than most.
You continue the display, the vibration,
the shimmer, the rustling of 150
feathers all moving together. She walks
to the dominant male. He had been
displaying to another female. She waited
for him. Year six, your best display.
The light is exactly right. The angle is
correct. The lower train is at peak
development, the eye spot iridescence
running at full saturation in the
morning sun.
You have been in this lek for four years
and you know every variable and today
every variable is correct. A peahen
approaches. She watches for a long time.
She watches the lower train, the
shimmer, the density of the fan. She has
visited two other males this morning.
She chooses you. This is the thing six
years of building was for.
The six months of 3% daily energy, the
two years of displaying an inferior
train, the mornings at the edge of the
lek when no one approached.
This specific moment, this specific
choice, is what all of it was building
toward. It lasts approximately 10
seconds. Research shows that
approximately half of peahens mate with
more than one male per season.
Three days later, she mates with the
dominant male. Then she lays her eggs
and raises the chicks alone. You are not
involved. You will not know the chicks.
Your contribution to the next generation
is the 10 seconds and the genes and the
eye spots. In August, the tail falls
out. Not one feather, all of them.
The 150 feathers that took six months of
3% of your daily energy to construct,
the 1 and 1/2 m of bronze and green and
iridescent blue that the peahen assessed
in 3 seconds, they fall to the ground
over the course of a few weeks. And the
most spectacular bird in this forest
becomes a brown
nondescript bird that looks like a
slightly larger version of the females.
You stand in the pile of your own
feathers. The regrowth starts
immediately. Small pin feathers pushing
through the beginning of next season's
train. 7 months to regrow it. Then the
lek again. Then the display.
Then the peahen visits three males and
chooses the one with the best lower
train iridescence. This is every year
for up to 40 years
in every lek across India and Sri Lanka.
Right now, there are male peacocks in
full display. Each one has spent 6
months and 3% of its daily energy
building a train. Each one has learned
the light. Each one is vibrating 150
feathers in the morning sun. Research on
lek behavior consistently finds the same
pattern. The top one or two males in a
lek account for a disproportionate share
of all matings.
The males below them display just as
hard with trains nearly as impressive in
the same light to the same peahens and
get significantly fewer approaches.
Sometimes none. They display anyway.
They cannot not display. The compulsion
to fan and vibrate and hold the angle of
the light arrived at year two and it
will not leave until they are dead. In
August, everyone's tail falls out. In
September, everyone starts building
again. Drop a peacock emoji if any of
this hit you. And there is one more
animal that spends its entire life
building toward a single moment of being
chosen.
It does not have feathers. It cannot
display. It just makes a sound and
waits. Next video.
