subtitles.plaintext:
You drag yourself out of the egg and
your face is already trying to kill
something. Not chewing, not searching,
hunting. Folded under your mouth is a
second jaw. Spring-loaded, ready, and it
was built before you were because body
has been planning this since before you
hatched. You are a dragonfly. The one on
tea towels, the one your grandmother
thinks brings good luck, the one people
get tattooed on the wrist to mean
freedom. This is what that looks like
before the postcards. You can't fly. You
don't have wings. You have armor and a
face that shoots and you live at the
bottom of a pond in the cold and the
dark and you will live down here for a
long, long time. Not for a week, not for
a month, not for a year, for four.
Four entire years in the mud. And the
pretty version, the one with the wings,
gets four weeks. And the beautiful
thing with the wings, the one everyone
loves that only gets four weeks, here's
the deal you were born into. Those four
years are spent doing one thing,
surviving a pond that is trying to eat
you every single second. And if you make
it, if you're one of the almost none who
last, you'll climb a reed in the dark,
split your own body open, and pull a
winged thing out of yourself for 1 hour.
That new thing can't fly, can't run,
can't fight. And the worst part isn't
the four years.
It isn't the pond. It's that the most
dangerous hour of your entire life is
the one right after you finally become
beautiful.
Just wait for it. You're hungry. You
hatched hungry. You don't move toward
the tadpole. The rule is you are the
ambush. The water moves things toward
you. The tadpole's tail brushes a leaf.
It turns. Its body lines up with your
face 1/30 of a second. The jaw under
your face fires forward on a hinge,
hooks the tadpole, folds back in. The
tadpole is now inside you.
It never saw you. You are 5 days old.
You just did the thing your body was
built for. You got it right on the first
try. It works.
It actually works.
This is the only good moment you will
have for 3 years. Something is hunting
you. It is 40 times your size and it is
looking right at you. Your body decides
before you do. You contract a set of
muscles inside your rectum and a jet of
water fires out of your back end. You
shoot three body lengths into the weeds.
The dragonfly nymph's only escape
mechanism is a butt rocket. You wait 20
minutes.
You breathe through your back end until
the fish loses interest, which is also
why you escaped, which is the most
undignified survival mechanism in the
entire animal kingdom. A fish almost ate
you and you saved yourself by
farting.
8 days old. 3 years to go. You molt.
Your old armor cracks down the back and
you pull yourself out of it. For 10
minutes, you are soft and white and you
cannot fight anything. A newt finds the
nymph next to you doing the same.
The newt eats her in three bites. You
eat a mosquito larva. You eat a worm.
Down here, the math doesn't care.
Winter. The pond freezes. Your heart
slows to one beat every 2 minutes.
You sit in cold black mud for 4 months.
Not eating. Not moving. You don't have
anything that thinks. The ice cracks. A
frog is awake.
It is between you and the only escape
route. You fire your jet sideways. You
make it. 200 of you hatched in this
pond. 80 made it through the first week.
40 made it through the first year. 12
are still alive after 3 years. You are
one of them. You don't know that. You
don't know what siblings are.
You've been a stomach with armor in a
pond for 3 years, and you have never had
a single thought. By your fourth year,
you are large. You are one of the
biggest things in this pond. There is
exactly one thing down here that can
still kill you. It's another one of you.
A dragonfly nymph's deadliest predator
for most of its life is a bigger
dragonfly nymph. You have eaten dozens
of smaller ones without a thought. Now
you are the smaller one. It doesn't
rush.
It doesn't have to. It learned the same
rule you did before it hatched. Times
you are the ambush, the water moves
things towards you times, and right now
the thing the water is moving is you.
You back away slowly. One leg at a time.
You do not fire your jet. The burst of
movement is exactly what its face is
waiting for. You hold still in the open
water in full view for 10 minutes while
a larger version of yourself decides
whether you are worth the strike. A
water beetle crosses between you. The
bigger nymph's face fires at the beetle.
It chose the easier meal. You are alive
because, for once, something else was
smaller than you. Four years of
surviving everything in this pond, and
the closest you came to dying was
looking into your own face. Then, one
morning in your fourth spring, something
inside you changes. Your legs want the
surface upward. For the first time in
your entire life, upward. You climb out
of the water. The air feels wrong, thin,
too cold against the wet armor. You've
never felt it before. Your body doesn't
stop. You grip the reed. You hold still,
and then your back splits open. The
shell you have worn for 4 years splits
open, and something pulls itself out of
you headfirst. It is also you. You hang
upside down from the body you used to
live in.
Your wings are folded against your back
like wet paper. You will not be able to
move for 1 hour. A sparrow lands two
stems over. It looks at you. You can't
turn your head. You can't fly.
You don't have the face that fires
anymore. The sparrow takes off. You hear
what happens to the nymph emerging on
the next reed. Your wings keep
inflating. It comes back. A breeze comes
through the reeds.
Your reed bends.
Its grip slips and it flies.
It doesn't come back. Your wings finish
hardening. You let go of the reed. And
for the first time in 4 years, you are
not in the water. You are in the sky.
You can fly in six directions: forward,
backward, sideways, up, down, hover. No
other insect on this planet can do this.
Your eyes have 30,000 lenses.
Your great great great ancestors had
2-ft wingspans and ruled the sky 300
million years ago before there were
birds, before there were flowers. You
are the best flying animal that has ever
lived. You have 28 days to enjoy it.
Most of those days, this happens. A male
grabs you out of the sky. Hooks on the
end of his abdomen, actual hooks. They
clamp onto the back of your neck and he
drags you through the air attached to
him by your skull.
He forces your body into a position the
textbooks call the wheel. He doesn't
fertilize you first. He has another job.
He scoops out the previous male. He has
a tool for it, a scoop
on his body.
Dragonflies evolved a tool specifically
for scraping rival sperm out of females
before adding their own.
4 years in a pond, 4 weeks in the sky.
And the reward is being neck clamped by
a flying creature with a custodial
appendage. He lets go.
He flies off. You keep flying, you drop
your eggs in the water,
the same pond you crawled out of, about
200 of them. Most won't hatch.
Of the ones that do,
most won't make the first week.
Of the few that survive 4 years of
underwater warfare, most will be eaten
while their wings are still wet.
That was the promise. It wasn't a fish.
It wasn't a frog. It was the 1 hour
where the new body doesn't work yet, in
full view of every bird waking up around
the pond. You got lucky.
The sparrow couldn't grip the reed. It
learned though. It came back the next
morning. You die 3 days after laying
your eggs. A frog eats most of you. Ants
finish the rest. 3,000 species of
dragonfly on Earth.
300 million years of the same loop.
4 years in a pond.
4 weeks in the sky.
Eaten with wet wings.
Over and over and over. In the mud at
the bottom of the pond, one of the 200
eggs you laid is hatching. Six legs, no
wings.
A face that doesn't fit a face. It
doesn't know about the sky yet. It has 4
years to find out, if it's lucky. So,
life as a dragonfly might be rough, but
there's another animal out there that
has it way worse. Trust me, it's wild.
Check out the video and see for
yourself.

subtitles.plaintext:
You hatch from an egg and immediately
fall into the dark. You will not see the
sky again for 17 years. You are not
sleeping. You are awake down here
tunneling, feeding on root sap, growing
through five body stages over 17 years,
aware of the dark, aware of the roots,
aware of the slow passage of seasons
through the temperature of the soil. And
when you finally come out, you will have
4 weeks to do everything your species
needs you to do. Then, you will die. 17
years. 4 weeks. That is the deal. Your
body is counting, not consciously.
Through changes in the root sap, spring
chemistry, winter chemistry, your body
reads each cycle and increments
something, some biological counter that
nobody has ever fully understood, toward
the number 17. Some cicadas get the
count wrong. A warm spring that mimics
the seasonal signal too early. A cold
year that blurs the boundary between one
cycle and the next. Something in the
root sap that reads like a cycle when it
isn't. The counter ticks to 17 before 17
years have passed or after, and the
cicada emerges alone. No brood. No
millions of siblings. No wall of sound
carrying for miles. Just one cicada
surfacing into a forest that has moved
on without it. It sings. Nothing
answers. You are going to be one of
them. Skip forward. You are 3 years
underground. You are the size of a
fingernail. You have molted twice, shed
your outer shell, and grown a new,
larger one each time. You move through
the soil, find roots, feed almost
continuously because the sap is thin,
and you need a great deal of it to grow.
Above you, seasons cycle through the
root chemistry. Spring sap, summer sap,
the thin, cold sap of winter when the
tree pulls its resources down. Your body
reads each one. 3 4 are
five. In year four, you molt for the
third time. In the dark, alone, you shed
your own skin.
The old shell splits along your back and
you pull yourself out of it, legs, head,
the whole shape of you, and leave it
behind in the soil. You are soft for a
few hours, pale, larger than before.
The new shell hardens around you in the
dark and you lock back onto the root and
you keep feeding. Nobody sees this. It
happens in the dark and the root is
there and the counter keeps going. Six,
seven.
Skip forward 10 years. You are close to
adult size now, still wingless, still in
the dark. The forest above you has
changed. Saplings become trees, old
trees fallen.
You have been feeding on this forest for
a decade and the forest does not know
you exist. Above you, right now, the
brood is underground, too. Millions of
them. In 14 states, all counting. And
And no all reading the same root
chemistry you are reading. All
incrementing toward the same number. You
are counting with them. Your count is
wrong. Skip forward year 16. Your eyes
have begun to turn red. This is not a
decision.
Your body's counter has reached a
threshold and the chemistry has shifted
and the eyes are turning red and
emergence is coming and there's nothing
you can do about the timing of it. You
begin building the exit tunnel. A
vertical shaft, half an inch wide,
running straight up through the soil.
You stop just below the surface. The
last half inch of earth between you and
the sky. The trigger is temperature.
The soil at 8 in depth must reach
exactly 64°F,
not approximately, exactly. Your body
will not break through until it does.
You wait. 16 years and 11 months
underground, 1 in from the sky. You've
been underground for 17 years. 1 in from
the sky. Drop A if you'd have broken
through early. A warm week in April, the
soil hits 64°. You break through the
surface, the light is overwhelming. You
have not seen light in 17 years.
You climb the nearest tree trunk, wings
wet and folded, exoskeleton still soft.
You wait for the sound. There is no
sound. The forest is a normal forest on
a normal April morning. No roar of
emergence.
No wall of sound. No millions of
siblings breaking the surface alongside
you. Just birds doing what birds do and
a squirrel in the undergrowth and a
woodpecker working at a tree somewhere
to the left. Because the emergence is
not happening. You emerged alone, but
the sun is on your back. For 17 years,
your world was the cold of soil at
depth.
The specific temperature of roots in
winter, the thin warmth of summer
conducted downward through 6 in of
earth. You have never felt direct
sunlight before this moment.
It hits your exoskeleton now and every
receptor in your body is registering
something it has no category for. Warm
in a way nothing underground was ever
warm. You cling to the bark and the sun
moves across you and for this one
specific moment before the silence has
fully registered, this part is correct.
This part is everything you were built
for.
Then you wait for the sound. Your
exoskeleton hardens over 6 hours. Your
wings dry. You turn dark, the black and
orange of an adult cicada and your
timbal, the vibrating membrane on the
sides of your body,
begins to fire. 100 decibels. The sound
carries for a mile in every direction.
It is the loudest sound any insect on
earth produces and you are producing it
alone in a forest that has no context
for a single cicada song in April, and
every bird within a quarter mile has
turned its head toward you. This is what
17 years was for.
This specific sound at this specific
frequency that a female of your species
will respond to with a click, a precise
rhythm, a frequency that only she makes
and only you are listening for.
You were built for this. The song is
perfect. The song is everything. Nothing
clicks back. You sing for a day, 2 days,
3 days. The sound carries for a mile.
The mile is empty. The females who would
have answered are underground still
counting, or they came and went already
and their bodies are decomposing in the
leaf litter below you. Your song is
perfect.
Your timing is wrong. On the fourth day,
a bird lands on the branch. Not a
predator drawn by the roar of emergence
from miles away, just a bird.
Doing what birds do on April mornings in
a forest that has nothing unusual
happening in it. It regards you for a
moment. The survival strategy of your
species is predator satiation. Emerge in
such overwhelming numbers that predators
eat until they cannot eat anymore, and
millions of you survive anyway.
The strategy works because of the brood.
You are not millions. You are one cicada
on a branch in April. You are still
singing when the bird moves. Somewhere
in this forest, 6 weeks before you
emerged, a female straggler laid her
eggs. They are hatching now.
Tiny nymphs, white, the size of ants
dropping from a branch one by one,
falling to the forest floor, immediately
burrowing. Each one finding a root, each
one locking on. The forest floor closes
over them. They are in the dark now,
awake, feeding, beginning to count.
Their count will be wrong, too, or it
will be right.
The same warm spring that fooled you may
have fooled their mother. Or they count
correctly and emerge with the brood and
the forest roars and they are
statistically spared. They do not know
which yet.
They are 1-year-old and underground and
the root sap is turning cold. Brood X is
the largest periodical cicada brood on
Earth. 14 states. In 2021, it emerged
population densities reached 1 and 1/2
million per acre in some areas. The
sound was audible from space
instruments. News stations covered it
for weeks. It is underground right now.
Every nymph from the 2021
emergence is in the soil counting.
They have been underground since 2021.
They will not surface until 2038. They
are awake down there tunneling, feeding,
reading the root sap. Most of them are
counting correctly. Some of them are
not. In 2038, on a Tuesday morning in
May, when the soil hits 64°,
the ground across 14 states will move
and the sky will fill with sound and for
4 weeks, the largest insect emergence on
Earth will happen again.
And in that same forest, a few weeks
later, one more cicada will break the
surface alone. It will climb a tree. It
will begin to sing. The sound will carry
for a mile. 17 years underground for 4
weeks above ground. And some of them get
the count wrong. Drop A if that hit you.
And if you want to see another animal
whose life is somehow even harder, it's
right there.

subtitles.plaintext:
You crack out of your egg and your
species is 37 million years old, not
something like you. You,
the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs 66
million years ago, your lineage was in
the water when the sky went dark and it
was still in the water when the sky
cleared. The design was already correct.
Nothing has needed to change.
And right now the design is 20 cm long,
wet with egg membrane, blinking in June
heat, and of the 37 siblings in this
nest,
80% will be dead before next summer. The
question is, which ones? You do not know
you are 20 cm long. You do not know what
20 cm means.
You know warmth and cold and the
specific vibration of your mother moving
on the bank and the sound of your
siblings breathing in the water around
you.
You know the signals your body was born
running. Stay shallow, go still, read
the surface. That is the entire map you
have. It is going to have to be enough.
Before you have been in the water 24
hours, your mother is going to put you
in her mouth. These are the jaws that
will one day generate the strongest bite
force of any living animal on Earth.
Nearly 3,000 lb per square inch, enough
to go through the shell of a snapping
turtle. Your entire body fits inside
them and for 45 seconds, it is going to
be the safest you will ever be in your
life.
Before you hatch, the summer decides
something about you that you will carry
forever. Your mother built this nest
from rotting marsh grass, the rotting
generates heat. 3° C is the entire
difference between hatching male and
hatching female. A cloud on a Tuesday
had more say over what you are than you
did. She has not eaten in 60 days. She
is there when you start calling from
inside the shell.
She tears the nest open and picks you
up. It is dark. There is filtered green
light through the gaps in her teeth. You
can feel every step she takes through
the vibration in her throat. Her breath
is warm.
Nothing in the swamp can reach you. She
reaches the waterline.
She opens her jaws. Cold water hits your
whole body at once. She is already
turning back for the next one. That
moment, the warmth, the darkness, the
filtered light,
the total safety of being carried lasted
45 seconds. It was the safest you will
ever be. You didn't know that while it
was happening. 24 of you in the shallows
now. You can feel your siblings through
the water, the small pressure of their
movement, the warmth of bodies close
together. Your mother is a dark shape on
the bank. The swamp is enormous and loud
and completely new and you have no map
for any of it except the one that
arrived with you. Stay close, stay
shallow, read the surface.
The heron arrives the same afternoon. It
has been fishing this bank since before
your nest was built. It reads the
surface, picks the sibling in open
water, and strikes before the water
reacts.
Your mother charges it. It lifts off 50
m and waits. You are in the reeds.
Something, a shadow, a vibration moved
you there. You don't know this, saved
you. Skip forward. The first week runs
through you like this. A raccoon at dusk
on the wrong side of the pod. A
largemouth bass from below on day four.
You feel the pressure change and you are
already moving shallow before the strike
lands. Something that was beside you is
not beside you anymore. Day six, a
juvenile alligator moves through your
section of the reeds close enough that
you feel the current from its tail. By
the end of the first week, the pod is
smaller, your mother is still here,
you are still in it. Those are the only
facts that matter. If you think you'd
have made it out of the first week, drop
in comments. Be honest. Skip forward.
You are 4 months old, 14 in long. You
know this water now, every depth change,
every section of bank, where the
raccoons come. The hunting has started.
You catch a frog on the bank and your
tail does the slow flick, that means
correct. And your mother is not here.
She moved on last week, no announcement.
She was there in the morning and by
evening her watchfulness was simply
gone. This is what growing up means for
an alligator. Not a transition, an
absence where something was. The heron
is on the far bank.
You go still. A frog lands on the bank 2
ft away. Everything fires
simultaneously. The lock, the weight
shift, the jaw ready. The stalk takes 10
seconds. The strike is done before the
frog registers anything.
Your tail does the slow flick, that
means correct. This is what the 37
million years was building toward. 4
seconds of the design working exactly as
it was built to work.
Then the heron moves on the far bank and
you go still again. The swamp does not
pause for the 4 seconds you just had.
Skip forward.
January. You are in the shallow channel
when the vibration arrives. Not from
above, from the water itself. A low
frequency your body has never felt.
Every system cuts.
You are not breathing in a way that
moves the water. An adult male, 8 ft,
moving toward you. Adult alligators eat
juveniles not from aggression, because
you are the size of prey.
The 37 million years of shared lineage
does not register at this distance. Your
yellow stripes are the exact color of
dead marsh grass in the shadow of the
bank. You are not a hatchling in the
reeds.
You are a shape that does not move. He
passes 2 m from you. You feel every step
through the water. You do not move for 1
hour. Not from caution, because your
body has not cleared the signal.
The still and wait runs until every
frequency in the water is wind and
current and nothing with 200 kg behind
it. When you finally move, the sun is
low.
Skip forward.
Spring, 8 months old, 18 in long. Of the
24 hatchlings that entered the water on
hatching morning, 10 are still alive.
Not the strongest 10.
The 10 for whom the geometry where they
were standing each time the thing that
kills alligators came through went right
instead of wrong. You are one of the 10.
That is all you are and it is
everything.
Skip forward.
3 years. You are 4 ft long. It is dawn.
The heron is on the bank ahead of you
and it lifts off before you reach it.
Not because you threatened it. Because
the calculation of risk has shifted and
the answer came back wrong for it. Below
4 ft you were prey. Above 4 ft you are
the swamp's problem, not its victim. You
did not earn this.
3 years of going still in time. 3 years
of the geometry going your way on enough
of the mornings that mattered. Your body
does not age the way other bodies age.
No fixed decline.
You will simply accumulate a foot a year
and if nothing kills you, you will reach
4 m and live for 50 years. Here, when
the road that borders this marsh is long
gone. The same animal. The same water.
The same posture. Your species was
always going to produce this. The
question was whether it was going to be
you. Researchers at Rockefeller Wildlife
Refuge in Louisiana have been tagging
alligators since the 1970s.
One female tagged in 1979 was recaptured
in 2016, 37 years.
She had been in the same section of
marsh the whole time. She didn't know
she was extraordinary. She was just
still there. She was carried in her
mother's jaws in August 1979.
She went still in the reeds when males
passed. She reached 4 ft and the herons
began to lift off. That is what is in
the stillness. For every alligator that
gets to that stillness, that is what is
in it. If you made it through the first
week, drop a dot, and the next animal's
first year makes this look easy. It's
right there.

subtitles.plaintext:
You are born the most capable predator
in this building. You are also
completely blind, completely deaf, and
the size of a tea bag. These two facts
are going to define the next 15 years of
your life. Day one, your eyes are sealed
shut and your ears are sealed shut and
the entire world is warmth and smell and
the sound of heartbeats. But your nose
is already running at full capacity. 40
million scent receptors more than a
human will ever have reading the air
before you have any other way to read
anything. You know your mother by smell.
You know each sibling by smell. You can
track the warmth gradient across the
nest to within a centimeter. You are
blind, deaf, and helpless. You are also
already the most sophisticated chemical
detection system in this building. Week
two.
Your eyes open. The world arrives all at
once. Shapes, light, the blur of your
mother's face, the movement of siblings.
Your ears unseal 4 days later and the
sound arrives on top of all of it. The
creak of the room, the hum of something
electrical in the wall, your mother's
breathing. Every single thing is new and
enormous and you have no way to know yet
which of it matters. Your legs don't
work properly. You fall over. You get
up. You fall over again.
But your paws are already doing
something your legs aren't. The kneading
reflex, the grip, the reaching. The
hunting starts in the paws before it
starts anywhere else. Week four. A piece
of fluff moves across the floor. You
don't decide anything. Your entire body
decides before you do, every system
firing simultaneously. Pupils blowing to
full black, weight shifting to your back
legs. The world narrowing to the
movement of that piece of fluff and
nothing else. You have never hunted
anything. You have never been taught to
hunt. Your mother has not shown you a
single thing about how this works. You
sprint. You catch it in both paws.
Your jaw does the bite, the specific
neck bite that goes between the
vertebrae, the one that ends things
fast. The bite your body knew before you
had a body to know it with. It is a
piece of fluff.
You kill it in under a second. Your tail
does the slow deliberate flick that
means correct. Everything is installed.
Everything works.
You are 4 weeks old and you are already
exactly the animal you were built to be.
Month two. A human comes and takes you
home. You were born in a house with a
garden and a field beyond it and the
smell of open ground coming through
every window.
You are taken to a flat. You assess it
in 20 minutes. Every corner, every
surface, every window. You already know
its dimensions. You already know it
completely. You sit at the window.
Outside, a pigeon on the ledge 2 m away
through the glass. Your jaw starts
moving the kill bite, the one that goes
between the vertebrae, practicing on
air.
The pigeon doesn't know you exist. This
is your territory now. 60 square meters,
one window, one pigeon you cannot reach.
Your ancestor chose this.
10,000 years ago, a wildcat walked
toward a human settlement and made a
calculation. Warmth, food, shelter, and
walked in. Nobody invited it. The cat
decided. This is what it decided for
you. Somewhere around month three, at
2:00 in the morning, you are going to
sprint full speed from the bedroom to
the bathroom to the kitchen and back
again for no reason the human can see.
They are going to film it. They are
going to post it. Millions of people are
going to watch it and call it the
zoomies and laugh. You are going to be
doing that three or four times a week
for the next 15 years.
And every single time, there is going to
be a reason, the same reason, a reason
nobody who filmed it understood. Inside
the wall, something is moving. You know
exactly what it is. 9 cm behind the
plaster, moving left toward the skirting
board. You can hear its claws on the
pipe.
You can smell it through the gap. Every
system has come online. Pupils blown,
ears locked, weight shifted forward,
back legs coiled. You are absolutely,
completely ready. The wall doesn't open.
You sit in front of it for 2 hours. The
human waves a hand in front of your
face. You don't respond.
They post a video, my cat has lost his
mind. You have not lost your mind. You
are doing exactly what your mind was
built to do. The mind just didn't come
with a wall.
At 3:00 a.m., your body wakes you up and
says, "Now." Not a sound, not a
movement.
Your internal clock, the same one your
ancestors have been running for millions
of years, has been tracking the dark.
And 3:00 in the morning is when prey is
slowest, and cats see best. And every
chemical in your body is saying the same
thing at the same time. Go. You go. Full
speed from the bedroom to the hall, off
the wall, over the sofa, back to the
bedroom, back to the hall.
Your heart rate has tripled. Your pupils
are all the way open.
Your body is doing everything it was
ever built to do. Moving fast through
territory, reading every corner,
covering ground. There is nothing to
catch. There is never anything to catch.
4 minutes.
Then, it stops. You sit in the middle of
the hall, breathing. You lick a paw
once. You go back to sleep. The human is
standing in the doorway. They have
filmed it on their phone.
In the comments, 8,000 people are going
to write, "Why do cats do this?"
You do this because you are a predator
whose hunt signal fired into an empty
flat in the middle of the night, and
your body had no way to finish the
sequence except to run. You do this
three or four times a week
for 15 years. If your cat does this,
drop in the comments. I want to know how
many of you have been filming this
without knowing what it was. There are
good years.
The flat finds its shape. At noon, the
sun comes through the south window and
hits a specific patch of kitchen floor
and you lie in it for 2 hours and your
body is warm all the way through and the
3:00 a.m. signal hasn't fired yet.
And the wall is quiet and nothing is
wrong. She comes home at 6:00. You are
at the door. She puts her face in your
fur. These are the good years. The
design is still running. It is just
running quietly.
You bring her a bird in October. Not
because you are hungry,
because she is part of your territory
and your territory is your family and
your family needs to eat and this is
what you do for family. You spent 40
minutes on this.
The stalk in the back garden, real
territory, real ground, the first proper
hunt you have had since the piece of
fluff in week four.
The kill was clean. You placed it on the
doormat, arranged correctly, and sat
beside it. She comes home and stops in
the doorway. You watch her face.
This is the moment, the moment the
provider sees what you have brought and
the effort is recognized. She makes a
sound you have not heard before. She
does not pick up the bird.
She backs away from it. You have given
her the best thing you know how to give,
the fullest expression of care your
design contains.
This is love in the only language you
were built to speak. She puts it in a
bag and puts the bag in the bin. You sit
on the doormat for a while after.
You watch where the bag went. You have
not understood what happened, but when
she comes over and strokes you once on
the head, you allow it. You always allow
it. At 11 years old, you still go out
before dawn. Your joints feel the cold
now. The left hip, especially on wet
mornings.
But you go anyway. The garden at 5:00
a.m. is still the garden at 5:00 a.m.
The long grass at the fence, the cold
air full of information your nose is
still perfectly capable of reading. You
go still, full lock. The weight shifts,
the pupils go wide, the jaw begins the
movement it always begins when prey is
close. Your body doesn't know it's 11.
Your body is exactly what it always was.
The same body that killed the piece of
fluff in week four, unchanged. The bird
is in the grass. You stalk here for 4
minutes. You miss. Not by much. You were
fast, you are still fast. But not quite
as fast as the bird. You sit in the wet
grass. She comes to the back door and
calls your name. You have known this
sound for 11 years, the specific
frequency of it, the way it rises at the
end. You turn and go to her. She picks
you up, both arms, her face pressed into
the top of your head. The warmth comes
through her coat. Your purring starts
before you decide anything. The hunt is
still there. It will always be there. It
just didn't work this morning. This
does. There are 600 million domestic
cats on Earth. Every single one of them
started like this. Blind in the dark,
nose already running, eyes opening in
week two. The prey drive firing in week
four on whatever moved a piece of fluff,
a shadow, a fly. And then a human, and a
flat, and a wall, and a window with
birds on the other side of it. Every
single one of them is doing this right
now. Somewhere a cat is sprinting
through an empty flat at 3:00 a.m. with
nowhere to go. Somewhere a cat has
brought something dead to a human it
considers family and is sitting on a
doormat watching where the bag went. The
design was built for a different world.
It runs in this one anyway. If you have
a cat, go look at it right now. Really
look at it. Because that thing sleeping
on your sofa killed its first prey in
week four. And has been trying to kill
things for you ever since.
And that might be the most loyal thing
any animal has ever done. Drop a comment
if any of this explained something your
cat has been doing for years.
And if you want to see another animal
whose life is even harder, it's right
there.

to the moment it waits by the door for someone who isn't coming back.

subtitles.plaintext:
You are born reaching for someone who
isn't there yet. Eyes sealed, legs
useless. The world is just warmth and
smell. Mother, siblings, and underneath
all of it, something different.
Something your body has already decided
matters more than anything else in the
room. She isn't even here. You haven't
met her. You are 6 hours old and you are
already trying to get to her. That
feeling, that specific urgency, will be
with you every single day of the 12
years you are alive. It will never once
feel like enough. 6 weeks later, she is
going to live to 80.
You are going to live to 12. There will
be a Tuesday morning when they carry you
into a small cold room and she sits on
the floor with you the moment you
arrive, the way she always does, and you
put your head on her leg one last time.
Your tail will be going. It is always
going. The first night alone is the
worst night of your life and you don't
survive it. Exactly, you just get to the
other side of it. They put you in the
kitchen with a gate across the door and
a blanket that smells like the breeder's
house, which doesn't smell like her, and
then the lights go off and you are alone
for the first time in your 8 weeks of
existence. You cry. Not performance,
your chest actually hurts. Your mother
is gone. Your siblings are gone. Every
smell that meant safety is gone. There
is one smell left that means anything
and it is coming from above you, from
behind the ceiling, and you cannot reach
it. You cry until your throat gives out.
You push your nose under the gate and
press it to the gap at the floor and
breathe her in from a distance and that
is the only thing that gets you to 4:00
in the morning. At 4:00, she comes
downstairs. She was awake, too. She sits
on the kitchen floor in her pajamas and
puts you in her lap and you press your
face into her chest and your whole body
stops shaking. She is warm. She is here.
Everything that was wrong is temporarily
not wrong. This is the best thing you
have ever felt. You will spend the rest
of your life trying to get back to this
exact feeling. You will get close,
sometimes the park, the couch, her arms
after a long day,
but never quite this completely, never
again this fully, because you will never
again be small enough that she can hold
all of you at once. 9 weeks later, she
leaves for work and your body does
something you have no language for. You
hear the keys, you hear the bag, you
know these sounds now, they are the
sounds that come before the worst thing.
The worst thing is the door. The door
closing with her on the other side of
it. She leaves, the door closes.
You sit in front of it for 4 minutes and
then your chest does the thing it did on
the first night, the actual physical
hurt, the same alarm, except this time
she doesn't come back at 4:00 in the
morning. This time, the door just stays
closed. You howl. The neighbors hear it.
You scratch at the door until your paws
bleed. You eat the corner of the kitchen
counter trying to find something to do
with your mouth that isn't screaming.
You knock over the bin and tear through
it looking for anything that smells like
her, a receipt, a hair tie, a wrapper
from something she ate last week. You
find a sock. You lie down with the sock.
You lie there for 7 hours with the sock.
When she gets home, the kitchen is
destroyed and you are so flooded with
relief that you spin in circles for 30
seconds and then press your entire body
weight against her legs and she sits on
the floor with you and the wreckage all
around her and says your name. Every
day. You do this every day for 12 years.
Not because you choose to, because your
body was built for a world where alone
meant dead. It never learned the
difference between gone for the day and
gone forever. It never needed to, until
now. Few years passed. Sunday. The lead
comes off and for a while nothing is
wrong. The ball leaves her hand and you
go full speed, all four paws off the
ground at the same time. Ears back,
completely gone. You don't decide to
run. Your body is already running. This
is the one moment where the design and
the life it was designed for are
perfectly matched. Nothing is missing.
Nothing is misaligned. You bring it
back. She throws it again. You go again.
14 times.
14 times her arm goes back and 14 times
you go completely without reservation,
everything you have. No hesitation at
the edge. She sits in the grass and you
put the ball in her lap and she wraps
both arms around you and neither of you
moves for a while. The sun on your coat,
her smell all around you. The map
correct. This is it. If you could keep
one day forever, it would be this one.
This exact arrangement. Her arms and the
grass and the ball and the knowledge
that she is right here. You will have
about 600 Sundays in your life. You
don't know that yet. You are 2 years
old. In every biological way that
matters, you are 14. You age 7 years for
every one of hers. While she turns 23,
you hit 35.
While she turns 26 and starts thinking
seriously about her life, you are 49,
your muzzle going gray at the edges,
your hips starting to feel the cold
mornings. She knows this. She knew it
when she got you. She decided the years
were worth it. You were not part of that
conversation. You don't have years. You
have today.
Today she is here and the ball is
somewhere under the couch and her smell
is the first thing you read every time
you walk into a room. Today is the whole
thing. Today is always the whole thing.
You have about 4,000 todays. You've used
over 1,000 already. When you are 3, a
man starts coming to the house. You read
him completely the first time he comes.
Shoes, hands, jacket, lining. 20 minutes
of your nose working while he stands
very still and lets you finish. He
passes. You have a nose more accurate
than any lie detector ever built and he
passes. One evening, she comes home and
he is already there and she goes to him
first. You are at the door. You are
always at the door when the key turns.
She comes in, drops her bag, and her
eyes go to him before they find you. And
she crosses the room to him before she
reaches down for you. It takes 4
seconds. She doesn't notice.
She reaches down for you after hand on
your head. She says your name and your
tail goes because your tail always goes
when she says your name. But those 4
seconds are in your body now. You don't
have language for them. You only have
the feeling of the door open and her
moving away from you. And the specific
quality of waiting that you have been
doing since you were 8 weeks old, but
never quite like this. You bring him the
ball. He throws it. You bring it back.
You add him to the map. You add
everyone. When you are 4, she goes away
for 3 days and something in your chest
cracks open. He stays. He feeds you. He
throws the ball once in the garden and
you bring it back and drop it at his
feet and then walk to the front door and
sit down and don't move. He doesn't
smell like her. The house doesn't smell
right. Every time you pass the front
door, you press your nose to the gap at
the bottom and check and she is not
there and the map has a hole in it the
size of everything. Day two, you stop
eating. Your stomach just closes. He
puts the bowl down. You look at it, look
at the door. She gets back on day three,
9:00 at night. You hear her key from the
top of the stairs and your legs go out
from under you getting down them. You
crash into her the moment the door
opens. You cry the actual sound from the
first night, the same one, and she drops
everything and sits on the floor and you
climb into her lap and press your face
into her neck and your whole body is
shaking. She is laughing. She thinks it
is sweet. She does not know that to you
this was 3 days of the world ending. She
doesn't know because you cannot tell
her. You cannot tell her anything. You
only have this, the shaking, the face in
her neck, the tail going even while the
rest of you is coming apart. There are
good years. Genuinely, uncomplicatedly
good years. They move somewhere with a
garden. You learn every inch of it in an
afternoon. The fence line, the corner
where the fox comes, the patch under the
hydrangea that smells different from the
rest. You add all of it. The rhythm
locks in. Her alarm at 7:00, the kettle,
the lead at 8:00. Her car at 6:00 in the
evening, which you hear from inside the
house 2 minutes before she turns into
the street and you are already at the
door before her key reaches the lock.
You are 6. In dog years, 42. The gray is
at your muzzle now. Your hips give you
trouble on cold mornings. But the lead
goes on at 8:00 and the car comes at
6:00 and on Sundays the ball leaves her
hand and you still go less far than
before, slower coming back, but
completely every time. She still has
both arms for you when you bring it
back. These are the good years. You
don't know they are the good years. You
think this is just what everything is.
She takes you to the park on a Sunday in
October. The air is cold, leaves coming
down. She throws the ball and you go
still. At 8 years old, completely. Your
legs are slower than they were at 2.
Your hips tighten in the cold and you
feel the getting back more than the
going out. None of that stops you. The
ball is in the air and your body knows
where it's going and nothing about that
has changed. Nine times. Nine times her
arm goes back and nine times you go
completely, everything you have. No
reservation, no hesitation at the edge.
On the ninth, you're slower and she
walks out to meet you halfway across the
park. She sits in the grass and you put
your head in her lap and she wraps both
arms around you properly, both arms, her
face in your neck, the way she did on
the first night before things got
complicated and neither of you moves.
The leaves come down on both of you. The
man is close by, his shoulder against
hers.
You can hear another dog somewhere in
the trees. The cold is deep in your coat
now. Her arms are the specific weight of
her arms. You are 8 years old,
biologically 56.
In the park, in this light, with both
her arms around you, none of that is
true. You don't know you're saying
goodbye to the park. She doesn't know it
either.
That is the one mercy in any of this.
Her eyes are closed. Your tail is going.
The last morning is a Tuesday in
January. Your back legs stopped being
reliable 2 weeks ago. She carries you to
the car. You know these arms, the
specific grip, the warmth through her
coat. She has carried you before, when
you were small, when you got hurt that
summer. You know them. The vet's room
smells the same as it always has.
She sits on the floor before they have
finished checking you in. She has done
this since your first appointment, when
you were 12 weeks old and the table was
cold and too high.
She sat on the floor then, and you
climbed into her lap, and she has sat on
the floor at every single appointment
since.
Her hand is on your ear before you have
finished settling. You put your head on
her leg. 10,000 times. In the kitchen,
after a long day. On the couch, she told
you twice you weren't allowed on.
In the park, with the leaves coming down
and both her arms around you.
Every time you needed to say the only
thing you have ever known how to say,
"I'm here. I'm staying.
This is where I am." You put it there
one more time. You don't know this is
the last time. The design doesn't
include last times.
You only know the leg is there and the
hand is on your ear, and both of those
things are correct, and so everything is
correct. Your tail is going. It is
always going. There are 470 million pet
dogs on Earth. Right now, somewhere a
dog is lying in front of a door that
just closed with a sock. Somewhere a dog
is pressing its nose to a gate at 4:00
in the morning.
Somewhere a dog is on a park lawn in
October with both arms around it. Tail
going, not knowing. None of them know.
That might be the only thing in this
that doesn't completely suck. Life as a
dog is rough, but there's another animal
out there that has it way worse. Trust
me, it's wild. Check out the video and
see for yourself.

Why It Sucks To Be Born As a Fire Ant

When the flood comes, the colony doesn't drown.
It turns itself into a raft.
Hundreds of thousands of ants lock bodies together
and float for weeks.
The ones on the outside drown.
They are replaced by the ones rotating in from inside.
You are one of those ants on the outside.

This is the full life of a fire ant —
from the moment you hatch to the moment the flood takes you.

subtitles.plaintext:
A worker is licking you before you
finish hatching. You're not even fully
out of the egg and she's already
cleaning you head to abdomen, fast and
methodical, not gentle, not slow.
She has 900 other larva to get to before
the hour is out. You have 30 seconds to
smell right. If the chemical coating on
your body matches the colony, you live.
If it doesn't, if something is slightly
off, if the humidity in this chamber
shifted your egg chemistry just wrong
enough, the same workers who cleaned you
will carry you to the refuse pile. No
second check, no warning, just the pile.
You smell correct. The worker moves on
before you've taken your first step. A
few weeks from now, this colony is going
to need a life raft. It will build one
out of its own workers linking bodies
together, stacking them across open
floodwater, keeping the queen dry in the
center while the outer edge holds the
waterline. The colony will survive. The
workers on the outer edge mostly won't.
You're going to be on the outer edge.
You're a larva. You can't walk. You
can't see. You open your mouth and
workers feed you and that's the entirety
of your existence for the next 2 weeks.
While you sit there eating, a decision
is being made. The workers controlling
your food supply are deciding what
you'll become, not the queen. The queen
lays the eggs. That's her whole job.
What comes out of those eggs, soldier,
worker, reproductive, that's up to
whoever is rationing the food. More food
means a soldier. Soldiers have jaws that
can shear through beetle shell. Their
heads are wide enough to plug a tunnel
entrance. When enemies break through,
they lock themselves in place and hold
the gap with their own skull while
workers pack mud around them from
behind. They live to fight. They're
genuinely terrifying. Less food means a
worker, small, fast, the kind the colony
needs in the hundreds of thousands. You
get less food. Nobody chose this for you
specifically.
The colony needed more workers and
soldiers this week and you were next in
line. That's the whole decision. You
pupate. Two weeks pass.
You bite through your casing. You're
soft and pale and still hardening when
the first larva lands in your legs. You
have a job. You tend larva. You lick
them clean, feed them from your own
stomach, rotate them toward heat or away
from moisture depending on what the
chamber needs.
You make the same trips through the same
tunnels in the same direction for 14
hours at a stretch. Skip forward. When a
larva dies, and some die every day, you
carry it to the refuse chambers.
Same motion you used to carry food. The
dead ones are lighter. One morning, a
worker in the tunnel ahead of you stops.
She doesn't fall.
She just stops walking mid-step in the
middle of the trail. The larva she was
carrying rolls gently off her. Another
worker picks it up without slowing down.
She's 5 weeks old. Workers live about 5
weeks. That's it. No injury, no attack,
no particular reason.
The fuel just runs out and the legs stop
and that's the end. You step around her.
Someone will carry her to the refuse
chambers in an hour or two, whenever the
trail signal routes a worker close
enough.
She won't wait long. You have the same 5
weeks. You're 3 weeks in. The trail
keeps moving.
You keep moving. Then one day the trail
splits. A section of tunnel has
partially collapsed. Soil shifted
overnight. The passage narrowed to
almost nothing.
The workers ahead of you are routing
around it, taking a detour that adds 4
minutes to the trip. You watch them go.
Then you push into the gap anyway. Your
body fits, barely.
You drag the larva through sideways, one
leg at a time, and come out the other
side in the main passage with the trail
running straight ahead. You beat the
detour by 4 minutes. Nobody noticed.
The trail doesn't reward you. No signal
says well done. You just arrive at the
nursery first and set the larva down and
turn around and go back through the gap
again. But, you found it. And now you
know it's there. Your assignment
changes. You're a forager now. You come
out of the tunnel and the world is
enormous. You've spent 3 weeks in the
dark in tunnels you could measure in
centimeters.
Out here, a blade of grass is taller
than a building. The heat is immediate
and total. The sky is just open in every
direction and running through all of it,
clear as a road, the trail. Pheromone
path laid by the workers before you,
thick with information. Where to go, how
far, what's at the end. Your antennae
read it and your legs follow. You don't
decide to forage, foraging just happens
to you. The trail leads to a dead
cricket a hundred body lengths out. You
bite in.
Your stinger drives venom into the
tissue, a chemical your species makes
that almost nothing else on Earth
produces, that burns on contact with
skin,
that makes every animal in this
ecosystem take a wide path around any
mound they recognize. You weigh less
than a grain of rice. But, the colony
you belong to has made armadillos run,
driven deer away from water sources, and
killed animals the size of newborn
calves when they stepped on a mound. The
fear is real. It's just not yours.
It's the colony's. You personally
contributed one sting to a dead cricket.
You tear off your piece and carry it
back down the trail. You'll make this
trip 60 or 70 times before your legs
give out. You feel it before you hear
it, a vibration in the tunnel floor,
rhythmic and heavy and getting closer.
Then, the ceiling cracks. Light floods
in. The alarm pheromone hits the air and
your body is already running toward the
gap before you've processed anything.
Fire ants don't flee. Every other insect
runs from a threat. Fire ants run at it.
You reach the breach with hundreds of
others and pour out onto the anteater's
snout. You bite. You sting, the venom
hits skin and burns and the anteater
flinches.
400 workers stinging simultaneously is
enough. The anteater swings its head,
drags itself backward through the grass,
retreats. You're back in the tunnel
before the gap is sealed. Workers are
already packing soil into the breach
relay lines, moving dirt from the inside
out, mandible load by mandible load. The
mound has been attacked and repaired in
8 minutes. 8 minutes.
That's the colony's entire response to a
predator the size of a building. Not a
retreat, not a regrouping. 8 minutes and
the trail is running again like nothing
happened. You were on that snout. The
colony's takeaway is 8 minutes. The
trail is still running, you get back on
it. The next few days are quiet, no
vibrations, no alarm pheromone.
The trail runs, the food comes in, the
mound keeps growing. You take your gap
in the collapsed tunnel every time,
saving 4 minutes off the trip. Arriving
at the nursery a little ahead of the
workers who don't know about it yet.
This is as close to good as it gets down
here. The trail runs, you run it,
the colony hums. You don't know it yet,
but this is the last quiet stretch. It's
been raining for 6 hours when the water
comes in through the entrance tunnels.
You feel the cold before you see it.
Pressure moving up through the soil,
reaching the lower passages, then the
nursery.
Larvae start to float off the chamber
floor.
Workers grab them immediately and the
signal fires colony wide and 50,000
workers are running before you finish
your thought. You grab a larva and run.
The lower chambers fill behind you as
you climb. You don't look back, you
reach the surface. Skip forward. At the
surface, workers are already linking.
Mandibles grip legs, bodies lock onto
bodies.
No signal for this or maybe the signal
is just the flood itself. The shared
pressure of 10,000 workers arriving at
once, all doing the same thing they've
done for a hundred million years.
The raft builds from the outside edge
inward. You set down your larva, a
worker takes it and pulls it toward the
center. You feel a grip on your foreleg,
a worker behind you locking in. You grip
the worker in front of you. You are
placed on the outer edge. The water
rises.
The raft lifts. You are below the
waterline. The cold hits your body all
at once, not gradually, just suddenly
wrong, but you hold. The workers around
you hold.
Air is trapped in the spaces between
your bodies and you breathe from those
pockets, slow and still. The raft is
alive.
It holds itself together by the grip of
every worker in it. The queen is
somewhere near the center. Eight workers
around her at all times, none of them
letting her feet touch the water.
She doesn't know you're here. She
doesn't need to know. You are the wall
between her and the flood. A fish rises
beneath you and presses its mouth
against the edge of the raft. Workers
sting it. It leaves. Even here, half
submerged, mid flood, moving on open
water, the colony is not something that
gets eaten. The fear is still real.
Hours pass. The cold works deeper into
your body. Workers rotate on the
surface, but the cycle is slow and the
flood is long and not everyone rotates
back up before the raft catches on a
root. Workers at the front start
climbing. The signal moves back through
the mass. You feel the bodies ahead of
you begin to release and you release too
and pull yourself up onto the root, then
the bark, then dry ground. You climb,
waterlogged.
Slower than you should be, your legs
working, but not right, something in the
cold that doesn't fully reverse.
The colony is on dry ground.
The queen is already surrounded by
workers scouting for a new mound site.
The trail is re-establishing before
you've stopped dripping. The colony
doesn't stop. The moment workers find
solid ground, they start digging nursery
chambers first, then the queen's room,
then food storage. The trail
reestablishes in hours.
By morning, larva are being fed and
foragers are running routes and the
mound is rising from soil that didn't
exist as a mound yesterday. You carry a
larva to the nursery and set it down. A
few weeks ago,
before you knew what a flood was, before
you knew what a raft was, you were told
the colony is going to save itself by
using your body as a life raft. The
workers on the outer edge mostly won't
make it. The colony survived. You get
back on the trail. There are 300 fire
ant colonies in a single acre of
infested ground.
Each one holds up to half a million
workers.
The queen lays 1,500 eggs a day without
pause. The colony doesn't track
individuals.
It tracks density, the number of workers
in each tunnel, the chemical pressure of
the trails, the volume of the food
supply. When density drops, the queen
produces more. The number stays
constant.
What's inside the number changes
constantly. Three days after the flood,
your legs stop cooperating. The cold
held too long and something in your body
doesn't come back from it. Your front
legs work, your middle legs are slow.
Your back legs drag. You carry one more
larva from the nursery to the food
chambers slower than the workers behind
you.
One of them steps around you, then
another.
The larva is heavier than it should be.
You set it down. You stop. A worker
steps over you.
She has somewhere to be. 15 minutes
later, another worker picks you up and
carries you to the refuse chamber.
You go in the same pile as the larva who
didn't make it and the workers who ran
out of weeks before the flood and the
ones who held the outer edge until they
couldn't. The trail doesn't pause. In
the nursery,
an egg cracked open while you were being
carried to the pile. A worker is licking
it clean right now, head to abdomen,
fast and methodical. It smells correct.
Life as a fire ant might be rough, but
there's another animal out there that
has it way worse. Trust me, it's wild.
Check out the video and see for
yourself.

subtitles.plaintext:
You crack out of your egg and your heart
is already running at 1,200 beats a
minute. Not because something scared
you. Not because something is wrong.
Because that is simply the price of
being what you are. You are the size of
a bumblebee. You weigh less than a
paperclip. You are completely blind. And
the egg beside you in this nest, the one
that was there when you started cracking
through your shell,
isn't going to hatch. It was never going
to hatch. You don't know that. You don't
know anything yet. You open your mouth.
Your mother built this nest from spider
silk because it is the only material on
Earth that stretches as you grow. Right
now, you are warm and fed and you have
no idea what you are. Skip forward. You
are a few weeks old and you have
discovered the only thing that matters.
You are always hungry. Not sometimes.
Not when food is scarce. Always. Every
15 minutes of every hour you are awake,
your body needs fuel. Go long enough
without it and your body starts
consuming itself, burning muscle,
burning organ.
Go a little longer than that and the
whole thing stops. You do not understand
any of this. You only know the feeling
and the feeling never goes away. Skip
forward. Your mother teaches you by
doing. She hovers at a flower, pulls
back, hovers again.
She is not explaining. She does not have
time and neither do you. You try. Your
bill misses completely and you smack
face first into the side of the flower.
You try again. Again. On the fourth
attempt, you get it. The nectar hits
your tongue and for a fraction of a
second, the feeling goes away. Then it
comes back. Go find another flower. When
you finally fly, really fly, it is
astonishing. Not flapping, rotating.
Your shoulders move in a way no other
birds can. You hover.
You reverse.
You hold perfectly still in open air and
the world does not move underneath you.
You are the smallest thing in this
canopy and for one moment it feels like
the canopy was built for something
exactly your size. Then the sun moves
behind a cloud. The temperature drops
2°. The feeling comes back. Go find a
flower. The light goes and your body
does something that if someone found you
doing it, they would think you were
dead. Your temperature drops 50°. Your
heart goes from 1,200 beats a minute to
fewer than 50. You stop reacting to
sound. You stop reacting to touch. You
are not asleep. You are something closer
to off. This is the only way you make it
through the night. Your body burns
almost nothing in this state, just
enough to keep the cells from dying. Not
because you chose this.
Not because you learned it. Because
anything that couldn't do this is
already gone. You are descended from
every hummingbird that made it through
the night before you. That is the only
reason you exist. You cannot wake up.
You cannot run. You cannot do anything
except hold the branch with locked toes
while the night passes over you. The owl
doesn't find you tonight. Tomorrow night
you'll do this again. Every night for
the rest of your life. Waking takes
almost an hour. You shiver through all
of it, muscles firing and releasing,
heating you from the inside because the
sun is not fast enough. Your stomach is
completely empty. The shivering is
burning what little you have left. The
second your wings are warm enough, you
go. You don't stretch. You don't look
around. You go straight to the nearest
flower because there is nothing else.
This is the first thing you do every
morning. Every morning for your entire
life. You've survived the nights. You've
survived the hunger. And now you find
out something nobody tells you about
hummingbirds. You are furious. Not
defensive. Not cautious.
Furious. In a way that makes no sense
for something your size. Last week you
spent 40 minutes chasing a red-tailed
hawk out of your airspace. It weighed
400 times more than you. It left. You
claim three flowers. Just three. That is
your whole world right now. Three
flowers, a line of nectar, and the
absolute conviction that nothing else is
allowed near them. The fight that gets
you there leaves your opponent with a
bill tip broken, clean off against
something hard. That detail tells you
how many times he has fought before.
Something is on the branch beside your
largest flower. You have flown past it
14 times today. It has not moved once.
You've worked these flowers for 3 days.
You know this spot. You trust this spot.
You come in from the left the way you
always do, bill extended, already
thinking about the next flower. You
don't see it. You don't have time to see
it. One moment you are flying toward the
flower. The next moment something has
you. You beat your wings hard. Harder.
The wings that can fly backwards,
that moved fast enough to leave a hawk
standing still in the air. They beat and
beat and nothing changes. The mantis
weighs almost exactly what you do. It
has been here since before you started
this morning. It has been doing nothing
for 4 hours and it is better at waiting
than you are at anything. Some
hummingbirds escape this. The ones that
don't are simply gone. Nobody finds
them.
Nobody notices. The colony keeps working
the flowers. You have to be one of the
ones that escapes. You sit on a branch
across the garden. Still, your chest is
moving faster than it should be. The
mantis is still on the stem. It has
already reset. It is going to be there
tomorrow. Your flowers are on the other
side of it. Here is what you are when
everything is working. You have
memorized every flower in your
territory, their locations, and the
exact time each one refills after the
last visit. You run a feeding schedule
more precise than most things with a
brain 10 times the size of yours. You
hold a fixed position in open air with
sub-centimeter drift. Researchers who've
measured this cannot fully explain how.
When something comes for you, you are
somewhere else before it decides to
move. You are the most precisely
engineered living thing at this scale.
Everything about you works and none of
it is enough to change what is coming
because you were built to do this for 3
years. Maybe five if nothing goes wrong.
And the thing that is going to end you
isn't a predator. Isn't the cold. Isn't
the hunger. It's August. Skip forward.
Something changes in August. You start
eating like something that knows it has
to. Every flower. Every insect. All day
past the point where it makes sense. Fat
builds along your back and belly and
throat until you have nearly doubled in
weight. Your body is storing everything
it can find. You don't know why. You
just can't stop. You reach the coast and
there is nothing ahead of you but ocean.
You have never seen the ocean before.
You don't know what it is. You don't
know what 500 miles means.
Something in you simply lifts off. 500
miles. No flowers. No insects. No land.
If you go down, you drown.
There is nothing between you and the
water and the water cannot hold you. You
fly through the night burning through
everything your body built over the last
2 weeks. You are dropping weight with
every wingbeat. If the wind turns, you
won't make it. If a storm builds behind
you,
you won't make it. You don't know any of
this. You are just flying because
something in you says to fly. Every year
some don't make it. They are not weaker.
They are not worse. The wind just went
the wrong way. Rig workers find them
every year. Tiny birds on the railings,
hundreds of miles from land, completely
spent, unable to lift off. The workers
leave sugar water and step back.
Sometimes the bird drinks. Sometimes it
lifts off again and continues. Sometimes
it doesn't. The workers who've seen this
say they remember every one. You make it
across. You find land. And before you do
anything else, before you rest, before
you look around, you find a flower. You
are one of 340.
Every single species of hummingbird
lives only in the Americas. None
anywhere else.
As if this one corner of the planet
decided to run this particular
experiment and kept going. The smallest
is the bee hummingbird, 2 and 1/4 inches
long, weighs less than a dime. Its heart
runs at the same rate as yours. It goes
through the same nights. The same
hunger.
The same crossing. Just smaller. The
rufous hummingbird travels 3,000 miles
each year. The longest migration
relative to body size of any bird on
Earth. It does this alone. It has no one
to follow. It just goes. You run this
for 3 years. Maybe five.
Some make it to nine. The oldest
ruby-throated hummingbird ever found was
9 years and 2 months old. She was
recaptured by researchers in West
Virginia banded years earlier. Still
going. She crossed the Gulf 18 times. 18
times she stood at the edge of that
coast and felt something in her body say
go. 18 times she went. 18 nights of open
water with nothing below.
18 mornings waking up shivering and
going straight to the nearest flower.
She didn't know she was extraordinary.
She didn't know she'd made it 18 times.
She just knew it was August and
something in her said go. So she went.
There is one more animal that makes a
crossing like this. It has no wings. It
has no way back. And it doesn't get to
do it 18 times.
Next video.

subtitles.plaintext:
You're in the dark. Something is wrong
with your body. Your legs don't feel
like legs anymore. Your head is soft
where it shouldn't be. There's a warmth
spreading through you that isn't
temperature. It's your own tissue
breaking down, muscle dissolving into
liquid, organs coming apart at the
cellular level.
You are right now approximately 70%
soup. This is not a nightmare. This is
Tuesday. This is the thing that happens
to every butterfly in the middle of
their one and only life, whether they're
ready for it or not. You are inside a
chrysalis and you are being taken apart
so that something new can be built from
the pieces. And here's the thing about
butterflies that nobody who's ever
stopped to watch one floating through a
garden actually knows the Dissolving is
not the worst part of the story, not
even close. The worst part happens near
the end, on the last good day. After you
survived everything, the wasps that
tried to lay eggs inside you, the birds,
the spiders, the storms, after you've
done the one thing you were built to do.
What finally gets you is something
that's been quietly breaking since the
day you were born and you won't even
notice it happening until it's too late
to matter. Keep watching. Back up a few
weeks to where this started. You're on a
leaf the size of a football field.
At least that's what it feels like when
you're a caterpillar a few millimeters
long, soft-bodied, newly hatched,
gripping the surface with six stubby
legs while the world around you moves in
ways you don't understand yet. Wind,
shadows, the vibration of something
landing nearby. Your mother chose this
leaf.
She tasted dozens before she landed on
this one. She has sensors on her feet
that read plant chemistry and she was
looking for a specific toxin. She found
it here. Now you eat it. You eat almost
constantly. You need to increase your
body weight by a thousand times before
you can pupate, which means every waking
hour is feeding. Leaf after leaf,
methodical, moving along the surface,
chewing through everything in reach. And
as you eat the plant's toxins, they
don't digest. They collect. They build
up in your tissue, in your skin, in the
fat you're storing.
The brighter your colors get, the yellow
rings darkening, the pattern sharpening,
the more poisonous you become and the
more clearly you advertise it. A bird
lands on the branch above you. It
watches you for a moment, tilts its
head, and pecks. One bite. Then it spits
you out and shakes its beak against the
bark trying to get rid of the taste. It
doesn't come back. You've been alive for
two weeks and you've already turned
yourself into something too dangerous to
eat. Nobody taught you that. Your
mother's choice of leaf did it before
you were born. First win. You're three
weeks old, halfway through a leaf, when
something lands on your back. You feel
the weight, something small, barely
there. Your body registers it and does
nothing.
You keep chewing, the weight lifts,
gone in four seconds. What just
happened? A parasitic wasp, smaller than
your thumbnail, walked along your back
with its antennae down reading your body
chemistry. When it found the right spot,
the soft tissue between two segments, it
drove its ovipositor through your skin
and injected a cluster of eggs directly
into your body. Then it flew away. You
didn't fight. You couldn't. By the time
your nervous system registered the
landing, the wasp was already gone. The
eggs hatch inside you over the next few
days.
The larva that emerge are careful. They
navigate around your vital organs
feeding only on your fat reserves,
keeping you alive because a dead host is
no use to them. You keep eating. You
keep growing. From the outside, you look
completely healthy, plump, well-fed. On
the inside, you are a nursery for
something that will eventually need to
get out. Some caterpillars that reach
the chrysalis stage never produce a
butterfly.
The chrysalis splits open and wasps pour
out dozens of them and whatever was
growing inside is gone. The butterfly
that should have been there simply never
exists. You keep eating. You won't know
which kind of story you're in until the
very end. The urge comes without
warning. One morning, you stop eating
mid-leaf. Something in your body has
shifted a chemical signal that overrides
everything else.
You climb down from the plant, find a
bare stem, and begin to spin.
Silk from a gland near your mouth looped
around yourself in slow rotations, layer
after layer, until you're encased in a
hard shell the color of old jade. Then
darkness.
Stillness. And then you start to feel
it, not pain exactly, but a wrongness,
like your body is not where it was.
Like the boundaries of your own shape
have become uncertain. What's happening?
Your own cells are releasing enzymes
that break down muscle, organ, and
connective tissue. Not remodeling,
dissolving. Within hours, almost
everything you were made of is fluid. If
someone cut the chrysalis open right
now, there would be no caterpillar
inside, no half-formed butterfly, just a
warm brownish liquid and a few clusters
of cells floating in it. Those clusters
are called imaginal discs.
They've been inside you your entire life
as a caterpillar, dormant, waiting,
carrying instructions for something you
had no idea you were going to become.
A wing compressed into a handful of
cells waiting for the right chemical
signal to start building. An eye, a new
nervous system, clean, carrying almost
nothing from before.
In the liquid of what used to be your
body, they begin to assemble. A wing
forms from material that was recently
your third leg. An eye builds itself
from tissue that was part of your gut.
Two weeks pass in complete darkness and
then a crack of light splits the shell.
You push out wet, crumpled wings folded
flat against your back like wet paper.
You grip the empty casing and hang
upside down.
Your wings need to expand before they
harden and the only way that happens is
fluid pumped through the veins by your
own muscles. Over the next hour, you
cannot be helped. If something, anything
assists you out of the chrysalis before
this process completes, your wings will
harden in the wrong shape. You'll never
fly.
You'll drag yourself across the ground
until something finds you. You hang, you
pump, you wait. The wings dry and
stiffen. You open them for the first
time.
They catch the light like stained glass.
You launch from the stem and the air
takes you. You have two weeks. The first
thing you find is a clearing, a patch of
sunlight in the forest canopy, maybe 4 m
across, the kind of warm, open space
that females pass through when looking
for mates. You land on a twig at the
edge, open your wings to the sun, and
wait. Within 10 minutes, another male
appears from the far side. You spiral
upward together. It looks effortless
from below, two bright shapes turning in
the light. What it actually is, two
animals burning through reserves they
can't replace, fighting for a patch of
warm air. No teeth, no claws, just speed
and endurance. You outlast him. He peels
off and finds another clearing somewhere
else. You drink from a flower proboscis
uncoiling into the base of the petals,
pulling up nectar. This is the only way
you can feed now. Your caterpillar mouth
is gone. You have no way to eat solid
food, no way to consume protein.
Everything you have left is what you
built before you dissolved and you are
spending it down hour by hour. You learn
the clearing's dangers fast. A praying
mantis on the third flower from the
left, arms folded, perfectly still, the
color of the petals. You read it from 2
m away.
You find a different flower. A spider
web catches the light at the wrong angle
near the east side of the clearing, a
fractional shimmer in your peripheral
vision. You adjust course without
thinking. A bird dives from above on day
four and you drop 3 m in less than a
second, change direction mid-fall, and
land in the undergrowth before it can
follow. Your wings chip at the edges.
A small piece of the left lower wing
disappears after a close pass on day
six. You fly exactly as well as before.
More chips. Still fine.
Still fast. On the 10th day, a female
crosses the clearing. You rise, she
rises. The spiral this time is
different, slower, closer. A mutual
reading of chemistry at near range. You
descend together onto a broad leaf in
the shade at the clearing's edge. You
mate. It takes the rest of the
afternoon. She's still uncertain and so
are you.
When it's done, she flies. She has her
own work now, finding the right leaf,
tasting dozens until she finds the one
with the right toxins, laying your eggs
one by one on the underside. You stay on
the leaf for a while. The sun is low.
The clearing is warm. Your wings rest
open catching the last of the light.
Everything you were built for is
complete. This is the peak, the exact
top of the arc. Hold on to it. Your left
wing has been tearing along a vein since
day eight. You didn't notice because the
tear was small enough that your body
compensated without telling you a
fractional adjustment to your flight
angle, a tiny extra load on the right
side to keep you level. It felt like
nothing. It was nothing until it wasn't.
You lift off from the leaf, three
wingbeats in, the vein finishes tearing.
The left wing folds wrong, just
slightly, just enough. You list, you
correct, you overcorrect.
Each correction costs energy you don't
have, burning harder on the right side,
fighting your own wing just to stay
level. You find a branch and grip it.
This is what the promise was about. Not
the wasp, you survived that. Not the
birds, you read every one. Not
starvation.
The thing that got you was a structural
crack that started forming on the day
you emerged and widened with every
single flight since then. By the time it
finished, you had done everything.
Everything worked.
Your eggs are on the right leaf with the
right toxins glued to the underside by a
mother who tasted dozens before she
chose. The story continues without you.
You don't take off again. There are
19,000 species of butterfly on this
planet. Most adults live between 1 and 4
weeks.
Some live days. The painted lady
migrates 10,000 km, the longest
butterfly migration ever recorded. The
generation that flies out doesn't
survive the return trip. Their
descendants make the journey back with
no map, no memory, no one to follow.
Just chemistry in the cells pointing
roughly the right direction, assembled
from soup, carrying instructions from
something that dissolved months before
they existed. Every butterfly you've
ever watched drifting through a garden
was doing this, burning down the last of
what a caterpillar built on a clock they
didn't choose with wings that were
already slowly chipping, looking for a
clearing in the right light, trying to
get the timing right. Life as a
butterfly might be rough, but there's
another animal out there that has it way
worse. Trust me, it's wild. Check out
the video and see for yourself.
